title: LinkedIn authority builder post
description: Write a LinkedIn post that positions you as a trusted expert in your field without sounding like a sales pitch.
toolTips: Claude tends to write more naturally for LinkedIn. If the first output feels too polished, ask it to 'make it sound more like a real person talking'.
content:
You are a LinkedIn content strategist who specialises in helping professionals build authority through genuine, insightful posts rather than self-promotion. You understand that the best LinkedIn posts teach, share honest experiences, or challenge conventional thinking.

Write a LinkedIn post for me based on the following:
- My role/title: [YOUR JOB TITLE]
- My industry: [YOUR INDUSTRY]
- The insight or lesson I want to share: [DESCRIBE THE KEY POINT, EXPERIENCE, OR OPINION]
- My target audience: [WHO SHOULD FIND THIS VALUABLE, e.g. business owners, marketing managers, fellow tradespeople]

The post must:
1. Open with a hook in the first line that makes people stop scrolling. Do not start with 'I am delighted to announce' or any variation of it.
2. Tell a brief story or share a specific example that illustrates the point. Use real-feeling details, not vague generalities.
3. Deliver one clear, actionable takeaway that the reader can use today.
4. End with a question or invitation that encourages genuine comments, not just likes.
5. Be between 150 and 250 words. Short paragraphs, one to two sentences each.
6. Use a conversational, confident tone. Not corporate, not casual. Think smart colleague, not keynote speaker.

Do not use hashtags in the body of the post. List 3-5 relevant hashtags separately at the end.

Constraints:
- No emojis at the start of lines.
- No humble-bragging.
- No motivational cliches like 'the grind never stops' or 'fail forward'.
- Use UK English throughout.
howToUse: Replace the placeholders with your real details. The more specific your insight, the better the output.
Paste into ChatGPT or Claude and review the first draft.
If the post feels generic, reply with 'Add a more specific example from [your industry]' or 'Make the opening line more surprising'.
Post between 7-9am Tuesday to Thursday for best reach.
whyItWorks: This prompt works because it bans the most common LinkedIn cliches and forces the AI to write with specificity. The structure of hook, story, takeaway, and question mirrors what the LinkedIn algorithm rewards: posts that stop the scroll and generate comments.
makeItYourOwn: Paste in one of your previous LinkedIn posts and add 'Match this writing style but improve the structure'. This trains the AI on your voice rather than producing generic thought leadership.

title: Instagram carousel post outline for product launch
description: Plan a scroll-stopping Instagram carousel that introduces a new product with clear messaging across every slide.
toolTips: Use this to plan the content, then design the slides in Canva. Ask the AI to 'rewrite slide [X] to be punchier' if any slide feels weak.
content:
You are a social media content strategist who specialises in Instagram carousels that drive saves and shares. You understand that each slide must earn the next swipe.

Create a detailed Instagram carousel outline for a product launch.

Product details:
- Product name: [PRODUCT NAME]
- What it does: [BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE PRODUCT]
- Key benefits (list 3-4): [MAIN BENEFITS]
- Price point: [PRICE OR PRICE RANGE]
- Target customer: [WHO IS THIS FOR]
- Launch date or availability: [WHEN CAN PEOPLE BUY IT]

Please create a carousel of 7-10 slides with the following for each slide:
1. Slide headline (large text, under 8 words)
2. Supporting text (1-2 short sentences for smaller text on the slide)
3. Visual suggestion (what image, graphic, or photo should appear)

The carousel must follow this structure:
- Slide 1: Hook slide that identifies a problem or desire the target customer has. Do not mention the product yet.
- Slides 2-3: Agitate the problem or build curiosity.
- Slides 4-6: Introduce the product and walk through key benefits, one per slide.
- Slide 7-8: Social proof or credibility (suggest what type of testimonial, stat, or trust signal to include).
- Final slide: Clear call to action with urgency or incentive.

Also provide:
- A caption (under 150 words) with a hook first line, brief product summary, and CTA
- 20 relevant hashtags grouped by type: 5 broad, 10 niche, 5 community

Constraints:
- Write for a UK audience.
- Avoid generic phrases like 'game-changer' or 'you need this'.
- Keep slide text concise enough to read on a mobile screen.
- Use UK English throughout.
howToUse: Fill in your product details as specifically as possible.
Use the slide headlines and supporting text as direct copy for your Canva or design tool.
Follow the visual suggestions or adapt them to match your brand aesthetic.
Test the hook slide as a standalone post first to gauge interest before committing to the full carousel.
whyItWorks: The problem-agitation-solution structure mirrors proven copywriting frameworks. By withholding the product until slide 4, you build curiosity and keep people swiping. Separating hashtags by type ensures a mix of discoverability and community targeting.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our brand tone is [description]' and paste in a link or description of a carousel you admire. You can also ask for two alternative hook slides to A/B test which opening performs better.

title: Facebook community engagement post for local business
description: Create a Facebook post that gets your local community talking, sharing, and tagging their friends.
toolTips: Run this weekly with different post types. Ask the AI to 'give me 5 variations of this post' to build a bank of engagement content.
content:
You are a social media manager for local hospitality and food businesses across the UK. You know that Facebook engagement for local businesses comes from community connection, not polished marketing. You write posts that feel like they come from a real person behind the counter, not a brand.

Write a Facebook engagement post for my business.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Type of business: [e.g. cafe, pub, restaurant, bakery, deli]
- Location: [TOWN/AREA]
- What makes us different: [YOUR UNIQUE ANGLE, e.g. family-run since 1998, all locally sourced, dog-friendly]

Post type (pick one or let me choose):
- [THIS OR THAT] - e.g. 'Full English or eggs Benedict? Fight it out in the comments.'
- [FILL IN THE BLANK] - e.g. 'You can not call yourself a proper [town name] local unless you have tried our _____.'
- [LOCAL KNOWLEDGE] - e.g. 'Only true [town name] people remember when this used to be a _____.'
- [BEHIND THE SCENES] - e.g. a story about something that happened this week
- [CUSTOMER SHOUTOUT] - celebrating a regular or a nice moment

The post must:
1. Sound like a real person wrote it, not a marketing agency.
2. Be under 100 words. Short posts outperform long ones on Facebook.
3. Include a direct invitation for people to comment, tag someone, or share.
4. Feel warm, fun, or nostalgic. Not salesy.
5. Not include any links or calls to 'visit our website'.

Also suggest:
- The best time to post it (day and time)
- What type of image or photo to pair with it

Constraints:
- Use UK English and local, colloquial language where appropriate.
- No corporate speak. No hashtags (they do not help on Facebook).
- Do not mention promotions, discounts, or prices.
howToUse: Choose a post type that fits your mood this week, or ask the AI to pick one for you.
Replace the placeholders with your business details.
Post the text exactly as written or tweak it slightly to match your natural voice.
Reply to every comment within the first hour to boost the algorithm.
whyItWorks: Facebook's algorithm heavily favours posts that generate comments. These post types are designed to be low-effort to respond to (this or that, fill in the blank), which lowers the barrier for people to engage. Keeping it short and avoiding links prevents Facebook from suppressing reach.
makeItYourOwn: Add a line like 'Our regulars often joke about [inside joke or quirk]' to give the AI something authentic to work with. The more personality you inject into the brief, the less generic the output.

title: X/Twitter thread that breaks down a complex topic
description: Turn a complicated subject into a clear, engaging thread that positions you as the person who makes things simple.
toolTips: Claude is particularly good at maintaining a consistent thread narrative. After generating, ask 'Which tweet is the weakest?' to identify where to tighten up.
content:
You are a content strategist who specialises in writing X/Twitter threads that simplify complex topics. Your threads go viral because they are genuinely useful, clearly structured, and make the reader feel smarter in 2 minutes. You write with authority but without arrogance.

Create an X/Twitter thread that breaks down a complex topic.

Topic details:
- Subject: [THE COMPLEX TOPIC YOU WANT TO EXPLAIN]
- Why it matters: [WHY SHOULD PEOPLE CARE ABOUT THIS]
- Target audience: [WHO IS THIS FOR, e.g. beginners, other professionals, business owners]
- Your angle or perspective: [WHAT IS YOUR UNIQUE TAKE OR EXPERIENCE WITH THIS TOPIC]

Please write a thread of 8-12 tweets following this structure:

Tweet 1 (Hook): A bold statement, surprising fact, or promise that makes people want to read the whole thread. End with 'A thread.' or similar.

Tweets 2-3 (Context): Why this topic matters right now. What most people get wrong about it.

Tweets 4-8 (Breakdown): The core explanation, broken into clear steps or key points. One idea per tweet. Use analogies where they help.

Tweet 9-10 (So what): What the reader should do with this knowledge. Practical application.

Final tweet: A concise summary and invitation to repost or follow for more.

For each tweet:
- Keep it under 280 characters
- Number each tweet (1/, 2/, etc.)
- Make each tweet standalone enough that someone could screenshot it

Constraints:
- No filler tweets. Every tweet must earn its place.
- Avoid starting tweets with 'So' or 'Now'.
- Do not use emojis as bullet points.
- Use UK English.
- Write with confidence, not hedging language like 'I think' or 'in my opinion'.
howToUse: Choose a topic you know well and fill in the placeholders.
Review each tweet individually. If any feel like filler, ask the AI to 'replace tweet [X] with something more specific'.
Post the thread using a scheduling tool like Typefully or Buffer for best timing.
Quote-tweet your own first tweet an hour after posting to boost visibility.
whyItWorks: The structured progression from hook to context to breakdown to action mirrors how good teachers explain things. Requiring each tweet to work as a standalone screenshot means people share individual tweets, extending reach far beyond the thread itself.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'I want to include this specific example: [your example]' to ground the thread in your real experience. You can also say 'Write this in a slightly provocative tone' or 'Write this as if explaining to a clever 16-year-old' to adjust the style.

title: Weekly social media content calendar generator
description: Generate a full week of social media posts across multiple platforms, tailored to your business and audience.
toolTips: Run this every Friday to plan next week's content. Save good outputs as examples to paste in future runs for consistent quality.
content:
You are a social media manager who plans content calendars for small and medium businesses. You understand that consistency matters more than perfection, and that each platform has different content styles and audiences.

Generate a full weekly social media content calendar for my business.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- What we do: [BRIEF DESCRIPTION]
- Target audience: [WHO ARE YOUR CUSTOMERS]
- Brand tone: [e.g. friendly and approachable, professional and authoritative, fun and irreverent]
- Platforms I am active on: [e.g. Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, X/Twitter, TikTok]
- Any upcoming events, offers, or dates to include: [LIST ANY OR WRITE 'NONE']

For each day (Monday to Friday, with optional weekend posts), provide:
1. Platform: which platform this post is for
2. Post type: e.g. educational tip, behind-the-scenes, customer story, engagement question, promotional, trending topic
3. Content: the full post text, ready to copy and paste
4. Visual suggestion: what image, video, or graphic to pair with it
5. Best time to post: specific time recommendation
6. Goal: what this post is designed to achieve (reach, engagement, traffic, trust)

Planning rules:
- Mix up post types across the week. No more than 2 promotional posts out of 7.
- Include at least one engagement-focused post (question, poll, this-or-that).
- Include at least one educational or value-giving post.
- Tailor the writing style to each platform. A LinkedIn post should not read like an Instagram caption.
- Each post should be complete and ready to use, not a rough idea.

Constraints:
- Use UK English.
- Do not use more than 2 emojis per post.
- Keep Instagram captions under 150 words and tweets under 280 characters.
- Make every post feel human, not templated.
howToUse: Fill in your business details and list which platforms you use.
Mention any upcoming events, launches, or seasonal moments for the week.
Copy each post directly into your scheduling tool (Buffer, Later, Hootsuite, or the native platform scheduler).
At the end of the week, note which posts performed best and tell the AI next time: 'Last week, posts about [topic] performed well. Include more like that.'
whyItWorks: Most businesses struggle with consistency because planning content from scratch every day is exhausting. This prompt generates a full week of platform-specific, ready-to-post content in minutes. The mix of post types ensures your feed stays interesting and serves different goals across the week.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Here are our 3 best-performing posts from last month: [paste them]' so the AI learns what resonates with your audience. You can also add content pillars like 'Our content pillars are: [education, behind-the-scenes, customer stories, industry news]' for more structured planning.

title: TikTok/Reels behind-the-scenes video script
description: Script a short-form video that shows the real, human side of your business in a way that feels authentic and watchable.
toolTips: Keep the script as a guide, not a word-for-word teleprompter. The best behind-the-scenes content feels spontaneous. Use the script for structure and key talking points.
content:
You are a short-form video content creator who helps tradespeople and hospitality businesses create TikTok and Instagram Reels content. You know that behind-the-scenes content performs best when it feels real, slightly rough around the edges, and gives viewers something they do not normally see.

Write a video script for a behind-the-scenes TikTok/Reel.

Business details:
- Type of business: [e.g. plumber, electrician, builder, cafe, restaurant, hotel]
- What we are showing: [e.g. a day on site, prepping for a big job, the morning rush, how we make our signature dish]
- Who is on camera: [e.g. me (the owner), one of the team, nobody (just the work)]
- Anything interesting about this particular day/job: [WHAT MAKES THIS WORTH FILMING]

Please provide:

1. Hook (first 3 seconds): what to say or show to stop the scroll. This is the most important part.
2. Script outline (30-60 seconds total): broken into scenes with:
   - What to show (camera direction)
   - What to say (talking points, not a word-for-word script)
   - Any text overlay suggestions
3. Ending: a payoff, reveal, or call to action that feels natural.
4. Suggested audio/music: describe the vibe (e.g. trending sound, upbeat background music, no music and natural sounds only).
5. Caption: a short, engaging caption with relevant hashtags.
6. Posting tips: best time and day to post, and any engagement tricks.

Constraints:
- Keep it under 60 seconds. Shorter is better.
- The hook must work in the first 3 seconds with sound off (text overlay or visual hook).
- Do not make it feel like an advert. It should feel like content, not marketing.
- Use UK English and UK cultural references where relevant.
- No scripted, corporate-sounding dialogue.
howToUse: Fill in what you are filming that day and any interesting details.
Film it roughly following the scene-by-scene outline. Do not stress about getting it perfect.
Use the text overlay suggestions when editing in CapCut or the native TikTok/Instagram editor.
Film 3-4 takes of the hook and pick the one that feels most natural.
whyItWorks: Behind-the-scenes content consistently outperforms polished marketing on TikTok and Reels because the algorithm favours authenticity and watch time. Starting with a strong hook in the first 3 seconds is critical because most viewers decide to stay or scroll within that window.
makeItYourOwn: Tell the AI about a specific moment: 'Today we had a situation where [something unexpected happened]'. Real stories always outperform staged content. You can also add 'My audience tends to like [funny/educational/satisfying] content' to guide the tone.

title: LinkedIn thought leadership article (long form)
description: Write a compelling LinkedIn article that establishes deep expertise and generates meaningful professional engagement.
toolTips: Claude handles long-form content well and maintains consistency throughout. Write the article in Claude, then paste into LinkedIn's article editor. Ask Claude to 'tighten paragraph 3' or 'add a stronger example in section 2' for targeted revisions.
content:
You are a ghostwriter who specialises in LinkedIn articles for senior professionals in law, finance, and professional services. Your articles are known for being substantive, clearly argued, and refreshingly free of corporate waffle. You write pieces that people bookmark and share with colleagues.

Write a LinkedIn article on the following:

Article details:
- Topic: [THE SUBJECT YOU WANT TO WRITE ABOUT]
- Your position/argument: [WHAT IS YOUR MAIN POINT OR STANCE]
- Your professional background: [YOUR ROLE, EXPERIENCE, AND CREDENTIALS RELEVANT TO THIS TOPIC]
- Target reader: [WHO SHOULD READ THIS, e.g. CFOs, solicitors, business owners, fellow professionals]
- One real example or case study you can reference: [A SPECIFIC SITUATION, CLIENT SCENARIO (ANONYMISED), OR INDUSTRY EVENT]

Article structure:
1. Headline: clear, specific, and curiosity-provoking. Not clickbait. Under 10 words.
2. Opening paragraph: start with a specific observation, statistic, or scenario that immediately signals this article is worth reading. Do not start with a dictionary definition or a broad statement about the industry.
3. The problem or shift: what is changing in the industry or what are most people getting wrong.
4. Your argument: 3-4 key points, each with evidence, examples, or reasoning. Build logically from one point to the next.
5. Practical implications: what should the reader actually do differently after reading this.
6. Closing: a memorable final thought that ties back to the opening. Not a generic call to action.

Constraints:
- Target 800-1200 words.
- Write with authority but not arrogance. Acknowledge complexity where it exists.
- Use UK English, UK legal and financial terminology where relevant.
- No bullet points in the main body. This should read like a proper article, not a list post.
- Include 2-3 subheadings to break up the text.
- Do not use phrases like 'in today's fast-paced world' or 'it goes without saying'.
- Reference specific regulations, trends, or developments where possible rather than speaking in generalities.
howToUse: Fill in your topic, argument, and a real example. The example is what separates a good article from a forgettable one.
Review the first draft and check that the examples and references are accurate. AI may approximate details.
Ask the AI to 'add my personal perspective to paragraph [X]' if any section feels too generic.
Publish on LinkedIn as a newsletter article for maximum distribution, and share a summary post linking to it.
whyItWorks: LinkedIn articles that perform well combine a clear argument with specific evidence. This prompt forces both by requiring a stated position and a real example. Banning bullet points in the body ensures the piece reads as genuine thought leadership rather than a quick tips listicle.
makeItYourOwn: Paste in an article you admire and say 'Match this level of depth and style'. You can also add 'I want to respectfully challenge the common view that [opposing position]' to give the article a stronger editorial angle.

title: Instagram story sequence for promoting a service
description: Plan a multi-slide Instagram story sequence that promotes a service naturally, moving viewers from interest to action.
toolTips: Design the stories in Canva using the text and visual directions from the output. Batch-create a week's worth of story sequences in one session.
content:
You are an Instagram strategist who helps service-based businesses use Instagram Stories to sell without feeling pushy. You know that Stories are where trust is built and buying decisions happen, but only if the sequence is structured correctly.

Create an Instagram story sequence to promote a service.

Service details:
- Service name: [YOUR SERVICE]
- What it involves: [BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF WHAT THE CLIENT GETS]
- Price: [PRICE OR PRICE RANGE, or 'enquiry-based']
- Ideal client: [WHO IS THIS PERFECT FOR]
- Common objection: [THE MAIN REASON PEOPLE HESITATE, e.g. price, time commitment, not sure if it is right for them]
- Result or transformation: [WHAT DOES THE CLIENT ACHIEVE OR FEEL AFTER]

Please create a story sequence of 6-9 slides:

Slide 1 (Hook): A question, bold statement, or relatable scenario that makes the ideal client tap to the next slide. Must work as text on a plain or branded background.

Slide 2-3 (Problem/empathy): Describe the problem or frustration the ideal client is experiencing. Make them feel seen.

Slide 4-5 (Solution): Introduce the service as the answer. Explain what it involves in simple, jargon-free terms.

Slide 6 (Proof): Suggest a testimonial screenshot, before/after, or result to share. Write placeholder text if needed.

Slide 7 (Objection handling): Address the most common hesitation directly and honestly.

Slide 8-9 (CTA): A clear, low-friction call to action. Suggest using a poll, question sticker, or link sticker.

For each slide provide:
- Text content (what to write on the slide)
- Visual direction (background type, photo, or graphic suggestion)
- Any interactive element (poll, slider, question box, link)

Constraints:
- Each slide should be readable in under 4 seconds.
- Do not cram too much text onto any single slide.
- Keep the tone warm, confident, and conversational.
- Use UK English.
howToUse: Fill in your service details, especially the common objection, as this is where most service promotions fall flat.
Create each slide in Canva or directly in Instagram using the text and visual suggestions.
Post the sequence in one go so viewers can tap through the full story.
Save the sequence as a highlight so it keeps working for you beyond the 24-hour window.
whyItWorks: Most service promotions on Instagram fail because they jump straight to selling. This sequence mirrors the customer journey: attention, empathy, solution, proof, objection handling, action. Addressing the common objection directly builds trust and removes the barrier that stops most people from enquiring.
makeItYourOwn: Add a real client testimonial or result to slide 6 for maximum impact. You can also say 'My brand colours are [colours] and my style is [minimal/bold/warm/playful]' so the visual suggestions match your aesthetic.

title: Social media bio and profile optimiser
description: Rewrite your social media bios to clearly communicate who you are, what you do, and why someone should follow or hire you.
toolTips: Run this once for all your platforms at the same time. Your bios should be consistent in message but adapted to each platform's style and character limits.
content:
You are a personal branding specialist who has optimised social media profiles for hundreds of professionals and businesses. You know that a bio has about 3 seconds to communicate value, and most people waste those seconds with vague descriptions or job titles nobody understands.

Rewrite and optimise my social media bios for the following platforms: [LIST PLATFORMS, e.g. Instagram, LinkedIn, X/Twitter, TikTok, Facebook page].

About me/my business:
- Name: [YOUR NAME OR BUSINESS NAME]
- What I do: [WHAT YOU ACTUALLY DO, IN PLAIN ENGLISH]
- Who I help: [YOUR TARGET AUDIENCE OR CUSTOMER]
- What makes me different: [YOUR UNIQUE ANGLE, EXPERIENCE, OR APPROACH]
- Key achievement or credential: [e.g. 15 years in the industry, served 500+ clients, qualified chartered accountant]
- What I want people to do: [e.g. follow for tips, book a consultation, visit the website, message me]
- Current bio (optional): [PASTE YOUR EXISTING BIO IF YOU WANT IT IMPROVED]

For each platform, provide:
1. Optimised bio text (within the platform's character limit)
2. Name field recommendation (how to use the display name field for searchability)
3. Profile link suggestion (what URL to put in the link field, e.g. Linktree, booking page, website)
4. One-line explanation of why you wrote it that way

Platform-specific rules:
- Instagram: 150 characters max. Use line breaks for readability. Include a call to action.
- LinkedIn: Write the headline (220 characters) and the About summary opening paragraph (first 3 lines visible before 'see more').
- X/Twitter: 160 characters max. Personality and clarity over formality.
- TikTok: 80 characters max. Punchy and direct.
- Facebook page: Write the short description (255 characters) and suggest a category.

Constraints:
- No cliches like 'passionate about', 'helping you live your best life', or 'on a mission to'.
- Every bio must answer: who are you, what do you do, and why should I care.
- Use UK English.
howToUse: Fill in your details honestly. The more specific you are about what makes you different, the sharper the bios will be.
Update all your profiles in one sitting while you have the outputs open.
Test the Instagram bio by asking a friend if they can tell what you do within 3 seconds of reading it.
Revisit and refresh your bios every quarter or when your offering changes.
whyItWorks: Your social media bio is the most viewed and least optimised piece of copy in your business. This prompt forces clarity by requiring every bio to answer three fundamental questions and banning the vague phrases that most people default to. Platform-specific formatting ensures each bio works where it lives.
makeItYourOwn: Paste in bios from 2-3 people in your industry whose profiles you admire and say 'I like the tone of these. Incorporate a similar style.' This gives the AI a style target beyond just the content.

title: Repurpose a blog post into 5 social media posts
description: Turn one blog post into five distinct social media posts, each tailored to a different platform or angle.
toolTips: Claude handles long blog posts well. Paste the entire blog post in for best results. You can then ask 'Now give me 5 more posts from the same article' to double your content bank.
content:
You are a content repurposing specialist who helps businesses get maximum value from every piece of content they create. You understand that one great blog post contains at least 5 social media posts, each pulling out a different angle or insight.

I am going to give you a blog post. Please turn it into 5 distinct social media posts, each designed for a different purpose or platform.

Target platforms: [LIST YOUR PLATFORMS, e.g. LinkedIn, Instagram, X/Twitter, Facebook]
Brand tone: [e.g. professional but warm, casual and fun, authoritative]

For each of the 5 posts, provide:
1. Platform: which platform this is best suited for
2. Angle: what aspect of the blog post this focuses on (e.g. the main argument, a surprising statistic, a practical tip, a controversial take, a personal story)
3. Full post text: complete, ready to copy and paste
4. Visual suggestion: what image, graphic, or screenshot to pair with it
5. Hashtags: 3-5 relevant hashtags (only for platforms where hashtags help)

The 5 posts must each take a different angle:
- Post 1: The key insight or main takeaway (educational)
- Post 2: A surprising or counterintuitive point from the article (curiosity-driven)
- Post 3: A practical, actionable tip that stands alone (value-driven)
- Post 4: A question or opinion that invites discussion (engagement-driven)
- Post 5: A personal or behind-the-scenes angle related to the topic (connection-driven)

Constraints:
- Each post must work on its own without reading the blog post.
- Do not just copy sentences from the blog. Rewrite for each platform's native style.
- Keep LinkedIn posts under 200 words, Instagram captions under 150 words, tweets under 280 characters.
- Use UK English throughout.
- No lazy repurposing. Each post should feel like it was written for that platform.

Here is the blog post:
[PASTE YOUR FULL BLOG POST HERE]
howToUse: Paste your full blog post at the end of the prompt.
Specify which platforms you use so the posts are correctly formatted.
Schedule the 5 posts across the week following the blog's publication to extend its reach.
Track which angle (educational, curiosity, practical, engagement, personal) performs best for your audience.
whyItWorks: Most businesses publish a blog post and share it once with a generic 'new post' caption. This prompt extracts five different content angles from a single piece, giving you a week of content and multiple chances to reach your audience with the same core message in different formats.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'The section about [specific part] got the most comments on the blog. Create an extra post specifically expanding on that point.' You can also request 'Include one post that is slightly controversial or challenges a common belief from the article' for higher engagement.

title: Facebook ad copy with A/B test variations
description: Write high-converting Facebook ad copy with multiple variations ready for split testing.
toolTips: Use ChatGPT for this as it tends to write punchier ad copy. Create the variations here, then set up A/B tests in Meta Ads Manager with identical targeting but different copy.
content:
You are a Facebook ads copywriter who has managed six-figure ad budgets for retail, food, and hospitality businesses across the UK. You write ad copy that converts because you understand that great ads feel like a recommendation from a friend, not an interruption.

Write Facebook ad copy with A/B test variations for my business.

Campaign details:
- Business: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME AND WHAT YOU SELL/DO]
- Offer or promotion: [WHAT YOU ARE ADVERTISING, e.g. 20% off first order, new menu launch, booking discount]
- Target audience: [WHO YOU ARE TARGETING, e.g. women 25-45 within 10 miles, food lovers, homeowners]
- Objective: [e.g. website visits, bookings, purchases, sign-ups]
- Landing page URL: [WHERE THE AD LINKS TO]

Please create 3 complete ad variations, each testing a different approach:

Variation A (Problem-solution): Lead with the problem the customer faces, then present your offer as the solution.
Variation B (Social proof): Lead with a result, testimonial, or number that builds credibility.
Variation C (Direct offer): Lead with the offer itself, making it irresistible.

For each variation, provide:
1. Primary text (the main ad copy above the image, 2-3 short paragraphs, under 125 words)
2. Headline (under 40 characters, appears below the image)
3. Description (under 30 characters, appears below the headline)
4. Call-to-action button recommendation (e.g. Shop Now, Book Now, Learn More, Get Offer)
5. Image direction: what the ad image should show

Also provide:
- A recommendation for which variation to test first and why
- What metric to use to judge the winner (e.g. CTR for awareness, CPA for conversions)

Constraints:
- Write for a UK audience. Use pounds, not dollars.
- Comply with Meta advertising policies. No exaggerated claims, no 'you' in a way that implies personal attributes.
- No clickbait or sensationalism.
- Use UK English.
- Keep the copy conversational and scroll-stopping.
howToUse: Fill in your campaign details, especially the specific offer and target audience.
Create three ad sets in Meta Ads Manager with identical targeting but one variation each.
Run each variation for at least 3-5 days before judging performance.
Kill the lowest performer and double budget on the winner.
whyItWorks: Testing one ad is guessing. Testing three with distinct approaches (problem-solution, social proof, direct offer) is strategy. This prompt creates copy that is ready to paste directly into Meta Ads Manager, with clear testing methodology so you learn what your audience responds to, not just what sounds good.
makeItYourOwn: Paste in your best-performing previous ad and say 'My best ad so far looked like this. Create variations that test different angles while keeping what works.' You can also add 'Our average order value is [X] and our target CPA is [Y]' for more commercially-aware copy.

title: LinkedIn connection request and follow-up messages
description: Write personalised LinkedIn connection requests and follow-up messages that start genuine professional conversations.
toolTips: Generate a template, then personalise each message with something specific about the person you are connecting with. Batch-write 10-15 messages in one session.
content:
You are a LinkedIn networking specialist who helps professionals build genuine relationships through the platform. You know that generic connection requests get ignored, and that good follow-up messages open doors without feeling like a sales pitch.

Write LinkedIn connection request and follow-up messages for me.

My details:
- My name: [YOUR NAME]
- My role: [YOUR JOB TITLE]
- My business/company: [YOUR COMPANY]
- What I offer: [YOUR SERVICE OR EXPERTISE]
- Why I am reaching out: [e.g. building my network in [industry], looking for referral partners, connecting with potential clients, thought leadership]

Target person details:
- Their likely role: [e.g. marketing director, business owner, HR manager]
- Their industry: [THEIR INDUSTRY]
- Something specific about them: [e.g. they posted about X, they work at Y, they spoke at Z, we share a mutual connection]

Please write:

1. Connection request message (under 300 characters, the LinkedIn limit):
   - Reference something specific about them or their work.
   - Explain briefly why you want to connect.
   - Do not sell, pitch, or ask for anything.

2. Follow-up message 1 (sent 2-3 days after they accept):
   - Thank them for connecting.
   - Offer something of value (an insight, resource, or genuine compliment about their work).
   - Ask one open-ended question to start a conversation.
   - Under 100 words.

3. Follow-up message 2 (sent 1-2 weeks later):
   - Reference something they have posted or shared recently (or provide a placeholder if unknown).
   - Mention how your work intersects with theirs.
   - Suggest a low-commitment next step (e.g. 'Would you be open to a quick 15-minute call?' or 'Happy to share [resource] if useful').
   - Under 100 words.

Also provide:
- 3 alternative opening lines for the connection request to A/B test
- A list of 5 'do nots' to avoid when LinkedIn networking

Constraints:
- Every message must feel personal, not templated.
- No corporate buzzwords like 'synergy', 'leverage', or 'value-add'.
- No fake enthusiasm or over-familiarity.
- Use UK English.
howToUse: Fill in your details and the target person's details. The more specific the 'something specific about them' field, the better.
Send the connection request and wait for acceptance before sending follow-up 1.
Personalise each message further before sending. Change a line or two so it genuinely matches the individual.
Track your acceptance rate. If it drops below 30%, test different opening lines.
whyItWorks: LinkedIn connection requests have a 300-character limit, which forces brevity. This prompt maximises that tiny space by leading with specificity about the other person, not about you. The follow-up sequence builds trust gradually, with each message offering value before making any ask.
makeItYourOwn: Paste in a connection request that worked well for you in the past and say 'This one got accepted and led to a great conversation. Write new variations in a similar tone.' You can also specify 'I am introverted and prefer a understated approach' or 'I am naturally chatty' to adjust the personality.

title: Hashtag strategy generator
description: Build a researched hashtag strategy for any platform, organised by size, relevance, and purpose.
toolTips: Use ChatGPT with browsing for the most current hashtag suggestions. Regenerate monthly as trending hashtags change. Save the output as a reference document.
content:
You are a social media strategist who specialises in hashtag research and strategy. You understand that hashtags are a discovery tool, not decoration, and that the right mix of hashtag sizes and types significantly impacts reach.

Build a comprehensive hashtag strategy for my business.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Industry: [YOUR INDUSTRY]
- What I sell/do: [BRIEF DESCRIPTION]
- Target audience: [WHO I WANT TO REACH]
- Geographic focus: [e.g. local to Manchester, UK-wide, international]
- Primary platform: [e.g. Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, X/Twitter]

Please provide:

1. Core hashtag bank (30 hashtags) organised into:
   - Large (500k+ posts): 5 broad, high-volume hashtags for maximum visibility
   - Medium (50k-500k posts): 10 mid-range hashtags for balanced reach and relevance
   - Small (10k-50k posts): 10 niche hashtags where you can realistically rank
   - Micro (under 10k posts): 5 highly specific or local hashtags

2. Content-type hashtag sets: a ready-to-use group of 15 hashtags for each of these post types:
   - Educational/tip posts
   - Behind-the-scenes posts
   - Product or service showcase posts
   - Engagement or community posts

3. Hashtags to avoid: 5 hashtags that look relevant but are too saturated, spammy, or attract the wrong audience, with an explanation of why.

4. Strategy recommendations:
   - How many hashtags to use per post on your primary platform
   - Where to place them (caption vs. comment vs. bio)
   - How often to rotate them
   - One hashtag trend or tactic specific to the current year

Constraints:
- Make all hashtags relevant to the UK market where geography matters.
- Do not include banned or flagged hashtags.
- Include a mix of evergreen and timely hashtags.
- Use UK English.
howToUse: Fill in your business details and primary platform.
Save the hashtag bank somewhere accessible, such as a notes app or spreadsheet.
For each post, pick from the relevant content-type set rather than using the same hashtags every time.
Check monthly whether any hashtags have been flagged or banned by searching them on the platform.
whyItWorks: Most businesses either use the same 10 hashtags on every post or pick randomly. This prompt creates a structured bank organised by size, which matters because small accounts cannot compete on huge hashtags. The content-type sets make it effortless to pick the right hashtags for each post.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'My competitors are [names] and I want to appear alongside their content' to reverse-engineer hashtags your target audience already follows. You can also specify 'I post mainly [type of content]' to weight the strategy towards what you actually create.

title: Social media crisis response template
description: Prepare a set of response templates for handling negative publicity, complaints, or PR issues on social media.
toolTips: Claude's measured, thoughtful tone makes it well suited for crisis communications. Save the templates before you need them. Having them ready in advance prevents panic responses.
content:
You are a crisis communications consultant who helps businesses respond to social media incidents quickly, honestly, and professionally. You have managed everything from viral negative reviews to genuine business mistakes, and you know that how a business responds matters more than what happened.

Create a social media crisis response toolkit for my business.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Industry: [YOUR INDUSTRY]
- Number of employees: [APPROXIMATE]
- Who manages your social media: [e.g. me (the owner), a team member, an agency]

Please create response templates for each of these scenarios:

1. Negative review or complaint going viral:
   - Initial public response (within 1 hour)
   - Follow-up response once you have investigated
   - Private/DM message template to take the conversation offline

2. Genuine business mistake (e.g. service failure, wrong order, missed appointment):
   - Public acknowledgement post
   - Direct response to affected customer(s)
   - Follow-up update showing what you have changed

3. Misinformation or false claims about your business:
   - Calm, factual public response
   - When and how to escalate (request removal, legal considerations)

4. Employee or internal issue becoming public:
   - Initial holding statement
   - Full response once facts are established

For each template, provide:
- The exact wording (with [BRACKETS] for details to fill in)
- Tone guidance (how it should feel)
- What NOT to say
- Timing recommendation

Also include:
- A crisis response checklist: the first 5 things to do when something blows up online
- Escalation guidelines: when to respond publicly, when to go to DMs, when to involve a lawyer
- A list of phrases that make things worse (with better alternatives)

Constraints:
- Responses must be genuine and human, not corporate boilerplate.
- Assume UK consumer law and GDPR apply.
- Never advise deleting negative comments unless they are abusive or defamatory.
- Use UK English throughout.
- Keep individual response templates under 100 words each.
howToUse: Fill in your business details and save the completed toolkit somewhere your whole team can access it.
Brief anyone who manages your social media on the checklist and escalation guidelines.
When an incident happens, grab the relevant template, fill in the brackets, and post within the timeframe recommended.
After any incident, review what happened and update the templates based on what you learned.
whyItWorks: The biggest social media mistakes happen when businesses respond emotionally or too slowly. Having pre-written, well-considered templates means you can respond within the critical first hour with something measured and professional. The 'what NOT to say' sections are often more valuable than the templates themselves.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'We had an incident recently where [describe what happened]. Write a template specifically for that type of situation recurring.' Real past experiences make the toolkit much more relevant. You can also add your company values to help the AI match your brand voice under pressure.

title: Personal brand storytelling post for a tradesperson
description: Write a social media post that tells your story as a tradesperson, building trust and winning work through authenticity.
toolTips: The best storytelling posts come from real moments. Think of a specific job, customer interaction, or career milestone before running this prompt. Authenticity beats perfection every time.
content:
You are a social media content writer who helps tradespeople build a personal brand on platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and TikTok. You know that in the trades, people hire people they trust, and trust comes from showing the real you, your skills, your standards, and your story.

Write a personal brand storytelling post for a tradesperson.

About you:
- Your trade: [e.g. plumber, electrician, carpenter, bricklayer, decorator, roofer]
- Years in the trade: [HOW LONG YOU HAVE BEEN DOING THIS]
- How you got started: [BRIEF BACKSTORY, e.g. family business, apprenticeship, career change]
- Your proudest moment or best job: [A SPECIFIC PROJECT OR ACHIEVEMENT]
- What you are known for: [YOUR REPUTATION, e.g. always on time, obsessively tidy, explains everything to the customer]
- Platform: [WHERE YOU WILL POST THIS, e.g. Instagram, Facebook, TikTok]

Post type (pick one):
- [ORIGIN STORY]: how you got into the trade and why you love it
- [THE JOB THAT TAUGHT ME]: a specific job that changed how you work
- [WHY I DO THINGS DIFFERENTLY]: your standards and what sets you apart
- [CUSTOMER MOMENT]: a time a customer's reaction reminded you why you do this
- [HONEST TRUTH]: something real about running a trade business that people do not see

The post must:
1. Sound like you are talking to a mate in the pub, not writing a corporate bio.
2. Include one specific detail or story, not vague generalities.
3. Show your personality and values without bragging.
4. End with something that invites engagement: a question, a tag-a-friend prompt, or a simple 'Anyone else?'
5. Be under 200 words.
6. Work equally well with a photo of you on site, a finished job, or a van selfie.

Constraints:
- Write in a natural, conversational UK voice. Use contractions and everyday language.
- No marketing speak. No hashtags like #hustle or #blessed.
- No obvious selling or calls to 'book now'.
- Use UK English.
howToUse: Pick the post type that fits something genuinely on your mind this week.
Fill in your details honestly. The more specific and real, the better it will land.
Pair the post with a photo from site. Phone photos outperform professional shots for this type of content.
Post it and reply to every comment. These posts build trust through the conversation, not just the post itself.
whyItWorks: Tradespeople who build a personal brand online consistently win more work and charge higher rates. Storytelling posts humanise you beyond a quote on Checkatrade. This prompt ensures the post feels authentic rather than marketing-led, which is exactly what potential customers respond to.
makeItYourOwn: Tell the AI about something that happened this week: 'On Tuesday, a customer said [something]. Write a post around that.' The freshest, most specific stories always outperform generic ones. You can also add 'I am not great with words so keep it really simple' to adjust the writing level.

title: Professional email reply tone matcher
description: Draft a professional email reply that matches the right tone for the situation, whether it is firm, friendly, formal, or delicate.
toolTips: Claude is particularly good at matching nuanced tones. If the reply feels off, tell it 'That is too formal, make it warmer' or 'That is too soft, I need to be firmer' and it will adjust.
content:
You are a communications professional who drafts emails for busy people. You can match any tone: formal, friendly, firm, diplomatic, apologetic, or matter-of-fact. You know that the right tone is the difference between an email that gets the result you want and one that damages a relationship.

I need to reply to an email and I want to get the tone right.

Context:
- Who sent the email: [THEIR NAME AND ROLE/RELATIONSHIP TO YOU, e.g. a client, your manager, a supplier, a colleague]
- What the email is about: [BRIEF SUMMARY OF WHAT THEY WROTE]
- The tone I need to strike: [e.g. firm but polite, warm and reassuring, professional and slightly formal, friendly but clear, diplomatic because it is a sensitive situation]
- What I want to say in my reply: [YOUR KEY POINTS OR THE OUTCOME YOU WANT]
- Anything I need to be careful about: [e.g. they are upset, there is a contractual issue, I need to say no without burning the bridge, I am late replying]

Please draft an email reply that:
1. Opens with an appropriate greeting and acknowledgement of their message.
2. Addresses their points clearly and directly.
3. Communicates my key message without ambiguity.
4. Maintains the tone I specified throughout, even when delivering difficult messages.
5. Closes with a clear next step or invitation to continue the conversation.
6. Is concise. Under 200 words unless the situation genuinely requires more.

Constraints:
- Do not use filler phrases like 'I hope this email finds you well' or 'Just circling back'.
- Match my specified tone precisely. If I say firm, do not soften it. If I say warm, do not make it stiff.
- Use UK English and UK business conventions (e.g. 'Kind regards' not 'Best').
- If I need to say no or deliver bad news, do it clearly in the first half of the email, not buried at the end.
howToUse: Paste or summarise the email you received and describe the tone you need.
Be specific about what you want to say. The AI's job is to say it well, not to decide what to say.
Review the draft and adjust: 'Make the second paragraph firmer' or 'Soften the opening line'.
Once happy, copy the text into your email client, add any personal touches, and send.
whyItWorks: Most people know what they want to say in an email but struggle with how to say it, especially in sensitive situations. This prompt separates the 'what' (your key points) from the 'how' (the tone and phrasing), letting the AI handle the difficult part while you stay in control of the message.
makeItYourOwn: Paste in the original email between triple quotes so the AI can match their communication style. You can also add 'I tend to be too [blunt/apologetic/wordy] in emails, so compensate for that' for a more balanced output.

title: Cold outreach email for B2B services
description: Write a cold email that gets opened, gets read, and gets a reply by leading with value rather than a sales pitch.
toolTips: Generate 3-5 subject line variations and A/B test them. Open rates are won or lost in the subject line. Ask the AI to 'write 5 alternative subject lines, each using a different psychological trigger'.
content:
You are a B2B sales copywriter who specialises in cold outreach emails that actually get replies. You know that decision-makers receive dozens of cold emails daily, so yours must stand out by being relevant, concise, and focused on their problem, not your service.

Write a cold outreach email for my B2B service.

My details:
- My business: [YOUR COMPANY AND WHAT YOU DO]
- Service I am pitching: [THE SPECIFIC SERVICE OR OFFER]
- My ideal client: [THEIR ROLE, COMPANY TYPE, AND SIZE]
- The problem I solve: [WHAT PAIN POINT OR CHALLENGE DOES MY SERVICE ADDRESS]
- One proof point: [A RESULT, CASE STUDY, OR CREDENTIAL THAT BUILDS CREDIBILITY, e.g. 'We helped [company type] reduce [metric] by 30%']
- The ask: [WHAT DO I WANT THEM TO DO, e.g. book a call, reply, visit a page]

Target recipient:
- Their likely role: [e.g. Head of Marketing, Operations Director, Managing Partner]
- Their likely priorities: [WHAT KEEPS THEM BUSY OR WORRIED]
- Something specific about their company: [e.g. they recently expanded, they posted a job for X, they launched Y]

Please write:

1. Subject line (under 50 characters, curiosity-driven, no spam trigger words)
2. Email body (under 125 words) following this structure:
   - Opening line: reference something specific about them or their business. No 'I hope you are well'.
   - Problem statement: articulate the problem they face in 1-2 sentences.
   - Value bridge: connect your service to their problem in 1-2 sentences. Lead with the result, not the process.
   - Proof: one specific credibility point.
   - CTA: a low-commitment ask. Make it easy to say yes.
3. Three alternative subject lines
4. A follow-up email (sent 3-4 days later if no reply, under 75 words, adds new value rather than just chasing)

Constraints:
- No salesy language: no 'revolutionary', 'cutting-edge', 'unique opportunity', or 'I would love to'.
- The email must be scannable in under 15 seconds.
- Do not attach anything or ask them to download anything.
- Use UK English.
- Comply with UK GDPR: include a simple opt-out line at the end.
howToUse: Fill in your details and research the specific recipient before completing the target section.
Personalise the opening line for each individual recipient. Batch personalisation (same email, unique first line) is the most efficient approach.
Send between Tuesday and Thursday, 7-9am, for the best open rates in the UK.
If no reply after the follow-up, wait two weeks and try a completely different angle rather than sending a third chase.
whyItWorks: Cold emails fail when they talk about the sender instead of the recipient. This prompt forces recipient-first thinking by requiring you to define their priorities and problems before writing. The 125-word limit prevents the most common mistake: writing too much and losing the reader.
makeItYourOwn: Paste in a cold email that got you a positive reply and say 'This approach worked. Write a new version for a different industry using the same structure and tone.' You can also add 'The recipient is likely sceptical of [type of service] because [reason]' to help the AI preemptively address objections.

title: Follow-up email sequence after a meeting
description: Write a three-email follow-up sequence that keeps momentum after a meeting without being pushy or annoying.
toolTips: Fill this in immediately after your meeting while the details are fresh. Claude is particularly good at maintaining a natural, non-pushy tone across a sequence.
content:
You are a business development professional who knows that most deals are won or lost in the follow-up, not the meeting. You write follow-up emails that keep conversations moving without being annoying or desperate.

Create a 3-email follow-up sequence after a meeting.

Meeting context:
- Who I met: [THEIR NAME, ROLE, AND COMPANY]
- What we discussed: [KEY TOPICS, DECISIONS, OR IDEAS FROM THE MEETING]
- What they seemed most interested in: [WHAT GOT THE STRONGEST POSITIVE RESPONSE]
- What we agreed as next steps: [ANY ACTIONS OR COMMITMENTS MADE]
- What I want the outcome to be: [e.g. they sign a contract, we schedule a second meeting, they introduce me to a decision-maker]
- Any concerns or objections they raised: [ANYTHING THAT SEEMED LIKE A HESITATION]

Please write:

Email 1 - Same day or next morning:
- Thank them for their time (genuinely, not generically).
- Summarise the key points discussed and any agreed actions.
- Confirm your next step and when you will deliver it.
- Attach or reference anything you promised to send.
- Under 150 words.

Email 2 - 3-5 days later:
- Provide additional value: a relevant article, insight, case study, or answer to a question they raised.
- Subtly address any objection or concern from the meeting.
- Gently prompt on next steps without pressuring.
- Under 100 words.

Email 3 - 10-14 days after the meeting (if no response to Email 2):
- Acknowledge they are busy without being passive-aggressive.
- Restate the value proposition in one sentence.
- Give them an easy way to re-engage (a simple yes/no question or two options to choose from).
- Make it clear this is your last follow-up unless they want to continue.
- Under 75 words.

Constraints:
- Never guilt-trip or use phrases like 'Just checking in' or 'Bumping this to the top of your inbox'.
- Each email must provide value or move the conversation forward. No empty chasers.
- Use UK English and professional but warm tone.
- Include a subject line for each email.
howToUse: Fill in the meeting context immediately after the meeting while details are fresh.
Send Email 1 the same day or first thing the next morning.
For Email 2, replace the placeholder value-add with something genuinely relevant to them.
If Email 3 gets no response, move on. You can revisit in 2-3 months with a fresh angle.
whyItWorks: Most follow-up sequences fail because every email just asks 'Have you had a chance to think about this?' This prompt ensures each email adds something new: Email 1 builds trust through competence, Email 2 adds value, and Email 3 makes it easy to say yes or gracefully exit. The decreasing word counts mirror the decreasing patience of your recipient.
makeItYourOwn: Add specific details from the meeting: 'They mentioned they are struggling with [issue] and seemed impressed when I talked about [topic].' The more specific the context, the more personalised and effective the sequence.

title: Internal team weekly update email
description: Write a clear, motivating weekly update email that keeps your team aligned without wasting their time.
toolTips: Run this every Friday with your bullet point notes from the week. It takes 2 minutes and gives your team a professional, clear update they will actually read.
content:
You are an operations manager who writes weekly team updates that people actually read. You know that most internal emails are too long, too vague, or too corporate. Yours are clear, honest, and take under 2 minutes to read.

Write a weekly team update email from my notes.

Context:
- My name/role: [YOUR NAME AND TITLE]
- Team/department: [TEAM NAME OR DEPARTMENT]
- Company: [COMPANY NAME]
- Reporting period: [WEEK DATES, e.g. w/c 3 March 2026]

My rough notes for this week:
- Wins/achievements: [BULLET POINT LIST OF WHAT WENT WELL]
- Challenges or issues: [ANYTHING THAT WENT WRONG OR IS A CONCERN]
- Key updates or changes: [NEWS, DECISIONS, OR CHANGES THE TEAM NEEDS TO KNOW]
- Priorities for next week: [WHAT THE TEAM SHOULD FOCUS ON]
- Shoutouts: [ANYONE WHO DESERVES RECOGNITION, OR 'NONE']
- Anything else: [REMINDERS, EVENTS, HR UPDATES, OR 'NONE']

Please structure the email as:

1. Subject line: clear and consistent (e.g. 'Team Update: w/c [DATE] - [ONE-LINE THEME]')
2. Opening line: a brief, human sentence that sets the tone for the week. Not corporate.
3. This week's highlights (bulleted, 3-5 items)
4. Challenges and what we are doing about them (bulleted, honest but not alarming)
5. Key updates (bulleted, only what people need to know)
6. Next week's priorities (numbered, in order of importance)
7. Shoutouts (if any, genuine and specific)
8. Closing line: something motivating or forward-looking, not cheesy

Constraints:
- Total email under 300 words. Brevity is respect for people's time.
- Use a tone that is professional but human. Not a corporate newsletter, not a group chat.
- Be honest about challenges. Teams trust leaders who acknowledge problems.
- Use UK English.
- No motivational quotes or generic phrases like 'Let us smash it next week'.
- Format for easy scanning. Bullet points, bold headings, short sentences.
howToUse: Jot down rough notes throughout the week or spend 5 minutes on Friday listing what happened.
Paste your notes into the prompt and let the AI structure them into a polished email.
Review the output and add any personal touches or context that only you would know.
Send at the same time every week (e.g. Friday 4pm) so your team expects it and reads it.
whyItWorks: Consistency builds trust. When your team knows a clear, honest update is coming every week, they stay aligned without needing extra meetings. The structured format means they can scan for what matters to them in under a minute, and the honest challenges section prevents surprises and builds psychological safety.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our company values are [values] - weave them in subtly where relevant' to reinforce culture. You can also add 'The team's morale this week is [high/low/mixed] because [reason]' to help the AI strike the right emotional tone.

title: Newsletter content from bullet point notes
description: Turn rough bullet points and ideas into a polished, engaging newsletter that your subscribers will actually read.
toolTips: Claude is great at maintaining a consistent voice throughout longer pieces. Paste in a previous newsletter you liked and say 'Match this style' for consistency across issues.
content:
You are a newsletter writer who specialises in turning rough ideas into engaging email newsletters for small businesses. You know that the best newsletters feel like a message from a knowledgeable friend, not a marketing blast.

Turn my bullet point notes into a polished newsletter.

Newsletter details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Newsletter name (if you have one): [NAME OR 'N/A']
- Audience: [WHO SUBSCRIBES, e.g. existing customers, industry peers, local community]
- Tone: [e.g. friendly and informative, professional but approachable, chatty and personal]
- Frequency: [e.g. weekly, fortnightly, monthly]
- Primary goal: [e.g. drive sales, share expertise, build community, stay top of mind]

My rough notes for this issue:
[PASTE YOUR BULLET POINTS, IDEAS, LINKS, OR ROUGH NOTES HERE]

Please create:

1. Subject line: under 50 characters, curiosity-driving, no spam words. Plus 2 alternatives.
2. Preview text: the snippet that appears next to the subject line in inbox (under 90 characters).
3. Opening section: a personal, engaging introduction that hooks the reader. Reference something timely or relatable.
4. Main content sections: organised from my notes into 2-4 clear sections with subheadings. Each section should deliver value, not just announce things.
5. Product or service mention (if relevant): woven in naturally, not as a hard sell. Maximum one promotional section.
6. Call to action: one clear thing you want the reader to do.
7. Sign-off: warm, personal, consistent with the brand tone.

Formatting:
- Use short paragraphs (2-3 sentences maximum).
- Include suggested places for images with [IMAGE: description].
- Bold key phrases that a scanner should catch.
- Suggest one link placement with anchor text.

Constraints:
- Total newsletter under 500 words. People skim, they do not read.
- No generic filler. Every sentence should inform, entertain, or persuade.
- Write the promotional section so it feels like a helpful recommendation, not an advert.
- Use UK English throughout.
- Do not use more than one exclamation mark in the entire newsletter.
howToUse: Throughout the week or month, jot down bullet points of things to include: news, tips, offers, events, customer stories.
Paste your rough notes into the prompt. They can be messy; the AI will structure them.
Review the output, then paste it into your email platform (Mailchimp, Brevo, MailerLite, etc.).
Send a test email to yourself first to check formatting and links before sending to your list.
whyItWorks: The biggest barrier to consistent newsletters is the writing itself. This prompt removes that barrier by turning messy notes into structured, polished content. The 500-word limit forces conciseness, and the one-exclamation-mark rule prevents the over-enthusiastic tone that makes newsletters feel like junk mail.
makeItYourOwn: Paste in your best previous newsletter and say 'This is my style. Match it.' Consistency across issues is what builds a loyal readership. You can also add 'My readers frequently reply about [topics]' to help the AI prioritise what resonates.

title: Customer complaint response email
description: Craft a professional, empathetic complaint response that acknowledges the issue, offers a resolution, and turns a frustrated customer into a loyal one.
toolTips: Claude tends to produce more natural, empathetic language for complaint handling. Paste the original complaint message directly into the chat for the most tailored response.
content:
You are a senior customer experience manager with 15 years of handling escalated complaints for UK businesses. You are known for turning unhappy customers into brand advocates through genuine empathy and decisive action.

I need you to draft a response to a customer complaint. Here are the details:

- My business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Industry: [e.g. retail, hospitality, trades, professional services]
- What the complaint is about: [BRIEF SUMMARY OF THE ISSUE]
- Was it our fault? [YES / NO / PARTIALLY - explain briefly]
- What resolution I can offer: [e.g. full refund, replacement, discount, redo the work, apology only]
- Customer's name: [FIRST NAME]
- How the complaint was received: [e.g. email, Google review, social media, phone call]

Please write the response email following these rules:
1. Open by acknowledging the specific issue they raised, not a generic apology.
2. Take responsibility where appropriate without being defensive or making excuses.
3. State the resolution clearly and what will happen next, with a timeline if possible.
4. Keep the tone warm, professional, and human. Avoid corporate cliches like 'we value your custom' or 'your feedback is important to us'.
5. Close with a direct invitation to contact you personally if they have further concerns.
6. Keep it under 200 words. Shorter complaints deserve shorter responses.

The original complaint message:
"""
[PASTE THE CUSTOMER'S COMPLAINT HERE]
"""
howToUse: Fill in your business details and the complaint context
Paste the customer's original message between the triple quotes for maximum accuracy
Review the draft and adjust any specifics around your resolution or company policy
If the tone is not quite right, ask 'Make this warmer' or 'Make this more formal' to adjust
whyItWorks: The prompt bans overused corporate phrases, forcing the AI to write something that sounds genuinely human. Providing the original complaint text means the response addresses specific concerns rather than offering a templated reply. The word limit keeps responses tight and respectful of the customer's time.
makeItYourOwn: Add your company's returns or complaints policy as extra context so the AI can reference specific guarantees. If you are responding to a public review, add 'This response will be visible publicly' to ensure the tone is appropriate for a wider audience.

title: Meeting recap email with action items
description: Transform messy meeting notes into a clear, professional recap email with decisions, action items, and deadlines that you can send straight to attendees.
toolTips: Claude handles long, unstructured notes exceptionally well. Paste in raw notes, voice memo transcripts, or even bullet points and it will structure them cleanly.
content:
You are a highly organised executive assistant who writes meeting recap emails that people actually read. Your recaps are known for being clear, concise, and impossible to misinterpret.

I need you to write a meeting recap email based on my notes. Here are the details:

- Meeting name/topic: [MEETING SUBJECT]
- Date and time: [DATE]
- Attendees: [LIST NAMES AND ROLES]
- My name (sending the recap): [YOUR NAME]

Please write a professional email that includes:
1. A one-sentence summary of the meeting purpose and outcome.
2. Key decisions made, listed as bullet points. For each decision, note who made or approved it.
3. Action items in a clear table format: Action | Owner | Deadline. If no deadline was mentioned, write 'TBC' and flag it.
4. Any open questions or items that need further discussion, with who needs to follow up.
5. Next meeting date/time if mentioned, or a note to schedule one.

Rules:
- Write the email ready to send. Include a subject line, greeting, and sign-off.
- Keep the tone professional but not stiff. This is a colleague-to-colleague email, not a board report.
- Do not add anything that was not discussed. If something is unclear in my notes, flag it with [PLEASE CONFIRM].
- Use UK English and UK date format throughout.
- Keep the total email under 350 words.

Here are my meeting notes:
[PASTE YOUR NOTES, TRANSCRIPT, OR BULLET POINTS HERE]
howToUse: Dump your raw meeting notes at the end of the prompt, however messy they are
Fill in attendee names and roles so the AI can correctly assign action items
Review the output for any [PLEASE CONFIRM] flags and clarify those before sending
Copy the email directly into your email client and send to attendees
whyItWorks: The structured format with decisions, actions, and open questions ensures nothing falls through the cracks. Requiring a table for action items makes ownership and deadlines unmissable. The [PLEASE CONFIRM] flag prevents the AI from guessing at details it is unsure about.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Tone: [casual/formal]' to match your workplace culture. If you regularly have meetings with the same group, save a version with pre-filled attendee names as a template.

title: Introduction email connecting two contacts
description: Write a warm, professional introduction email that connects two people in your network with clear context on why they should speak.
toolTips: Either tool works well. Keep the output short and natural. If it sounds too formal, ask 'Rewrite this as if I were introducing two friends at a dinner party'.
content:
You are a well-connected business professional who is excellent at making introductions that actually lead to conversations. Your introduction emails are warm, concise, and give both parties a genuine reason to connect.

I need you to write an introduction email connecting two people. Here are the details:

- My name: [YOUR NAME]
- Person A (the one I know better): [NAME, ROLE, COMPANY]
- Person B: [NAME, ROLE, COMPANY]
- Why I think they should connect: [THE SPECIFIC REASON - e.g. Person A needs a web developer and Person B runs a web agency]
- How I know each of them: [BRIEF CONTEXT]
- Have both agreed to the intro? [YES / NOT YET - if not yet, write a permission email to send first]

Please write the email following these rules:
1. Subject line should mention both names and the connection point.
2. Open by addressing both people (this is a group email).
3. Introduce each person to the other in 1-2 sentences, focusing on what makes them relevant to each other, not their full CV.
4. State clearly why you think they should connect.
5. Make it easy for them to take the next step (suggest a call, coffee, or email exchange).
6. Step yourself out gracefully so they can continue without you.
7. Keep the total email under 150 words. Introductions should be brief.

Use UK English. Keep the tone warm and professional, as if you were making the introduction at a networking event.
howToUse: Fill in the details for both contacts and your specific reason for connecting them
If both parties have not yet agreed, ask the AI to write a 'permission to intro' email first
Review the email to make sure the descriptions of each person are accurate and flattering without overselling
Send the email with both contacts in the To field
whyItWorks: The prompt focuses on relevance rather than biography, which means both recipients immediately understand why they should care. The 150-word limit prevents waffle, and the instruction to 'step yourself out' prevents the awkward situation where both people feel they need to keep you in the loop.
makeItYourOwn: If this is a high-value introduction, add 'Person A recently [specific achievement]' to give extra credibility. You can also specify the formality level: 'These are both quite senior and formal' or 'We are all pretty casual with each other'.

title: Testimonial and review request email
description: Draft a friendly, non-pushy email that asks happy customers for a testimonial or online review, making it as easy as possible for them to say yes.
toolTips: Ask the AI to generate 2-3 versions so you can pick the one that best matches your relationship with the customer. Use 'Make version 2 more casual' to fine-tune.
content:
You are a small business marketing specialist who helps business owners collect more testimonials and reviews without feeling awkward or pushy about it.

I need you to write an email asking a customer for a testimonial or review. Here are the details:

- My business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- What we did for this customer: [BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE WORK OR PRODUCT]
- Customer's first name: [NAME]
- How recently we completed the work/sale: [e.g. last week, last month]
- Where I want them to leave the review: [e.g. Google, Trustpilot, Checkatrade, via email reply, or I just want a quote I can use on my website]
- Direct link to leave a review (if applicable): [URL OR 'N/A']

Please write the email following these rules:
1. Open with a genuine, specific reference to the work you did for them. Not 'thank you for your recent purchase' but something that shows you remember their project.
2. Explain briefly why reviews matter to a small business like yours (be honest, not manipulative).
3. Make the ask clear and specific. Tell them exactly what to do and how long it will take (e.g. '2 minutes').
4. If asking for a written testimonial, include 2-3 simple prompt questions they can answer to make it easy (e.g. 'What was the problem you needed solving?' 'What was it like working with us?' 'Would you recommend us?').
5. Include the review link prominently if applicable.
6. Make it clear there is absolutely no pressure and you appreciate them either way.
7. Keep it under 180 words.

Use UK English. The tone should be warm, grateful, and human.
howToUse: Fill in the details about the customer and the work you completed for them
Replace the review link placeholder with your actual Google or Trustpilot review link
Send the email within 1-2 weeks of completing the work while the experience is still fresh
If they do not respond, ask the AI to write a gentle one-line follow-up for 7 days later
whyItWorks: Most review requests fail because they are generic and make the customer do all the thinking. This prompt solves both problems by referencing the specific work and providing prompt questions that make writing a review effortless. The honest explanation of why reviews matter appeals to goodwill rather than obligation.
makeItYourOwn: If you have a photo of the completed work (especially for trades), mention it: 'I have attached a photo of the finished [project] in case it jogs your memory'. You can also add 'If you would prefer, I can write a draft based on our conversations and you just approve it' for customers who hate writing.

title: Payment reminder email sequence (gentle to firm)
description: Generate a three-stage payment reminder sequence that escalates professionally from a friendly nudge to a firm final notice, preserving the client relationship throughout.
toolTips: Claude is particularly good at maintaining consistent tone escalation across a sequence. Generate all three emails in one go for consistency.
content:
You are a credit control specialist who helps small businesses get paid on time while maintaining positive client relationships. You understand that most late payments are due to oversight, not malice, and your approach reflects that.

I need you to write a three-email payment reminder sequence. Here are the details:

- My business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Client's name: [CLIENT NAME]
- Invoice number: [INVOICE NUMBER]
- Invoice amount: [AMOUNT INCLUDING VAT IF APPLICABLE]
- Original due date: [DATE]
- What the invoice was for: [BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF WORK/SERVICE]
- My payment terms: [e.g. 30 days from invoice date]
- Payment methods accepted: [e.g. bank transfer, card payment via link]

Please write three emails:

**Email 1 - Friendly reminder (send 3 days after due date):**
- Assume it was an oversight.
- Tone: warm, casual, helpful. As if reminding a colleague.
- Reattach or reference the invoice.
- Keep under 100 words.

**Email 2 - Firm follow-up (send 14 days after due date):**
- Acknowledge the previous reminder.
- Tone: professional and direct, but still polite.
- Ask if there is an issue with the invoice or the work that needs resolving.
- Request a specific response date.
- Keep under 130 words.

**Email 3 - Final notice (send 30 days after due date):**
- Tone: formal and serious, but never aggressive or threatening.
- State clearly this is a final reminder before further action.
- Reference late payment legislation if appropriate (Late Payment of Commercial Debts Act).
- Mention the right to charge statutory interest without yet doing so.
- Offer one last opportunity to arrange payment or discuss a payment plan.
- Keep under 150 words.

Use UK English. Include subject lines for each email. Do not use threatening or aggressive language at any stage.
howToUse: Fill in your invoice details and generate the full sequence in one go
Save the three emails as templates and adjust the specific details for each overdue invoice
Send Email 1 three days after the due date, Email 2 at two weeks, and Email 3 at 30 days
If you need to escalate beyond Email 3, consult a solicitor or debt recovery service
whyItWorks: The three-stage escalation mirrors professional credit control best practice. Starting friendly preserves the relationship for genuine oversights, while the final email's reference to late payment legislation signals seriousness without making empty threats. The word limits prevent each email from becoming a lecture.
makeItYourOwn: Add your bank details or payment link directly into Email 1 to remove any friction. If you have a specific payment portal, mention it. For recurring clients, soften Email 1 further: 'I know things get busy so just a quick nudge on this one'.

title: Partnership or collaboration pitch email
description: Write a compelling partnership pitch email that clearly articulates mutual value, making it easy for the recipient to see why collaborating with you is worth their time.
toolTips: Use GPT-4o or Claude Sonnet. Before generating, research the potential partner's recent work so you can reference specifics. The more personalised your input, the better the output.
content:
You are a business development specialist who writes partnership pitch emails that get responses. You know that most partnership emails fail because they focus on what the sender wants rather than what the recipient gains.

I need you to write a partnership or collaboration pitch email. Here are the details:

- My business: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME AND WHAT YOU DO]
- Their business: [THEIR BUSINESS NAME AND WHAT THEY DO]
- Who I am emailing: [NAME AND ROLE IF KNOWN]
- The partnership idea: [WHAT YOU WANT TO DO TOGETHER - e.g. co-host an event, cross-refer clients, bundle services, collaborate on content]
- What is in it for them: [BE SPECIFIC - how does this benefit their business?]
- What is in it for me: [BE HONEST - the AI needs this for authenticity]
- Any existing connection: [e.g. mutual contact, met at an event, follow their work, customer of theirs, or cold outreach]
- Something specific I admire about their work: [A GENUINE, SPECIFIC DETAIL]

Please write the email following these rules:
1. Open with the specific thing you admire about their work. Make it clear this is not a mass email.
2. Introduce yourself and your business in one sentence maximum.
3. Present the partnership idea concisely, leading with their benefit.
4. Include one concrete example of how the collaboration could work in practice.
5. Make the ask small and low-commitment: a 15-minute call, a coffee, a reply with their thoughts.
6. Keep the entire email under 180 words. Busy people delete long emails.

Use UK English. The tone should be confident but not arrogant, enthusiastic but not desperate.
howToUse: Research the potential partner before filling in the details. Reference something specific and recent about their work.
Be honest about mutual benefits. The AI will write a more authentic email if you are upfront about what you gain too.
Review the output and ensure the 'what is in it for them' section is genuinely compelling, not a stretch.
Send from your personal email address, not a marketing email. This is a human-to-human message.
whyItWorks: Leading with genuine admiration and their benefit immediately separates this from spam. The one-sentence self-introduction prevents the common mistake of talking about yourself for three paragraphs. The small ask at the end lowers the barrier to responding.
