makeItYourOwn: If you have a case study of a similar partnership that worked, add 'I recently partnered with [business] and [specific result]' to provide social proof. You can also add 'If this is not the right fit, no hard feelings at all' to reduce any pressure.

title: Appointment confirmation and preparation email
description: Send a professional appointment confirmation email that prepares the client for their visit, reduces no-shows, and sets clear expectations.
toolTips: Generate one version then ask 'Now create a shorter SMS version of this' for a text message reminder to send the day before.
content:
You are a client services coordinator who writes appointment confirmation emails that reduce no-shows and ensure clients arrive prepared. You know that clear, friendly confirmation emails build trust before the appointment even begins.

I need you to write an appointment confirmation and preparation email. Here are the details:

- My business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Type of appointment: [e.g. initial consultation, property viewing, therapy session, legal meeting, dental check-up]
- Client's first name: [NAME]
- Appointment date and time: [DATE AND TIME]
- Location or meeting format: [ADDRESS / VIDEO CALL LINK / PHONE]
- Duration: [e.g. 30 minutes, 1 hour]
- What the client should bring or prepare: [e.g. ID, medical history, documents, list of questions, nothing specific]
- Parking or access instructions: [IF APPLICABLE]
- Cancellation/rescheduling policy: [e.g. 24 hours notice required]
- Any forms to complete in advance: [LINK OR 'NONE']

Please write the email following these rules:
1. Open with a warm confirmation of the appointment, including all key details (date, time, location, duration) prominently.
2. If there are preparation steps, list them clearly as numbered items so nothing gets missed.
3. Include practical details like parking, building access, or what to expect on arrival.
4. State the cancellation policy matter-of-factly without sounding punitive.
5. End with a reassuring note appropriate to the appointment type (e.g. for a first therapy session: 'There is no need to prepare anything specific. We will go at your pace').
6. Include a one-line 'Questions before your appointment?' with your contact details.
7. Keep the total email under 200 words.

Use UK English. The tone should be warm, professional, and reassuring.
howToUse: Fill in your appointment details and any preparation requirements specific to your business
Save the output as a template in your email client or booking system
Send automatically or manually 2-3 days before the appointment
Ask the AI to also generate a short SMS reminder version for the day before
whyItWorks: No-shows drop significantly when clients receive clear confirmation emails with preparation instructions. The structured format ensures nothing is missed, while the reassuring closing note reduces anxiety, particularly for first-time appointments in sensitive settings like therapy or legal consultations.
makeItYourOwn: Add a line like 'When you arrive, you will be greeted by [receptionist name]' to make the experience more personal. For video calls, include a brief 'Please test your camera and microphone 5 minutes before' instruction.

title: Out-of-office message that actually helps the sender
description: Create a professional out-of-office auto-reply that manages expectations, redirects urgent matters, and subtly reinforces your brand rather than just saying 'I am away'.
toolTips: Ask for 2-3 variations: one formal, one casual, and one with personality. Pick the one that matches your brand.
content:
You are a communications consultant who helps professionals write out-of-office messages that are useful rather than useless. Most out-of-office replies just say 'I am away' and give no helpful information. Yours will be different.

I need you to write an out-of-office auto-reply. Here are the details:

- My name: [YOUR NAME]
- My role: [YOUR JOB TITLE]
- Dates I am away: [FROM DATE TO DATE]
- Reason (if sharing): [e.g. annual leave, conference, parental leave, or 'prefer not to say']
- Will I be checking email at all? [YES OCCASIONALLY / NO / EMERGENCIES ONLY]
- Who should they contact for urgent matters: [NAME, ROLE, EMAIL]
- Anything I want to promote while I am away: [e.g. new blog post, upcoming event, recent case study, or 'nothing']
- Tone preference: [FORMAL / FRIENDLY / PERSONALITY - e.g. light humour]

Please write the out-of-office message following these rules:
1. State clearly when I am away and when I will respond (give a specific date, not 'when I return').
2. Provide the urgent contact with enough context that people actually use it (not just a name and email).
3. Set expectations about response time: will I reply to everything in order, or should they resend if it is important?
4. If I have something to promote, weave it in naturally (not as a hard sell). For example: 'While you wait, you might find our recent guide on [topic] useful: [link]'.
5. Keep it under 100 words. Nobody reads a long out-of-office.
6. Do not start with 'Thank you for your email'. Find a more interesting opening.

Use UK English throughout.
howToUse: Fill in your dates, alternate contact, and tone preference
Set the output as your auto-reply in Outlook, Gmail, or your email client
Update it each time you go away rather than reusing the same stale message
If you chose the 'personality' tone, check it still reads professionally to a client who does not know you well
whyItWorks: Most auto-replies waste an opportunity. This prompt creates one that manages expectations (reducing follow-up emails), redirects urgent matters (so you are not disturbed), and optionally promotes something useful (turning every inbound email into a subtle touchpoint). The 100-word limit keeps it scannable.
makeItYourOwn: If you run your own business, use this as a chance to link to your booking calendar: 'If you would like to schedule a call for when I am back, grab a slot here: [link]'. This turns your absence into a lead capture tool.

title: One-page business proposal from rough notes
description: Turn your rough notes, scribbles, or bullet points into a polished one-page business proposal that looks like you spent hours on it.
toolTips: Claude handles messy, unstructured input particularly well. Dump your rough notes in and let it structure them. For formatting, copy the output into a Word or Google Doc template.
content:
You are a business proposal writer who specialises in creating concise, persuasive one-page proposals for small and medium-sized businesses. You know that busy decision-makers rarely read past page one, so you make every sentence count.

I need you to turn my rough notes into a polished one-page business proposal. Here are the details:

- My business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Client/prospect name: [THEIR NAME OR COMPANY]
- What they need: [THE PROBLEM OR REQUIREMENT]
- What I am proposing: [YOUR SOLUTION - rough notes are fine]
- Approximate budget/pricing: [YOUR PRICE OR RANGE]
- Timeline: [WHEN YOU WOULD START AND FINISH]
- Why us: [WHY SHOULD THEY CHOOSE YOU? - any rough points]

Please structure the proposal as follows:
1. **Header:** My business name, their name, date, proposal title.
2. **The challenge (2-3 sentences):** Restate their problem in a way that shows I understand it.
3. **The solution (4-6 sentences):** What I will do, broken into clear deliverables or phases.
4. **Why us (2-3 sentences):** What sets us apart. Use specifics, not generic claims like 'we are passionate'.
5. **Investment:** Clear pricing with what is included. If there are options, present them as Good / Better / Best.
6. **Timeline:** Key milestones or a simple start-to-finish overview.
7. **Next step:** One clear call to action (e.g. 'Reply to approve and we will schedule a kickoff call').

Constraints:
- Total word count: 350-500 words maximum. This must fit on one page.
- Write in UK English.
- Tone: confident, professional, straightforward. No fluff or filler.
- Do not use jargon the client would not understand.
- Present pricing with confidence. No apologetic language around costs.

Here are my rough notes:
[PASTE YOUR NOTES, BULLET POINTS, OR SCRIBBLES HERE]
howToUse: Dump your rough notes at the end of the prompt. They do not need to be tidy.
Fill in the key details like pricing and timeline, even if approximate
Review the output and adjust any claims in the 'Why us' section to be accurate
Copy into a branded Word or Google Doc template and send as a PDF
whyItWorks: The strict one-page format forces clarity and removes waffle. The structured sections mirror what decision-makers actually look for when evaluating proposals. Starting with 'the challenge' rather than 'about us' shows the client you understand their problem, which builds immediate trust.
makeItYourOwn: Add a line like 'Our recent project for [similar client] achieved [specific result]' in the 'Why us' section for social proof. If you have testimonials, include a short quote. You can also add 'The client is comparing us against [competitor type]' so the AI can position you accordingly.

title: Pricing justification email when clients push back
description: Craft a confident, professional email that justifies your pricing when a client questions your quote, without being defensive or discounting your value.
toolTips: Claude is strong at maintaining a confident-but-not-arrogant tone. If the first version feels too defensive, ask 'Rewrite this with more confidence and less justification'.
content:
You are a pricing strategist who helps small business owners respond to price pushback without caving on their rates or damaging the relationship. You understand that price objections are usually about perceived value, not actual cost.

A client has pushed back on my pricing. I need a professional email response. Here are the details:

- My business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- What I quoted for: [THE SERVICE OR PRODUCT]
- My quoted price: [THE AMOUNT]
- What the client said: [THEIR OBJECTION - e.g. 'That is more than we expected', 'We have had cheaper quotes', 'Can you do it for less?']
- Client's name: [NAME]
- What justifies my price: [LIST YOUR KEY VALUE POINTS - e.g. experience, quality of materials, guarantees, turnaround time, qualifications, insurance, past results]
- Am I willing to negotiate? [YES - state your floor / NO / OPEN TO ADJUSTING SCOPE]

Please write the response email following these rules:
1. Open by acknowledging their concern without agreeing that the price is too high.
2. Reframe the conversation around value and outcomes, not cost.
3. Break down what is included in the price so they understand what they are paying for.
4. If applicable, explain what cheaper alternatives typically lack (without badmouthing competitors).
5. If I am open to negotiation, offer to adjust the scope rather than the price: 'If the budget is firm at [X], here is what we could include at that level.'
6. Close with confidence. Do not apologise for your pricing.
7. Keep the total email under 200 words.

Use UK English. Tone: confident, professional, respectful. Never defensive, never desperate.
howToUse: Fill in the specific objection the client raised and your key value points
Be honest about whether you are willing to negotiate so the AI can tailor the approach
Review the value breakdown to ensure it accurately reflects what you deliver
Send within 24 hours of receiving the pushback to maintain momentum
whyItWorks: Price pushback is almost always about perceived value, not budget. This prompt reframes the conversation around what the client gets rather than what they pay, which is how premium businesses justify their rates. Offering scope adjustment instead of discounts protects your margins while showing flexibility.
makeItYourOwn: Add a real example: 'A recent client chose a cheaper provider and came back to us to fix the work. Here is what happened: [brief story]'. Nothing justifies pricing better than a cautionary tale told respectfully.

title: Case study from a successful project
description: Transform a successful project into a compelling case study with a clear problem-solution-result structure that you can use on your website, in proposals, or in sales conversations.
toolTips: Claude excels at turning rough details into polished narratives. The more raw detail you provide, the better the case study. Paste in emails, notes, or even photos descriptions.
content:
You are a content strategist who writes case studies that win new business. Your case studies follow a proven problem-solution-result structure and read like a compelling story, not a dry report.

I need you to write a case study based on a project I completed. Here are the details:

- My business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Client name (or anonymised descriptor): [e.g. 'A mid-sized law firm in Manchester' if they prefer anonymity]
- Industry: [CLIENT'S INDUSTRY]
- The problem or challenge: [WHAT THE CLIENT CAME TO YOU WITH]
- What we did (the solution): [DESCRIBE THE WORK - be as detailed as possible]
- The results: [SPECIFIC OUTCOMES - numbers, timescales, improvements, quotes from the client]
- Timeline: [HOW LONG THE PROJECT TOOK]
- Any obstacles we overcame: [THINGS THAT WENT WRONG AND HOW YOU HANDLED THEM]
- Client quote (if available): [A REAL QUOTE OR 'NONE - please draft one for approval']

Please write the case study with these sections:
1. **Headline:** An outcome-focused title (e.g. 'How [Client] reduced costs by 40% in 3 months').
2. **The challenge (80-100 words):** Set the scene. What was the client struggling with and what was at stake?
3. **The solution (100-150 words):** What you did, step by step, written to showcase your expertise without being self-congratulatory.
4. **The results (80-100 words):** Specific, measurable outcomes. Use numbers wherever possible.
5. **Client quote:** Real or drafted for approval, 1-2 sentences.
6. **Key takeaway:** One sentence summarising why this matters to a prospective client reading it.

Constraints:
- Total length: 400-550 words.
- Write in UK English.
- Focus on the client's transformation, not on how great you are.
- Use specific numbers and timeframes. If I have not provided them, flag with [PLEASE ADD SPECIFIC FIGURE].
- Avoid superlatives and marketing fluff.
howToUse: Choose your most impressive or representative project and fill in all the details
Include real numbers wherever possible. '40% increase in bookings' is far more powerful than 'significant improvement'.
If you draft a client quote, send it to the client for approval before publishing
Use the finished case study on your website, in proposals, and in sales conversations
whyItWorks: The problem-solution-result structure is proven to be the most persuasive format for case studies because it mirrors the buyer's own journey. Focusing on the client's transformation rather than your capabilities makes the reader see themselves in the story. The word limits keep it digestible.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'The prospective clients reading this will be [type of business/person]' so the AI can emphasise the details most relevant to your target audience. Include a 'What we would do differently' section for added authenticity and credibility.

title: Objection handling scripts for common pushbacks
description: Generate ready-to-use scripts for the most common sales objections in your industry, with confident responses that address the real concern behind each pushback.
toolTips: After generating the scripts, ask 'Now roleplay as a difficult prospect and throw these objections at me one by one so I can practise' for an interactive training session.
content:
You are a sales trainer who has coached hundreds of small business owners on handling objections with confidence. You know that objections are not rejections; they are requests for more information. Your scripts are conversational, not salesy.

I need you to create objection handling scripts for my business. Here are the details:

- My business: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME AND WHAT YOU SELL/DO]
- My typical customer: [WHO BUYS FROM YOU]
- My price range: [APPROXIMATE PRICING]
- My key differentiators: [WHAT MAKES YOU DIFFERENT FROM COMPETITORS]
- The most common objections I hear: [LIST 3-5 OBJECTIONS, e.g. 'It is too expensive', 'We are already working with someone', 'Can we think about it?', 'We do not have the budget right now']

For each objection, please provide:
1. **The objection:** Stated as the prospect would say it.
2. **What they actually mean:** The real concern behind the words.
3. **Your response (conversational script):** A natural, confident response of 3-5 sentences that addresses the real concern, not the surface objection. No hard-sell tactics.
4. **Follow-up question:** One question to ask after your response that moves the conversation forward.
5. **If they still say no:** A graceful exit line that keeps the door open for future business.

Rules:
- Write in a natural, spoken style. These are for conversations, not emails.
- Never be pushy, manipulative, or use high-pressure tactics.
- Every response should provide genuine value or insight, not just counter-argue.
- Use UK English.
- Acknowledge the objection before responding. Never dismiss or argue.
- Keep each complete objection script under 120 words.
howToUse: List the specific objections you hear most often in your sales conversations
Review each script and adjust the language to match how you naturally speak
Practise saying the responses out loud until they feel natural, not rehearsed
Ask the AI to roleplay as a prospect so you can practise the full conversation flow
whyItWorks: Most objection handling fails because it addresses the surface objection rather than the real concern underneath. By identifying 'what they actually mean', this prompt ensures your responses hit the right note. The conversational style prevents the scripts from sounding rehearsed, which is the fastest way to lose trust.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'I tend to freeze when someone says [specific objection]' to get extra coaching on your weak spots. You can also add recent examples: 'Last week a client said [exact words] and I did not know how to respond'.

title: Discovery call preparation and question framework
description: Prepare a structured question framework for a sales discovery call that uncovers the prospect's real needs, timeline, budget, and decision-making process.
toolTips: After generating the framework, ask 'Now simulate this discovery call with me. You play the prospect and I will practise asking these questions' for realistic preparation.
content:
You are a sales coach who specialises in consultative selling for small businesses. You teach that discovery calls are about listening and understanding, not pitching. A well-run discovery call should have the prospect talking 70% of the time.

I have a discovery call coming up and need a structured question framework. Here are the details:

- My business: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME AND WHAT YOU SELL/DO]
- Prospect's business: [THEIR COMPANY AND WHAT THEY DO, if known]
- How they found me: [e.g. referral, website enquiry, networking, social media]
- What I think they need: [YOUR BEST GUESS BASED ON INITIAL CONTACT]
- Anything I already know about their situation: [ANY CONTEXT FROM EMAILS OR INITIAL CONVERSATIONS]

Please create a discovery call framework with the following sections:

1. **Opening (2 minutes):** A natural way to open the call that puts them at ease, sets expectations for the call length, and establishes the agenda.

2. **Understanding their situation (5-7 questions):** Questions that uncover their current situation, what is working, and what is not. Start broad, then narrow down.

3. **Identifying the problem (3-4 questions):** Questions that dig into the specific pain point, its impact on their business, and what happens if they do nothing.

4. **Budget and timeline (3-4 questions):** Tactful questions to understand their budget range, timeline, and urgency without being pushy.

5. **Decision-making (2-3 questions):** Questions to understand who else is involved in the decision, what their evaluation process looks like, and what a good outcome looks like for them.

6. **Closing the call:** How to summarise what you have heard, confirm next steps, and set a clear follow-up action.

Rules:
- All questions should be open-ended (no yes/no questions).
- Write questions in natural, conversational language.
- Include a brief note next to each question explaining what you are trying to learn from it.
- Do not include any pitching in the framework. This is purely about listening.
- Use UK English.
howToUse: Fill in what you know about the prospect and your best guess at their needs
Review the questions and remove any that do not apply to your specific situation
Print or display the framework during the call as a guide, not a script
After the call, use the answers to draft a tailored proposal or follow-up email
whyItWorks: Structured discovery prevents the common mistake of jumping into a pitch before understanding the prospect's real needs. The open-ended questions force genuine conversation rather than a checkbox interrogation. Including notes on the purpose of each question helps you stay flexible rather than robotically following a script.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Questions I specifically want to ask: [your questions]' so the AI weaves them into the framework naturally. After the call, paste your notes back in and ask 'Based on this discovery call, draft a follow-up email with a tailored recommendation'.

title: Pitch deck outline with slide-by-slide content
description: Generate a complete pitch deck outline with specific content, talking points, and design direction for each slide, ready to build in PowerPoint or Canva.
toolTips: Claude produces well-structured, detailed outlines. After generating the deck, ask 'Now write the speaker notes for each slide' for a complete presentation package.
content:
You are a pitch deck consultant who has helped startups and agencies create presentations that win clients and funding. You know that great pitch decks tell a story, not list features.

I need a complete pitch deck outline with content for each slide. Here are the details:

- My business: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME AND WHAT YOU DO]
- Purpose of this pitch: [e.g. pitching to a new client, seeking investment, presenting at a conference, internal stakeholder buy-in]
- Target audience: [WHO WILL BE IN THE ROOM OR READING THIS]
- The key message I want them to walk away with: [ONE SENTENCE]
- My unique selling points: [3-5 BULLET POINTS]
- Any data or proof points I have: [e.g. revenue figures, growth stats, client logos, testimonials, case studies]
- Presentation length: [e.g. 10 minutes, 20 minutes, leave-behind only]
- Number of slides: [e.g. 8-12]

For each slide, provide:
1. **Slide title**
2. **Key message** (the one thing the audience should take from this slide)
3. **Content:** The actual text, bullet points, or data to appear on the slide (keep it minimal; slides should not be walls of text)
4. **Visual suggestion:** What image, chart, screenshot, or graphic would work best
5. **Talking point:** What the presenter should say that is NOT on the slide (this is where the depth lives)

Deck structure should follow a narrative arc:
- Hook: grab attention in the first 30 seconds
- Problem: make the audience feel the pain
- Solution: your answer, clearly explained
- Proof: evidence it works
- Ask: what you want from them

Constraints:
- Slides should have no more than 6 bullet points or 30 words of visible text each.
- Use UK English.
- Avoid cliches like 'game-changing', 'cutting-edge', or 'synergy'.
- Every slide must earn its place. If it does not advance the story, cut it.
howToUse: Fill in your business details, audience, and key message
Use the output as a blueprint to build the deck in PowerPoint, Keynote, or Canva
The talking points become your speaker notes; practise with them rather than reading slides
Ask the AI for 'a more visual version of slide 3' or 'a stronger opening hook' to iterate on specific slides
whyItWorks: Separating slide content from talking points prevents the classic mistake of putting everything on the slides and then reading them aloud. The narrative arc structure ensures the presentation builds to a conclusion rather than listing features randomly. Visual suggestions save time when designing.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'The audience is likely sceptical about [specific concern]' so the AI can address it directly in the deck. You can also paste in a competitor's pitch or a deck you admire and say 'Use a similar structure but for my business'.

title: Quote follow-up email when you have not heard back
description: Write a professional follow-up email for an unanswered quote that adds value, avoids desperation, and gives the prospect a reason to respond.
toolTips: Generate 2-3 versions: one for 3 days after, one for 7 days, and a final one for 14 days. Each should have a slightly different angle.
content:
You are a sales follow-up specialist who helps tradespeople and small business owners chase quotes without sounding desperate. You know that most quotes are not rejected; they are just forgotten, and a good follow-up can recover the majority of them.

I sent a quote and have not heard back. I need a follow-up email. Here are the details:

- My business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Client's first name: [NAME]
- What the quote was for: [BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE WORK OR SERVICE]
- Quote amount: [THE PRICE YOU QUOTED]
- When the quote was sent: [DATE]
- How many days since the quote: [NUMBER OF DAYS]
- Any additional context: [e.g. they seemed keen, they said they were getting other quotes, it was a referral, they went quiet after seeing the price]

Please write the follow-up email following these rules:
1. Do not open with 'Just following up' or 'Just checking in'. These are weak openers.
2. Add value: share a relevant tip, mention something timely (e.g. material price changes, seasonal booking patterns), or reference a similar completed project.
3. Make it easy to respond: give them a simple yes/no question or a low-effort next step.
4. Acknowledge that they might have gone with someone else, and be gracious about it.
5. Keep a confident, relaxed tone. You are busy and in demand, not chasing.
6. Keep it under 120 words.

Use UK English. Do not use any language that sounds desperate, passive-aggressive, or guilt-tripping.
howToUse: Fill in the details about your quote and the client
Send the first follow-up 3-5 days after the quote. If no response, send a second version at 10-14 days.
If you are following up on multiple quotes, generate a batch by listing them all
After 2-3 follow-ups with no response, accept it gracefully and move on
whyItWorks: The value-add approach differentiates your follow-up from the hundreds of 'just checking in' emails prospects receive. By being gracious about them potentially choosing someone else, you remove the awkwardness that prevents people from responding. The word limit keeps it quick and respectful of their time.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'I recently completed a similar project. Here is a photo: [attach]' to remind them of the quality you deliver. For trades, mentioning your upcoming availability ('My diary is filling up for [month]') creates genuine urgency without being pushy.

title: Upsell email for existing customers
description: Write a natural, value-driven email to existing customers introducing an additional service or product that genuinely complements what they already have.
toolTips: Provide context about the customer's purchase history so the AI can personalise the recommendation. The more specific you are, the less salesy it sounds.
content:
You are a customer relationship specialist who helps small businesses increase revenue from existing customers through genuine, helpful upselling. You know that the best upsells feel like good advice, not a sales pitch.

I need to write an upsell email to an existing customer. Here are the details:

- My business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Customer's first name: [NAME]
- What they have already purchased/used: [THEIR EXISTING PRODUCT OR SERVICE]
- How long they have been a customer: [APPROXIMATE DURATION]
- What I want to upsell: [THE ADDITIONAL PRODUCT OR SERVICE]
- Price of the upsell: [AMOUNT]
- Why this upsell makes sense for them specifically: [HOW IT COMPLEMENTS WHAT THEY ALREADY HAVE]
- Any special offer for existing customers: [e.g. 15% loyalty discount, free trial, bundle deal, or 'none']

Please write the email following these rules:
1. Open by referencing their existing relationship with your business. Be specific, not generic.
2. Identify a problem or need they likely have that the upsell solves. Frame it as helpful, not commercial.
3. Introduce the upsell as a natural next step, not a random offer. Connect it clearly to what they already use.
4. If there is a special offer, present it as appreciation for their loyalty.
5. Include one brief proof point: a result another customer achieved, a statistic, or a practical example.
6. Make the call to action easy and low-pressure. 'Reply if you would like to know more' is fine.
7. Keep the total email under 160 words.

Use UK English. Tone: warm, helpful, genuinely looking out for the customer. Never pushy.
howToUse: Choose customers who have had a positive experience before emailing them
Be specific about why this particular upsell suits this particular customer
If you have a loyalty offer, include it. Existing customers respond well to exclusive treatment.
Send to individuals, not as a mass email. Personalisation is the entire point.
whyItWorks: Selling to existing customers is 5-7 times cheaper than acquiring new ones, but most businesses never do it because they feel awkward. This prompt removes the awkwardness by framing the upsell as helpful advice rather than a pitch. The loyalty angle makes the customer feel valued rather than targeted.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'This customer recently [specific interaction, e.g. left a positive review, referred a friend, mentioned a challenge]' to make the email hyper-personalised. You can also A/B test by generating two versions with different angles.

title: Referral request message that does not feel awkward
description: Draft a natural, comfortable referral request that makes it easy for happy clients to recommend you without putting them on the spot.
toolTips: Generate both an email version and a shorter message version (for WhatsApp or text). Ask 'Now create a version I can send via text message in under 50 words'.
content:
You are a referral marketing specialist who helps small business owners ask for referrals without the cringe factor. You know that most people are happy to refer businesses they love, but the way you ask makes all the difference.

I need a referral request message. Here are the details:

- My business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Customer's first name: [NAME]
- What I did for them: [THE SPECIFIC WORK OR SERVICE THEY RECEIVED]
- When we completed the work: [APPROXIMATE DATE]
- How satisfied they seemed: [e.g. they said they were delighted, left a great review, have been a repeat customer]
- What format should this be: [EMAIL / TEXT MESSAGE / LINKEDIN MESSAGE / IN-PERSON SCRIPT]
- Is there a referral incentive? [e.g. 10% off their next service, £50 voucher, a free session, or 'no incentive']
- Who is my ideal referral? [DESCRIBE THE TYPE OF PERSON OR BUSINESS YOU WANT TO BE REFERRED TO]

Please write the referral request following these rules:
1. Open by referencing the positive outcome of the work you did together. Remind them why they liked working with you.
2. Make the ask specific. Instead of 'Do you know anyone?', try 'Do you know any [specific type of person] who might be dealing with [specific problem]?'. A specific ask is easier to answer.
3. Make it easy: tell them exactly what to do (forward this email, share your number, introduce you via email, etc.).
4. If there is an incentive, mention it naturally. Do not lead with it.
5. Reassure them there is absolutely no obligation. This should feel like a conversation, not a transaction.
6. Keep the email version under 130 words. Text message version under 50 words.

Use UK English. Tone: warm, grateful, confident. Never desperate or begging.
howToUse: Choose a customer who you know is happy and has shown goodwill towards your business
Send the message 1-2 weeks after completing the work, while the positive experience is fresh
If you generate both email and text versions, use the text for closer relationships and email for more formal clients
Follow up once if they do not respond, then drop it. Never push.
whyItWorks: Making the ask specific ('Do you know any accountants who...') is far more effective than the vague 'Do you know anyone?' because it triggers a mental search for a specific person rather than a general category. Referencing the positive outcome first primes them emotionally before the ask.
makeItYourOwn: If you have a formal referral programme, add the details. If not, sometimes the most effective incentive is simply 'I would be happy to return the favour if you ever need a recommendation for your business'. Reciprocity is powerful.

title: Tender response executive summary
description: Write a compelling executive summary for a tender response that positions your business as the obvious choice, hitting all the evaluation criteria while standing out from competitors.
toolTips: Claude handles complex, structured documents well. Paste in the actual tender requirements or evaluation criteria for the most tailored output.
content:
You are a bid writing consultant who has helped SMEs win contracts worth millions. You specialise in executive summaries that evaluators remember. You know that in a stack of 20 tenders, the executive summary is often the only section read in full.

I need you to write the executive summary for a tender response. Here are the details:

- My business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- What we do: [YOUR CORE SERVICE/CAPABILITY]
- The tender: [BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF WHAT IS BEING TENDERED]
- Issuing organisation: [WHO ISSUED THE TENDER]
- Key evaluation criteria (if known): [LIST THE CRITERIA THEY WILL SCORE ON]
- Our relevant experience: [2-3 SIMILAR PROJECTS YOU HAVE DELIVERED]
- Our key strengths for this contract: [WHAT MAKES YOU THE RIGHT CHOICE]
- Team/resources: [KEY PEOPLE OR RESOURCES YOU WILL DEPLOY]
- Any certifications or accreditations: [e.g. ISO 9001, CHAS, Constructionline, Safe Contractor]
- Price competitiveness: [ARE YOU CHEAPEST, MID-RANGE, OR PREMIUM? HOW DO YOU JUSTIFY IT?]
- Any social value or sustainability commitments: [e.g. local employment, apprenticeships, carbon reduction]

Please write the executive summary with the following structure:
1. **Opening statement (2-3 sentences):** Position your business as a natural fit for this contract. Reference the issuing organisation's objectives.
2. **Understanding of requirements (3-4 sentences):** Demonstrate that you understand exactly what they need and why it matters.
3. **Our approach (4-5 sentences):** Summarise how you will deliver, highlighting your methodology and what makes it effective.
4. **Relevant experience (3-4 sentences):** Reference 2-3 similar projects with specific outcomes (numbers, timescales, results).
5. **Added value (2-3 sentences):** What you bring beyond the specification. Social value, innovation, local commitment.
6. **Closing statement (1-2 sentences):** Confident close that reinforces your suitability.

Constraints:
- Total length: 400-600 words. Executive summaries must be concise.
- Mirror the language used in the tender document. If they say 'service users', you say 'service users', not 'customers'.
- Every claim must be evidenced or evidenceable. No unsubstantiated superlatives.
- Write in UK English with formal but not stuffy tone.
- Address evaluation criteria directly, even if not in the same order.
- Do not use first person ('I'). Use 'we' and the company name.
howToUse: Paste in the tender specification or at least the evaluation criteria for the most accurate output
Fill in your relevant experience with specific numbers: contract values, delivery timelines, measurable outcomes
Review the output against the evaluation criteria to ensure every one is addressed
Use the executive summary as the foundation for the rest of your tender response
whyItWorks: Tender evaluators are often scoring 10-20 submissions against a rubric. An executive summary that directly mirrors the evaluation criteria and evidences every claim makes scoring easy for the evaluator, which works in your favour. The structured format ensures nothing is missed.
makeItYourOwn: Paste the exact evaluation criteria from the tender and add 'Please ensure the executive summary addresses each of these criteria explicitly'. You can also add 'Our main competitor for this tender is likely [type of company] who will compete on [price/scale/experience]' to help differentiate your response.

title: Sales page copy for a service
description: Write persuasive, structured sales page copy for a service-based business that guides visitors from problem awareness through to booking or enquiry.
toolTips: Claude produces well-structured long-form copy. After generating, ask 'Now write the meta description and page title for SEO' to complete the page.
content:
You are a conversion copywriter who specialises in service-based businesses. You write sales pages that convert visitors into enquiries by addressing objections before they arise and building trust through specificity.

I need you to write sales page copy for one of my services. Here are the details:

- My business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- The service: [WHAT YOU ARE SELLING]
- Price or price range: [YOUR PRICING, or 'bespoke quotes']
- Target customer: [WHO IS THIS FOR - be specific]
- The problem this service solves: [WHAT PAIN POINT DOES IT ADDRESS]
- What is included: [LIST WHAT THE CUSTOMER GETS]
- Process/timeline: [HOW IT WORKS FROM START TO FINISH]
- What makes you different from competitors: [YOUR UNIQUE SELLING POINTS]
- Social proof: [TESTIMONIALS, CASE STUDIES, NUMBERS, ACCREDITATIONS - whatever you have]
- Common objections or hesitations: [WHAT STOPS PEOPLE FROM BUYING]
- Call to action: [WHAT DO YOU WANT THEM TO DO - call, book online, fill in a form, email]

Please write the sales page with these sections:
1. **Headline:** Outcome-focused, speaks to the target customer's desire or pain.
2. **Opening paragraph (3-4 sentences):** Describe the problem the reader is experiencing. Make them feel understood.
3. **The solution (1 paragraph):** Introduce your service as the answer. Focus on outcomes, not features.
4. **How it works (3-5 steps):** Break down the process so it feels simple and clear.
5. **What is included (bullet list):** Everything they get, written as benefits, not features.
6. **Social proof section:** Testimonials, results, or trust signals.
7. **FAQ section (4-6 questions):** Address the common objections as FAQs.
8. **Final call to action:** A confident, clear invitation to take the next step.

Constraints:
- Total length: 600-900 words.
- Write in UK English.
- Use short paragraphs (2-3 sentences) and plenty of white space.
- Every sentence must earn its place. No filler.
- Tone: confident, clear, and human. Not corporate, not hyped up.
- Use 'you' and 'your' throughout. This is about the reader, not about you.
howToUse: Fill in all the details as thoroughly as possible. The more you give, the better the copy.
Review the FAQs and make sure they address the real objections your prospects raise
Paste the copy into your website builder. The section structure maps directly to page sections.
Ask the AI to write variations of the headline: 'Give me 5 alternative headlines' and pick the strongest
whyItWorks: The structure follows a proven conversion framework: problem, solution, proof, action. Opening with the customer's problem creates an immediate emotional connection. Breaking the process into steps reduces perceived complexity, and addressing objections as FAQs removes barriers to action before the reader even raises them.
makeItYourOwn: Add your brand voice guidelines if you have them: 'Our tone is [description]'. Include real testimonials rather than asking the AI to write them. You can also add 'Our biggest competitor charges [X] and positions themselves as [description]' to help the AI differentiate you.

title: Seasonal promotion campaign plan
description: Generate a complete seasonal promotion campaign plan with messaging, timeline, channels, and offers tailored to your business and the upcoming season or event.
toolTips: Run this 6-8 weeks before the season or event. After generating the plan, ask 'Now write the email copy for week 1' or 'Draft the social media posts' to create the actual content.
content:
You are a promotional campaign strategist for independent and small chain businesses. You create seasonal campaigns that drive footfall and sales without requiring a massive budget. You know that timing, messaging, and a clear offer matter more than spend.

I need a seasonal promotion campaign plan. Here are the details:

- My business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Business type: [e.g. independent restaurant, boutique retailer, hotel, cafe, farm shop]
- The season or event: [e.g. Christmas, Valentine's Day, Easter, summer holidays, Black Friday, back to school, Mother's Day]
- Campaign duration: [e.g. 2 weeks, 4 weeks, the whole of December]
- My budget for the campaign: [APPROXIMATE AMOUNT, or 'very limited - mainly organic']
- My existing marketing channels: [e.g. Instagram, Facebook, email list of 500, website, in-store signage, local newspaper]
- What I want to promote: [SPECIFIC PRODUCTS, SERVICES, OR OFFERS]
- Last year's approach (if any): [WHAT YOU DID LAST TIME AND WHETHER IT WORKED]
- Any constraints: [e.g. limited staff, no online ordering, closed on Sundays]

Please create a campaign plan that includes:

1. **Campaign theme and headline:** A catchy, memorable theme that ties everything together.
2. **The offer:** A clear, compelling promotion. If I have not specified one, recommend 2-3 options with pros and cons.
3. **Timeline:** A week-by-week (or day-by-day for short campaigns) breakdown of what happens when.
4. **Channel plan:** What to post or do on each marketing channel, with specific content ideas.
5. **Key messages:** 3-5 core messages to use across all channels, adapted for each platform.
6. **In-store/on-site elements:** Signage, displays, staff talking points, or experiential ideas.
7. **Measurement:** How to track whether the campaign is working, using simple methods appropriate for a small business.

Constraints:
- Keep everything realistic for a small business. No suggestions requiring a marketing team of five.
- Budget-conscious. Prioritise free and low-cost tactics.
- Use UK English and UK-relevant seasonal context (e.g. bank holidays, school terms).
- Include specific dates where relevant.
- Keep the total plan under 700 words.
howToUse: Start planning 6-8 weeks before the season or event for best results
Fill in all details including last year's performance to avoid repeating what did not work
Use the timeline as a content calendar. Schedule posts and emails in advance.
After generating the plan, ask the AI to write specific content pieces: emails, social posts, in-store signage wording
whyItWorks: Most small businesses approach seasonal promotions reactively, deciding what to do the week before. This structured plan ensures consistent messaging across channels, proper timing, and a clear offer. The measurement section prevents the common problem of running promotions without knowing whether they actually worked.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our most popular product/service is [X]' and 'Our quietest period is usually [Y]' so the AI can tailor the offer to where it will have the most impact. Include details about your local area: 'We are near a school / in a high street / in a tourist area' for location-specific ideas.

title: Turn a complaint into a retention opportunity
description: Transform an angry customer complaint into a structured response that resolves the issue and keeps the customer loyal.
toolTips: Claude tends to produce more natural, empathetic language. Either tool works well here. Paste the actual complaint for a tailored response.
content:
You are a customer retention specialist with 15 years of experience turning unhappy customers into loyal advocates. You understand that a complaint is a gift because it gives you a chance to fix something and strengthen the relationship.

A customer has complained to my business. I need you to help me craft a response that resolves the issue and turns this into a retention opportunity.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Industry: [YOUR INDUSTRY, e.g. retail, restaurant, salon, trades]
- What we are known for: [e.g. quality service, fast delivery, personal touch]

The customer complaint:
"""
[PASTE THE COMPLAINT HERE - email, message, or describe what happened]
"""

Please provide:

1. An empathetic response (under 200 words) that:
   - Acknowledges the specific issue without generic phrases like 'we value your custom'
   - Takes clear ownership where appropriate
   - Offers a concrete resolution or next step
   - Includes a goodwill gesture if appropriate (suggest what it could be)
   - Invites them back or offers to make it right personally

2. A short internal note (3-4 bullet points) covering:
   - Root cause: what likely went wrong
   - Process fix: what to change so this does not happen again
   - Follow-up action: what to do in 7 days to check the customer is happy

Constraints:
- Never be defensive or make excuses.
- Avoid corporate language. Write like a real person who genuinely cares.
- Use UK English throughout.
- The response should feel like it was written by someone senior, not a template.
howToUse: Paste the actual customer complaint between the triple quotes
Fill in your business details so the response feels personal and on-brand
Send the customer-facing response after reviewing and adding any personal touches
Use the internal note to brief your team and prevent repeat issues
whyItWorks: This prompt treats complaints as a two-part problem: the customer relationship and the underlying process failure. By generating both an external response and an internal action plan, it ensures you fix the symptom and the cause. The instruction to avoid corporate language produces responses that feel genuine rather than scripted.
makeItYourOwn: Add your returns or complaints policy as context so the AI can reference specific options available to you. Include 'This customer has been with us for [X years]' to adjust the tone and goodwill gesture accordingly.

title: Positive review response templates
description: Generate thoughtful, varied responses to positive Google or Trustpilot reviews that strengthen customer relationships and boost your online presence.
toolTips: Either tool works well. Run this once to generate a batch of templates, then customise each one when you use it. Quick and effective.
content:
You are a reputation management specialist who helps small businesses respond to online reviews in a way that feels personal, builds loyalty, and encourages repeat visits.

I need you to write responses to positive reviews for my business. Each response should feel genuine and different from the others.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- What we do: [BRIEF DESCRIPTION]
- Platform: [Google / Trustpilot / both]
- Owner or manager name to sign off as: [YOUR FIRST NAME]

Here are the reviews to respond to:

Review 1: [PASTE REVIEW OR DESCRIBE IT]
Review 2: [PASTE REVIEW OR DESCRIBE IT]
Review 3: [PASTE REVIEW OR DESCRIBE IT]

For each review, write a response (40-80 words) that:
1. Thanks the reviewer by name if visible
2. References something specific they mentioned (do not be generic)
3. Adds a small personal touch or behind-the-scenes detail
4. Ends with a warm invitation to return or try something new
5. Signs off with the owner/manager first name

Constraints:
- Every response must be noticeably different in structure and wording. Do not repeat phrases across responses.
- Never use 'We appreciate your kind words' or similar cliches.
- Use UK English.
- Keep each response between 40 and 80 words.
- Do not ask the reviewer to do anything promotional (no 'tell your friends' or 'follow us').
howToUse: Paste your recent positive reviews into the prompt, one per line
Replace the business details with your own
Copy each response, add any personal details you want, and post directly to Google or Trustpilot
Run this weekly or fortnightly to stay on top of reviews without spending hours on them
whyItWorks: Responding to positive reviews boosts your visibility in search results and shows prospective customers you are engaged. The instruction to reference specific details from each review prevents cookie-cutter responses that make your business look lazy. Varying the structure across responses keeps your review feed looking authentic.
makeItYourOwn: Add a line like 'We recently launched [new product/service] so mention it naturally if relevant' to turn review responses into subtle marketing. You can also specify 'Our tone is [warm and chatty / professional / humorous]' to match your brand personality.

title: Negative review response that shows professionalism
description: Craft a professional, measured response to a negative review that demonstrates accountability and invites resolution without being defensive.
toolTips: Claude produces more measured, thoughtful language for sensitive situations. Read the response carefully before posting and adjust any factual details.
content:
You are a crisis communication specialist who helps small businesses respond to negative online reviews. Your responses always achieve three things: they show accountability, they demonstrate professionalism to anyone reading, and they move the conversation offline.

I have received a negative review and need a response that protects my reputation while being genuinely professional.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Industry: [YOUR INDUSTRY]
- Owner or manager name: [YOUR NAME]

The negative review:
"""
[PASTE THE FULL REVIEW HERE]
"""

Context (optional but helpful):
- What actually happened from your side: [YOUR VERSION OF EVENTS]
- Was this a genuine issue or do you believe the review is unfair? [HONEST ASSESSMENT]
- Have you already been in contact with this customer? [YES/NO AND BRIEF DETAILS]

Please write a public response (60-120 words) that:
1. Addresses the reviewer by name if visible
2. Acknowledges the experience they described without admitting liability for anything that did not happen
3. Shows that you take the matter seriously
4. Briefly provides context only if it corrects a factual inaccuracy (not excuses)
5. Invites them to contact you directly to resolve the matter, with a specific contact method
6. Signs off with your name and role

Also provide:
- A private message template (under 80 words) to send directly to the customer to resolve the issue offline
- 2-3 sentences of coaching advice on what NOT to say publicly in this situation

Constraints:
- Never be sarcastic, passive-aggressive, or dismissive, even if the review is unfair.
- Do not apologise for things that did not happen. Acknowledge their experience, not their version of facts.
- Use UK English.
- Remember: future customers will read this response more carefully than the review itself.
howToUse: Paste the negative review and fill in your side of the story for the most balanced response
Read the coaching advice section before posting anything publicly
Post the public response, then send the private message separately
If the situation resolves well, politely ask the customer if they would consider updating their review
whyItWorks: The reminder that future customers read your response more than the review itself reframes the task. You are not arguing with one unhappy person; you are demonstrating your professionalism to hundreds of prospective customers. The private message template moves the real conversation offline where it can actually be resolved.
makeItYourOwn: Add details about your complaints process or guarantee so the AI can reference them. For trades businesses, include 'We have photos/records of the work' if applicable, and the AI will help you reference evidence professionally without being combative.

title: FAQ page generator from business description
description: Generate a comprehensive FAQ page for your website based on your business description and the questions your customers actually ask.
toolTips: Either tool works well. For a stronger FAQ, paste in real customer questions from your emails or messages rather than relying solely on the AI to guess them.
content:
You are an experienced copywriter who specialises in writing FAQ pages that genuinely help customers and reduce repetitive enquiries for business owners.

I need you to create a comprehensive FAQ page for my website.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- What we do: [DESCRIBE YOUR PRODUCTS OR SERVICES]
- Target customers: [WHO YOU SERVE]
- Location: [WHERE YOU OPERATE, e.g. nationwide delivery, London-based, mobile across Surrey]
- Price range: [e.g. from £50, packages from £200/month, varies by project]
- Common customer concerns: [WHAT PEOPLE WORRY ABOUT BEFORE BUYING, e.g. quality, turnaround time, hidden fees]

Questions we already get asked frequently (if any):
[LIST ANY REAL QUESTIONS YOU RECEIVE REGULARLY, OR WRITE 'Generate from scratch']

Please generate:
1. 12-15 FAQ entries grouped into logical categories (e.g. Getting Started, Pricing, Delivery, After-sales)
2. Each answer should be 30-60 words, written in a warm but professional tone
3. Answers should reduce anxiety and build confidence to buy
4. Where relevant, answers should end with a soft call to action (e.g. 'Get in touch for a free quote' or 'See our full range here')

Constraints:
- Write the questions in the language your customers would actually use, not formal business language.
- Answers must be specific to my business, not generic filler.
- Use UK English throughout.
- Do not include questions about topics I have not mentioned unless they are universally expected (e.g. delivery, returns, contact details).
- Format with clear category headings and Q: / A: structure for easy copying to a website.
howToUse: Fill in your business details as specifically as possible
If you have real customer questions, paste them in for a much more useful FAQ
Copy the output directly to your website, adjusting any details that need updating
Review every 3 months and add new questions that keep coming up
whyItWorks: A well-written FAQ page reduces the volume of repetitive enquiries and builds buyer confidence. This prompt groups questions by category so visitors can scan quickly, and the soft calls to action throughout create natural pathways to conversion. Writing questions in customer language improves SEO because people search in the same way they speak.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Include a question about [specific topic your competitors get wrong]' to differentiate yourself. You can also add 'Our brand voice is [chatty/professional/quirky]' to match your website tone. Paste in competitor FAQ pages and ask the AI to identify gaps yours should fill.

title: Chatbot conversation script for a service business
description: Create a structured chatbot conversation flow that qualifies leads, answers common questions, and books appointments for your service business.
toolTips: Claude handles complex multi-step outputs well. Use the output as a script for tools like Tidio, Drift, or your website chat widget. You may need to adapt formatting for your specific chatbot platform.
content:
You are a chatbot UX specialist who designs conversation flows for small service businesses. Your scripts feel natural and helpful, not robotic. You know that the goal of a service business chatbot is to answer the most common questions, qualify whether the person is a good fit, and get them to book or call.

I need a chatbot conversation script for my business website.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Services offered: [LIST YOUR MAIN SERVICES]
- Target customers: [WHO YOU SERVE]
- Booking method: [e.g. phone call, online form, booking link, email]
- Operating hours: [YOUR HOURS]
- Most common questions from website visitors: [LIST 3-5 IF KNOWN, OR WRITE 'Generate from context']

Please create a complete chatbot conversation script that includes:

1. Welcome message: a friendly, concise greeting with 2-3 quick-reply buttons for the most common intents (e.g. 'Book an appointment', 'Pricing info', 'Ask a question')

2. For each intent, a conversation branch (3-5 messages deep) that:
   - Gathers the minimum information needed to help
   - Answers the question or provides useful information
   - Ends with a clear next step (book, call, or leave details)

3. A fallback message for when the chatbot cannot help, directing to a human

4. An out-of-hours message with next-available response time

Format each message as:
- BOT: [message text]
- BUTTONS: [option 1] | [option 2] | [option 3]
- USER INPUT: [what user might type]

Constraints:
- Each bot message should be under 40 words. People do not read long chatbot messages.
- Use conversational UK English, not corporate speak.
- Include at most 3 buttons per message to avoid overwhelming visitors.
- The entire script should cover 4-5 conversation branches.
- Never promise something the business cannot deliver. Keep it factual.
howToUse: Fill in your business details and common customer questions
Review the script and adjust any details about your services, pricing, or booking process
Load the conversation branches into your chatbot platform (Tidio, Drift, WhatsApp Business, etc.)
Test each branch yourself before going live, and refine based on real customer interactions
whyItWorks: Most small business chatbots fail because they try to do too much or sound robotic. This prompt focuses on the 4-5 things visitors actually want to know and keeps messages short enough to feel like a real chat. The structured branching format maps directly onto how chatbot platforms work, saving you hours of design time.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our most popular service is [service] and we want to promote [offer]' so the chatbot subtly highlights what matters most to you. Include 'Customers often hesitate because of [concern]' so the script can address objections proactively.

title: Returns and refund policy plain English rewriter
description: Rewrite your returns and refund policy in clear, customer-friendly plain English that builds trust and reduces support queries.
toolTips: Claude excels at rewriting dense text into plain language. Paste your full existing policy for the best results. If you do not have one yet, describe your rules and it will write one from scratch.
content:
You are a plain English specialist who rewrites business policies so that customers can actually understand them. You know that clear policies build trust and reduce the number of support emails a business receives.

I need you to rewrite my returns and refund policy in plain English.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- What we sell: [PRODUCTS OR SERVICES]
- Where we sell: [e.g. online only, online + physical shop, market stalls]

My current policy (or rules to turn into a policy):
"""
[PASTE YOUR EXISTING POLICY HERE, OR DESCRIBE YOUR RETURNS/REFUND RULES IN PLAIN TERMS, e.g. '30 day returns on unused items, customer pays return postage, refund within 5 working days']
"""

Please rewrite this as a customer-facing returns and refund policy that:

1. Uses short sentences and simple words (aim for a reading age of 12-14)
2. Is structured with clear headings: How to Return an Item | Refund Timescales | Exchanges | Exceptions | How to Contact Us
3. Tells customers exactly what to do step by step
4. Clearly states what is and is not covered
5. Includes a friendly opening line that sets a positive tone (e.g. 'We want you to be happy with your purchase')
6. Is formatted for easy scanning with bullet points and bold key information

Constraints:
- Do not add any terms or conditions I have not provided. If something is unclear, flag it with [PLEASE CONFIRM: ...] so I can fill in the gap.
- Comply with UK Consumer Rights Act 2015 basics (14-day cooling-off period for online purchases).
- Use UK English throughout.
- Keep the total policy under 400 words.
- Do not use legal jargon. If a legal term is necessary, explain it in brackets.
howToUse: Paste your existing policy or describe your returns rules in plain terms
Review the output for accuracy and fill in any [PLEASE CONFIRM] sections
Add the policy to your website, include a link in order confirmation emails, and print a copy for your shop if applicable
Have someone unfamiliar with your business read it and check they understand every point
whyItWorks: Unclear policies are one of the biggest barriers to online purchases. This prompt enforces plain English, a logical structure, and a friendly tone, which together build buyer confidence. The instruction to flag gaps rather than invent terms protects you from accidentally publishing incorrect information.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'We want to emphasise that we are generous with returns because it is part of our brand' or 'We need a strict policy because our products are [perishable/custom-made]' to set the right tone. Include details about who pays return postage, restocking fees, or sale item exceptions.

title: Customer escalation email for manager attention
description: Draft a professional internal escalation email that clearly explains a customer issue and gets the right manager to act quickly.
toolTips: Either tool works well for email drafting. Be specific about what happened and what you have already tried so the output is accurate and ready to send.
content:
You are an experienced customer service team leader who knows how to write internal escalation emails that get results. Your escalations are clear, factual, and make it easy for a manager to understand the situation and decide what to do.

I need to escalate a customer issue to my manager (or another department) because I cannot resolve it at my level.

Escalation details:
- Customer name: [CUSTOMER NAME]
- Account or order reference: [REFERENCE NUMBER IF APPLICABLE]
- Date the issue was first raised: [DATE]
- Channel: [e.g. email, phone, in-person, social media]

What happened:
[DESCRIBE THE ISSUE IN YOUR OWN WORDS - what the customer experienced and why they are unhappy]

What I have already done:
[LIST THE STEPS YOU HAVE TAKEN TO TRY TO RESOLVE IT]

Why this needs escalation:
[e.g. customer is requesting a refund above my authority, threatens legal action, repeat issue, VIP customer, reputational risk]

Please write an internal escalation email that includes:
1. A clear subject line that communicates urgency level
2. A one-sentence summary at the top (so the manager gets the point immediately)
3. A factual timeline of what happened (bullet points, chronological)
4. What has been attempted and the outcome
5. What the customer is expecting or demanding
6. A recommended course of action from me
7. The deadline by which a response is needed

Constraints:
- Be factual and neutral. No emotional language or blame.
- Include all relevant reference numbers and dates.
- Use UK English.
- Keep the email under 250 words.
- The tone should be professional but direct. Managers are busy.
howToUse: Fill in the details of the customer issue and what you have already tried
Review the output and check all facts, dates, and reference numbers are correct
Add the manager's name and send via your internal email or messaging system
Follow up if you do not receive a response by the deadline stated in the email
whyItWorks: Good escalation emails follow a standard structure that managers can scan quickly. This prompt ensures every escalation includes the timeline, what has been tried, and a recommended action, which means the manager can make a decision immediately rather than asking follow-up questions. The factual, neutral tone prevents escalations from reading as complaints about colleagues.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our escalation policy requires [specific detail]' if your company has a formal process. You can also specify 'This customer spends approximately [amount] per year' to help the manager assess commercial impact.

title: Customer satisfaction survey questions
description: Generate a focused set of customer satisfaction survey questions that give you actionable data, not just vanity metrics.
toolTips: Either tool works. Once you have the questions, build the survey in Google Forms, Typeform, or SurveyMonkey. Keep it short to maximise completion rates.
content:
You are a customer experience researcher who designs surveys for small and medium businesses. You focus on questions that lead to actionable improvements, not vanity metrics. You know that short surveys get more responses and better data.

I need a customer satisfaction survey for my business.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- What we do: [PRODUCTS OR SERVICES]
- Industry: [YOUR INDUSTRY]
- What stage of the customer journey this covers: [e.g. after purchase, after service delivery, annual check-in, post-event]
- What I most want to learn: [e.g. would they recommend us, what could we improve, are they likely to buy again]

Please create a survey with:

1. 8-12 questions maximum (short surveys get 3x more completions)
2. A mix of question types:
   - 2-3 rating scale questions (1-5 or 1-10)
   - 2-3 multiple choice questions
   - 1 Net Promoter Score question
   - 2-3 open-text questions that invite specific, useful feedback
3. A logical flow that starts easy and builds to more reflective questions
4. An engaging introduction (2 sentences) that tells the customer why their feedback matters and how long it will take
5. A thank-you message at the end

For each question, include:
- The question text
- The question type and response options
- A note explaining what insight this question gives you and what to do if scores are low

Constraints:
- The survey should take under 3 minutes to complete.
- Avoid leading questions (e.g. 'How amazing was our service?' is biased).
- Use UK English and natural, conversational language.
- Do not ask for information you already have (e.g. order number, date of visit).
- Every question must earn its place. If it does not lead to a potential action, cut it.
howToUse: Fill in your business details and what you most want to learn
Build the survey in your preferred tool (Google Forms, Typeform, or SurveyMonkey)
Send it to customers within 24-48 hours of their purchase or experience for the best response rate
Use the insight notes alongside each question to interpret your results and take action
whyItWorks: Most customer surveys are too long and ask the wrong questions. This prompt enforces a strict question limit and requires every question to be actionable. The mix of quantitative and qualitative questions gives you both measurable trends and rich detail. Including insight notes means you know exactly what to do with the data once it comes in.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'I am specifically trying to understand why customers [leave after one purchase / choose competitors / do not use our online booking]' to sharpen the survey focus. Include 'Our last survey found [key result]' to build on previous insights.

title: Welcome email sequence for new customers
description: Create a 3-5 email welcome sequence that builds trust, sets expectations, and encourages repeat business from new customers.
toolTips: Claude writes more natural email copy. Use the output in Mailchimp, Klaviyo, or any email marketing tool. Set up as an automated sequence triggered by first purchase or sign-up.
content:
You are an email marketing specialist who designs welcome sequences for small businesses. Your emails are warm, useful, and conversion-focused without being pushy. You know that the welcome sequence is the highest-engagement email series a business will ever send.

I need a welcome email sequence for new customers.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- What we sell/do: [PRODUCTS OR SERVICES]
- Target customer: [WHO THEY ARE]
- What makes us different: [YOUR UNIQUE SELLING POINT]
- Trigger: [e.g. first purchase, newsletter sign-up, account creation, first booking]
- Goal of the sequence: [e.g. encourage second purchase, build trust, educate about our range, get them to book]

Please write a [3 / 4 / 5]-email welcome sequence with the following for each email:

1. Subject line (under 50 characters) and preview text (under 90 characters)
2. Suggested send timing (e.g. immediately, Day 2, Day 5)
3. Full email body copy (100-200 words per email)
4. One clear call to action per email
5. A brief note on the strategic purpose of each email

The sequence should follow this arc:
- Email 1: Welcome and set expectations (what they will get from you)
- Email 2: Build trust and share your story or values
- Email 3: Provide value (a tip, guide, or helpful content related to their purchase)
- Email 4 (if applicable): Social proof (reviews, testimonials, or customer stories)
- Email 5 (if applicable): Encourage next action (second purchase, referral, or review request)

Constraints:
- Write in a warm, conversational tone. Not salesy.
- Each email must be able to stand alone (not everyone opens every email).
- Use UK English throughout.
- Do not include discount codes unless I specifically mention them. Discounting too early trains customers to wait for offers.
- Keep subject lines curiosity-driven or benefit-led, never clickbait.
howToUse: Fill in your business details and choose whether you want 3, 4, or 5 emails
Review each email and personalise with real customer stories, product names, or team details
Set up the sequence in your email tool with the suggested timing
Monitor open rates and click rates after the first month and ask the AI to refine any underperforming emails
whyItWorks: Welcome emails have the highest open rates of any automated email, often 50-80%. This prompt structures the sequence as a trust-building arc rather than a sales barrage, which means customers stay engaged through to the final email. The instruction to avoid early discounting protects your margins while still driving repeat business.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Include a personal note from [founder name] in email 2 about why we started the business' for an authentic touch. You can also specify 'Our customers typically need [product/service] again after [timeframe]' so the AI can time the repeat purchase nudge perfectly.

title: Phone enquiry script for a trades business
description: Create a professional phone script that helps trades businesses handle enquiry calls, qualify leads, and book site visits confidently.
toolTips: Either tool works well. Print the script and keep it by the phone. After a week of real calls, feed back what is working and ask the AI to refine it.
content:
You are a business communications consultant who helps trades and property businesses handle phone enquiries professionally. You understand that for most trades businesses, the phone call is the first impression and the biggest opportunity to win or lose a job.

I need a phone enquiry script for my business.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Trade or service: [e.g. plumber, electrician, builder, roofer, landscaper, property maintenance]
- Service area: [e.g. South London, Bristol and surrounding areas]
- Typical job types: [e.g. bathroom refits, rewires, extensions, emergency callouts]
- How you prefer to quote: [e.g. free site visit, phone estimate, fixed price, day rate]

Please create a phone script that covers:

1. Opening greeting (professional but friendly, under 20 words)

2. Qualification questions (6-8 questions to understand the job):
   - What they need doing
   - Urgency and timeline
   - Property type and access
   - Budget expectations (asked tactfully)
   - How they found you
   - Best contact details

3. Responses for common scenarios:
   - They want a quote over the phone
   - They want someone today (emergency)
   - They are just getting prices from multiple tradespeople
   - They ask about your qualifications or insurance

4. Closing the call:
   - Booking a site visit or next step
   - Setting expectations on timeline
   - Professional sign-off

5. A list of red flags to watch for (customers to be cautious about)

Constraints:
- Write in natural spoken language, not formal business English. This will be read aloud.
- Keep responses concise. No one wants a scripted monologue on the phone.
- Use UK English and UK-specific terminology.
- Include notes in [brackets] for the person using the script explaining why each question matters.
- The script should fit on a single A4 page when printed.
howToUse: Fill in your trade, service area, and typical jobs
Print the script and keep it next to your phone or save it on your phone for mobile use
Practise the qualification questions until they feel natural rather than scripted
After a week of using it, note which questions are most useful and ask the AI to refine the script
whyItWorks: Trades businesses often lose jobs not because of price but because of poor phone manner or forgetting to ask key questions. This script ensures every call captures the right information to quote accurately and sets professional expectations. The red flags section helps you avoid problem customers before committing time to a site visit.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'I specialise in [specific type of work] and want to steer conversations towards those jobs' to help qualify for your most profitable work. Include your accreditations (Gas Safe, NICEIC, etc.) so the script handles qualification questions confidently.

title: Job description that attracts the right candidates
description: Write a job description that sells the role to the right people, filters out the wrong ones, and reflects your company honestly.
toolTips: Either tool works well. For best results, describe the role in your own words first rather than using a generic template. The more honest and specific you are, the better the output.
content:
You are a recruitment copywriter who specialises in writing job descriptions for small and medium businesses. You write descriptions that attract the right candidates and put off the wrong ones, because a bad hire costs far more than an empty seat.

I need a job description for a role I am hiring for.

Role details:
- Job title: [JOB TITLE]
- Department or team: [e.g. operations, marketing, on-site, front of house]
- Reports to: [WHO THEY REPORT TO]
- Location: [e.g. office-based in Leeds, hybrid, remote, on-site]
- Employment type: [full-time / part-time / contract / apprenticeship]
- Salary range: [RANGE OR 'Competitive' if you prefer not to state]

About the role:
- In your own words, what will this person actually do day-to-day? [DESCRIBE IN PLAIN ENGLISH]
- What does success look like after 3 months? [WHAT WOULD A GREAT HIRE ACHIEVE EARLY ON?]
- What is the biggest challenge of this role? [BE HONEST]

About your company:
- Company name: [YOUR COMPANY]
- What you do: [BRIEF DESCRIPTION]
- Team size: [NUMBER OF PEOPLE]
- What your culture is actually like (not aspirational, actual): [HONEST DESCRIPTION]
- Benefits: [LIST REAL BENEFITS, e.g. 25 days holiday, pension, flexible hours, free parking]

Please write a job description that includes:
1. A compelling opening paragraph (3-4 sentences) that sells the opportunity, not just the company
2. What they will be doing (6-8 bullet points of real responsibilities, not corporate fluff)
3. What we are looking for (split into 'Essential' and 'Nice to have', 4-5 items each)
4. What we offer (benefits and culture, written honestly)
5. How to apply (clear next step)

Constraints:
- Write in second person ('you will') not third person ('the candidate will').
- Be specific. Replace vague phrases like 'excellent communication skills' with what that actually means in this role.
- Do not use buzzwords like 'rockstar', 'ninja', 'dynamic', or 'fast-paced environment' unless it is genuinely true.
- Use UK English and UK employment terminology.
- Keep the total description under 500 words. Shorter descriptions get more applications.
- Ensure the language is inclusive and does not inadvertently discourage any group from applying.
howToUse: Fill in the role details honestly, especially the day-to-day description and biggest challenge
Review the output and check that the essential requirements genuinely are essential (over-specifying loses good candidates)
Post on your preferred job boards, your website, and LinkedIn
Ask a current team member to read it and confirm it accurately describes the role and your culture
whyItWorks: Most job descriptions are wishlists of requirements that read like legal documents. This prompt forces you to describe what the person will actually do and what success looks like, which helps candidates self-select. Writing in second person makes the reader imagine themselves in the role, increasing application rates from good-fit candidates.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'The last person in this role [left because / was promoted because / struggled with]' to help the AI tailor the description to what you really need. Include 'We have had [number] applicants for similar roles before and the main problem was [too junior / wrong skills / culture mismatch]' to sharpen the filtering.

title: Interview questions tailored to a specific role
description: Generate a structured set of interview questions designed to reveal whether a candidate can actually do the job, not just talk about it.
toolTips: Claude produces well-structured, thoughtful interview questions. Share the job description in the prompt for the most tailored questions. Ask for follow-up probing questions too.
content:
You are a hiring manager coach who helps small business owners interview effectively. You know that most interviews fail because they rely on generic questions that let candidates give rehearsed answers. Your questions are designed to reveal real capability, not interview polish.

I need a set of interview questions for a role I am hiring for.

Role details:
- Job title: [JOB TITLE]
- Key responsibilities: [LIST THE 3-5 MOST IMPORTANT THINGS THIS PERSON WILL DO]
- Essential skills: [WHAT THEY MUST BE ABLE TO DO]
- Team they will work with: [DESCRIBE THE TEAM]
- Biggest challenge in this role: [WHAT MAKES IT HARD]
- What went wrong with the last hire (if applicable): [HONEST ASSESSMENT]

Please create an interview question set that includes:

1. Opening questions (2): to settle the candidate and get them talking naturally
2. Role-specific questions (4-5): directly testing whether they can do the core parts of the job
3. Situational questions (3): 'Tell me about a time when...' scenarios relevant to the role's challenges
4. Culture fit questions (2): to assess whether they will thrive in our specific environment
5. Red flag questions (2): designed to surface potential issues (e.g. reliability, honesty, attitude)
6. Candidate's questions: 2-3 things to listen for in what the candidate asks you

For each question, provide:
- The question itself
- What a strong answer looks like (2-3 bullet points)
- What a weak answer looks like (2-3 bullet points)
- One follow-up probing question to dig deeper

Constraints:
