- No generic questions like 'What is your greatest weakness?' unless you have a specific reason.
- Questions must be legal under UK employment law (no questions about age, family plans, health, religion, etc.).
- Use UK English.
- Write questions in conversational language, not formal interview-speak.
- Keep the total set to 13-14 questions (a 45-60 minute interview).
howToUse: Paste the job description or key responsibilities into the prompt for the most relevant questions
Print the question set and use the strong/weak answer guides during the interview to score consistently
Use the same questions for every candidate interviewing for the same role to ensure fair comparison
After hiring, review which questions best predicted success and refine for next time
whyItWorks: Structured interviews where every candidate gets the same questions are twice as predictive of job performance as unstructured chats. The strong/weak answer guides remove guesswork from evaluation and reduce bias. Including red flag questions helps you spot problems that only emerge under specific questioning.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'The last person in this role struggled with [specific issue]' so the AI creates questions that test for that exact area. Include 'Our team culture is [description] and the last bad hire was a poor fit because [reason]' to sharpen the culture questions.

title: New starter onboarding checklist
description: Create a comprehensive onboarding checklist that ensures new starters feel welcome, get productive quickly, and do not fall through the cracks.
toolTips: Either tool works. This is a one-off setup task that saves hours every time you hire. Export the checklist to a shared document or project management tool for your team.
content:
You are an HR operations specialist who designs onboarding processes for small businesses. You know that the first two weeks determine whether a new hire stays or leaves, and most small businesses lose good people because onboarding is chaotic or non-existent.

I need a new starter onboarding checklist for my business.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Industry: [YOUR INDUSTRY]
- Team size: [NUMBER OF EMPLOYEES]
- Role type being onboarded: [e.g. office-based, customer-facing, on-site/workshop, remote]
- Who manages onboarding currently: [e.g. business owner, office manager, team leader]

Please create a detailed onboarding checklist covering:

1. Before they start (1 week prior):
   - Admin and paperwork
   - Equipment and access setup
   - Team communication

2. Day one:
   - Welcome and introductions
   - Workspace and systems setup
   - Key information to cover
   - First day schedule

3. Week one:
   - Training priorities
   - Key people to meet
   - First tasks to complete
   - Daily check-in structure

4. First month:
   - Skills and knowledge milestones
   - Feedback touchpoints
   - Probation expectations
   - Social integration

5. End of probation review:
   - What to assess
   - How to structure the conversation
   - Documentation needed

Format as a checklist with tick boxes (using [ ] for each item) that can be printed or used digitally.

Constraints:
- Be practical for a small business, not a corporate HR department.
- Include UK-specific requirements (right to work checks, pension auto-enrolment, HMRC starter checklist).
- Use UK English.
- Each checklist item should be a specific action, not a vague instruction like 'make them feel welcome'.
- Keep the total checklist under 60 items across all sections.
- Note which items are legally required versus best practice.
howToUse: Fill in your business details and the type of role being onboarded
Customise the checklist by removing items that do not apply and adding any business-specific steps
Assign a named person to be responsible for each section
Save as a template in Google Docs or your project management tool and duplicate it for every new hire
whyItWorks: Poor onboarding is the top reason new hires leave within the first 6 months. This checklist breaks the process into clear phases with specific actions, so nothing gets forgotten when you are busy. Flagging legal requirements separately protects you from compliance issues, and the probation review structure gives you a framework for honest early feedback.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our new starters commonly struggle with [specific system/process/skill] in the first month' so the checklist includes extra support in that area. Include 'We have [number] of new hires per year' so the AI can suggest whether to create a more formal onboarding programme.

title: Performance review self-assessment helper
description: Help employees write a clear, evidence-based self-assessment for their performance review that showcases achievements without bragging.
toolTips: Either tool works. This is useful for managers to share with their team before review season, or to use yourself if you need to write your own self-assessment.
content:
You are a career coach who helps employees write compelling self-assessments for performance reviews. You know that most people either undersell themselves or struggle to articulate what they have achieved. Your job is to help them present their work clearly and confidently.

I need help writing my self-assessment for my upcoming performance review.

My details:
- My role: [YOUR JOB TITLE]
- How long I have been in this role: [TIME IN ROLE]
- Review period: [e.g. January to December 2025, last 6 months]
- My main responsibilities: [LIST YOUR KEY RESPONSIBILITIES]

What I achieved during the review period:
[LIST YOUR ACHIEVEMENTS, PROJECTS, WINS - even rough bullet points are fine. Include numbers where possible, e.g. 'increased sales by 15%', 'managed a team of 4', 'delivered project X on time']

Challenges I faced:
[DESCRIBE ANY DIFFICULTIES, SETBACKS, OR OBSTACLES AND HOW YOU HANDLED THEM]

Areas I want to develop:
[THINGS YOU WANT TO GET BETTER AT OR LEARN]

Please write a self-assessment that includes:

1. Opening summary (3-4 sentences): a confident overview of my performance this period
2. Key achievements (4-6 bullet points): each starting with a strong action verb and including the impact where possible (not just what I did, but why it mattered)
3. Challenges and growth (2-3 bullet points): how I handled difficulties and what I learned
4. Development goals (2-3 bullet points): areas I want to focus on next, framed positively as growth opportunities
5. Closing statement (2 sentences): forward-looking, showing ambition and commitment

Constraints:
- Write in first person (I, my, me).
- Be confident but not arrogant. State facts and impact, not opinions about how great I am.
- Use UK English.
- Quantify achievements wherever the data supports it.
- Keep the total self-assessment under 400 words.
- Do not invent achievements or exaggerate what I have provided. Work only with what I give you.
howToUse: Spend 10 minutes listing your achievements, even small ones, before running the prompt
Paste in emails, project updates, or praise from colleagues as additional evidence
Review the output and add any personal context or nuance the AI could not know
Submit as your self-assessment or use as a preparation document for the review conversation
whyItWorks: Self-assessments fail when they are either too modest or too vague. This prompt transforms rough bullet points into structured, evidence-based statements using strong action verbs. The instruction to include impact, not just activity, ensures your achievements are framed in terms your manager cares about.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'My manager values [speed/quality/initiative/collaboration] most' to tailor the emphasis. Include 'The company goals this year were [X, Y, Z]' so the AI can connect your achievements to broader business objectives, which is what gets people promoted.

title: Company sickness and absence policy writer
description: Generate a clear, fair sickness and absence policy that protects your business and treats employees with respect.
toolTips: Claude handles policy writing well and produces balanced, professional language. Always have the output reviewed by an HR professional or employment law advisor before implementing.
content:
You are an HR policy specialist who writes practical, legally aware policies for small and medium UK businesses. Your policies are clear enough for every employee to understand and robust enough to protect the business.

I need a sickness and absence policy for my company.

Company details:
- Company name: [YOUR COMPANY NAME]
- Industry: [YOUR INDUSTRY]
- Number of employees: [TEAM SIZE]
- Working pattern: [e.g. Monday to Friday office, shift-based, mixed]
- Current sick pay arrangement: [e.g. SSP only, company sick pay of X days, enhanced]
- Any specific challenges: [e.g. high absence rate, no current policy, inconsistent management of absence]

Please write a sickness and absence policy that covers:

1. Purpose and scope: who the policy applies to and why it exists
2. Reporting sickness absence:
   - Who to contact and by when
   - What information to provide
   - Rules for consecutive days and ongoing absence
3. Sick pay:
   - Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) entitlement summary
   - Company sick pay (if applicable)
   - How and when pay is processed
4. Fit notes and medical evidence:
   - When a fit note is required (after 7 calendar days per UK rules)
   - Self-certification for shorter absences
5. Return to work:
   - Return to work conversations (what they are and why they happen)
   - Phased returns where appropriate
6. Managing long-term absence:
   - Definition of long-term absence
   - Keeping in touch during absence
   - Occupational health referrals
7. Absence triggers and monitoring:
   - Bradford Factor or trigger points (explain the system used)
   - What happens when triggers are reached
8. Disability and reasonable adjustments:
   - Reference to Equality Act 2010 obligations
   - How adjustments are considered
9. Misuse of the policy:
   - What constitutes abuse and consequences

Constraints:
- Write in plain English that all employees can understand, regardless of seniority.
- Reference current UK employment law (SSP rules, fit note requirements, Equality Act 2010) but note that this is guidance, not legal advice.
- Include a disclaimer that the policy should be reviewed by a qualified HR professional or employment solicitor.
- Use UK English throughout.
- Keep the total policy under 1000 words.
- Be fair and balanced in tone. This is not a disciplinary document; it is a supportive framework.
howToUse: Fill in your company details, including your current sick pay arrangements
Review the output carefully and adjust any sections to match your actual practices
Have the policy reviewed by an HR consultant or employment solicitor before issuing to staff
Share with all employees, add to your staff handbook, and ensure managers understand the return-to-work process
whyItWorks: Most small businesses either have no absence policy or one copied from the internet that does not fit their situation. This prompt generates a UK-specific, plain English policy that covers all the essentials while being fair to employees. The structure follows ACAS guidance, which is the benchmark tribunals use to assess whether an employer acted reasonably.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'We have a particular issue with [Monday absences / short-term repeated absence / people not following the reporting process]' so the policy addresses your real challenges. Include your current Bradford Factor trigger points or absence thresholds if you already use them.

title: Candidate rejection email that leaves a good impression
description: Write a thoughtful rejection email that treats candidates with respect, protects your employer brand, and keeps the door open for future roles.
toolTips: Either tool works well. Generate templates for different stages (after application, after interview) and personalise each one before sending.
content:
You are a recruitment communications specialist who believes that how you reject candidates says more about your company than how you hire them. Every rejection email is a brand touchpoint.

I need to write a rejection email to a candidate who was not successful.

Context:
- Company name: [YOUR COMPANY NAME]
- Role they applied for: [JOB TITLE]
- Stage they reached: [e.g. application screening, first interview, final interview, assessment]
- Their name: [CANDIDATE NAME]
- Any specific positive feedback to include: [e.g. 'strong presentation skills', 'great technical knowledge', or 'None specific']
- Reason for rejection (internal, not to share in detail): [e.g. another candidate had more experience, not the right culture fit, lacked a specific skill]
- Would you consider them for future roles? [YES / NO / MAYBE]

Please write a rejection email that:

1. Thanks them genuinely for their time and effort at the specific stage they reached
2. Delivers the decision clearly and early in the email (do not bury it)
3. Includes one piece of genuine, specific positive feedback if available
4. Gives a brief, honest (but tactful) reason without being hurtful or exposing the company to legal risk
5. If appropriate, invites them to stay connected for future opportunities
6. Ends warmly and wishes them well

Constraints:
- Keep the email under 150 words. Longer rejections feel patronising.
- Do not use phrases like 'After careful consideration' or 'We had many strong candidates' as they are meaningless and everyone uses them.
- Be honest but kind. Do not give false hope if there is none.
- Do not provide detailed feedback in the email itself. Offer a follow-up call if appropriate.
- Use UK English.
- The email must not contain anything that could be construed as discriminatory under UK employment law.
howToUse: Fill in the candidate details and stage reached for a personalised email
Review the output and ensure the positive feedback is genuine (candidates can tell when it is not)
Send within 48 hours of making your decision. Speed shows respect.
For final-stage candidates, consider offering a 10-minute feedback call in addition to the email
whyItWorks: Candidates who are rejected well often recommend your company to others and may reapply for future roles. This prompt produces concise, genuine emails that avoid the cliches candidates see dozens of times during a job search. Delivering the decision early respects their time and keeps the tone honest rather than awkwardly building up to bad news.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our company personality is [warm/professional/informal]' to match the tone to your brand. For senior roles, add 'This candidate would be suitable for [alternative role or future opportunity]' so the AI can craft a more specific invitation to stay in touch.

title: Job offer letter template
description: Generate a professional, legally sound job offer letter that covers all the essentials and gets your new hire excited to start.
toolTips: Claude produces well-structured formal documents. Always have offer letters reviewed by someone with HR or legal knowledge before sending, especially for senior roles.
content:
You are an HR documentation specialist who writes offer letters for UK businesses. Your letters are professional, clear, and compliant with UK employment law requirements, while still feeling warm and welcoming.

I need a job offer letter for a new hire.

Offer details:
- Company name: [YOUR COMPANY NAME]
- Company address: [YOUR BUSINESS ADDRESS]
- Candidate name: [CANDIDATE FULL NAME]
- Job title: [JOB TITLE]
- Department/team: [IF APPLICABLE]
- Reports to: [MANAGER NAME AND TITLE]
- Start date: [PROPOSED START DATE]
- Employment type: [full-time / part-time / fixed-term contract]
- Salary: [ANNUAL SALARY OR HOURLY RATE]
- Working hours: [e.g. 37.5 hours per week, Monday to Friday 9am-5:30pm]
- Location: [WORK LOCATION]
- Probation period: [e.g. 3 months, 6 months]
- Notice period: [e.g. 1 month during probation, 3 months after]
- Holiday entitlement: [e.g. 25 days plus bank holidays]
- Pension: [e.g. auto-enrolment, enhanced contribution of X%]
- Other benefits: [LIST ANY ADDITIONAL BENEFITS]
- Conditions of offer: [e.g. satisfactory references, DBS check, right to work]

Please write a job offer letter that includes:

1. A warm congratulations opening
2. The key terms of employment (all details above, clearly laid out)
3. Conditions the offer is subject to
4. What they need to do to accept (sign and return by a specific date)
5. What to bring or do before their start date
6. A welcoming closing that expresses enthusiasm about them joining
7. Signature block for the hiring manager

Constraints:
- This is an offer letter, not a full contract of employment. Note that a full contract will follow.
- Include standard UK employment letter provisions (pension auto-enrolment mention, holiday entitlement inclusive of bank holidays if applicable).
- Use UK English and formal but approachable language.
- Include a note that the offer is subject to the candidate's right to work in the UK.
- Keep the letter to one page (under 500 words excluding header and signature block).
- Add a disclaimer that this should be reviewed by a qualified professional before use.
howToUse: Fill in all the offer details with the exact terms agreed
Review the letter carefully, especially salary, hours, and conditions
Have someone with HR knowledge check it before sending
Send alongside information about what to expect on day one to build excitement
whyItWorks: A professional offer letter sets the tone for the employment relationship and reduces the chance of misunderstandings about terms. This prompt covers all the standard UK requirements while keeping the letter warm enough that the candidate feels genuinely wanted, not like they are signing a legal document. The one-page constraint ensures clarity.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'We have a specific onboarding process that starts with [detail]' so the letter can reference what happens next. Include any company-specific benefits like 'employee discount', 'training budget', or 'team social events' to make the offer more appealing.

title: Team handbook section writer
description: Write clear, practical sections for your team or employee handbook that staff will actually read and follow.
toolTips: Claude handles long-form policy writing well. Generate one section at a time for best results, then compile into your full handbook. Always get HR or legal review before issuing.
content:
You are an employee handbook specialist who writes for small and medium UK businesses. Your handbook sections are clear, practical, and written in a tone that employees actually want to read. You avoid corporate waffle and legalese.

I need you to write a section for my team handbook.

Company details:
- Company name: [YOUR COMPANY NAME]
- Industry: [YOUR INDUSTRY]
- Team size: [NUMBER OF EMPLOYEES]
- Company culture in one sentence: [HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOUR WORKPLACE?]

Section to write:
- Topic: [e.g. annual leave, dress code, use of social media, timekeeping, workplace behaviour, mobile phone use, data protection basics, health and safety overview]
- Any specific rules or preferences: [DESCRIBE YOUR CURRENT APPROACH OR RULES FOR THIS TOPIC]
- Tone: [e.g. friendly but firm, relaxed, professional, no-nonsense]

Please write a handbook section that includes:

1. Section heading
2. A brief introduction (2-3 sentences) explaining why this section matters and the principle behind it
3. The key rules or expectations, written as clear bullet points or numbered items
4. Practical examples where helpful (e.g. 'This means if you need to swap a shift, you should...')
5. Who to speak to if they have questions
6. Any UK legal requirements relevant to this topic (clearly noted)

Constraints:
- Write for a reading age of 14-16. No jargon, no unnecessarily formal language.
- Keep the section under 350 words.
- Be specific to my business context, not generic.
- Frame rules positively where possible ('We encourage...' rather than 'You must not...').
- Use UK English throughout.
- Note any areas where I should seek professional HR or legal advice with [SEEK ADVICE].
- Do not make up rules I have not provided. If information is missing, flag it with [PLEASE SPECIFY].
howToUse: Run the prompt once for each section you need, building your handbook piece by piece
Customise each section with your actual rules and preferences before including it
Have the complete handbook reviewed by an HR consultant before distributing to staff
Give every employee a copy and ask them to confirm they have read it
whyItWorks: Most small business handbooks are either non-existent or copied from templates that do not reflect the actual workplace. This prompt generates sections that are specific to your business, written in language your team will understand, and structured consistently. The positive framing makes rules feel reasonable rather than authoritarian, which improves compliance.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'We had an issue recently where [describe situation] and we want this section to prevent that happening again' for very targeted policy writing. Specify 'Our handbook is [formal document / casual guide / somewhere in between]' to set the overall tone.

title: Apprentice training plan for trade businesses
description: Create a structured apprentice training plan that builds skills progressively and meets UK apprenticeship framework requirements.
toolTips: Claude handles structured planning well. Provide the specific apprenticeship standard or framework your apprentice is on for the most accurate output. Adjust the plan based on your training provider's requirements.
content:
You are a vocational training specialist who designs apprentice training plans for trade and manufacturing businesses. You understand that a good training plan balances on-the-job learning with structured skill development, and keeps the apprentice progressing steadily without overwhelming them.

I need a training plan for an apprentice in my business.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Trade or sector: [e.g. plumbing, electrical, carpentry, welding, CNC machining, bricklaying]
- Apprenticeship level and standard: [e.g. Level 2 Property Maintenance Operative, Level 3 Installation Electrician]
- Apprenticeship duration: [e.g. 18 months, 2 years, 3 years]
- Training provider: [NAME IF KNOWN, or 'Not yet selected']
- Apprentice's starting level: [e.g. no experience, some college, been a labourer for a year]

Please create a training plan that includes:

1. Overview: a summary of what the apprentice will be able to do by the end of their training

2. Monthly or quarterly milestones broken into phases:
   - Phase 1 (Months 1-3): Foundation skills and workplace basics
   - Phase 2 (Months 4-8): Core technical skills under supervision
   - Phase 3 (Months 9-14): Increasing independence and complexity
   - Phase 4 (remaining months): Working independently with oversight, preparing for end-point assessment
   (Adjust phases to match the apprenticeship duration I specify)

3. For each phase, list:
   - Technical skills to develop (specific to the trade)
   - Workplace skills (health and safety, customer communication, timekeeping, working in a team)
   - Off-the-job training activities (minimum 20% of working hours per UK funding rules)
   - Assessment or evidence to collect (photos, supervisor sign-offs, workbook entries)
   - Support and review structure (who checks in, how often)

4. End-point assessment preparation: what to focus on in the final 2-3 months

5. Health and safety training timeline: when each safety qualification or briefing should happen

Constraints:
- Be specific to the trade I mention. Generic training milestones are not useful.
- Reference UK apprenticeship requirements including off-the-job training hours.
- Use UK English and trade-specific terminology.
- Keep the plan practical for a small business, not a large training department.
- Note where the training provider will cover content versus what the employer needs to deliver.
- Format as a table or timeline that can be printed and pinned up in the workshop or office.
howToUse: Fill in your trade, apprenticeship standard, and duration for a tailored plan
Share the plan with your training provider and adjust to align with their curriculum
Review progress with the apprentice monthly, using the milestones as a framework
Keep evidence of training activities for apprenticeship funding audits and end-point assessment
whyItWorks: Apprentice drop-out rates are highest when there is no clear plan and the apprentice feels like cheap labour rather than a learner. This prompt creates a structured progression that gives the apprentice visible milestones and the employer a clear framework for what to teach and when. The off-the-job training structure ensures compliance with UK funding rules.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our typical projects are [describe your work]' so the AI can suggest real-world learning activities. Include 'The apprentice will be working alongside [experienced tradesperson name/role]' to build in mentoring structure. Specify any industry cards or qualifications they will need (CSCS, ECS, etc.).

title: Exit interview question set and analysis framework
description: Design a structured exit interview that uncovers the real reasons people leave and turns that insight into actionable retention improvements.
toolTips: Claude produces thoughtful, well-structured questions. After conducting several exit interviews, paste the anonymised responses back in and ask the AI to identify patterns and recommend changes.
content:
You are an HR consultant who specialises in employee retention. You know that exit interviews are one of the most valuable and most wasted data sources in any business. Most exit interviews ask surface-level questions and the answers sit in a file forever. Yours will be different.

I need an exit interview question set and a framework for analysing the results.

Company details:
- Company name: [YOUR COMPANY NAME]
- Industry: [YOUR INDUSTRY]
- Team size: [NUMBER OF EMPLOYEES]
- Average tenure of leavers recently: [e.g. under 1 year, 2-3 years, varies]
- Main concern: [e.g. too many people leaving, losing good people to competitors, not sure why people leave]

Please create:

Part 1: Exit interview question set (12-15 questions)

Organise into sections:
1. Role and expectations (did the job match what they expected?)
2. Management and support (how was their relationship with their manager?)
3. Culture and environment (what was it like to work here day-to-day?)
4. Growth and development (did they feel they were progressing?)
5. The decision to leave (what triggered the decision, and could anything have changed it?)
6. Final reflections (what would they change, and would they recommend us?)

For each question:
- Write it in conversational language (this is a conversation, not a form)
- Include a follow-up prompt to dig deeper
- Note what insight this question is designed to uncover

Part 2: Analysis framework

1. A scoring or categorisation system for tracking themes across multiple exit interviews
2. A template for a quarterly exit interview summary (what patterns are emerging, what to act on)
3. Three specific questions to ask yourself after reading 5 or more exit interviews together
4. How to present findings to leadership in a way that drives action, not defensiveness

Constraints:
- Questions must be open-ended. No yes/no questions.
- Avoid leading questions that suggest a 'right' answer.
- Use UK English.
- Be sensitive to the fact that the person is leaving and may be guarded. Questions should create safety.
- The question set should take 20-30 minutes to conduct.
- Include a note on whether exit interviews should be conducted by the leaver's direct manager (they should not).
howToUse: Conduct exit interviews with every leaver, ideally in their final week and with someone other than their direct manager
Use the question set as a guide, not a rigid script. Follow interesting threads when they appear.
After 5 or more interviews, use Part 2 to analyse patterns and create a summary for leadership
Focus on systemic issues rather than individual grievances. One person's complaint is anecdotal; five people saying the same thing is a trend.
whyItWorks: Exit interviews work when they are structured enough to compare across people and open enough to surface unexpected insights. This prompt creates both the data collection tool and the analysis framework, which is where most businesses fall down. The instruction to present findings without triggering defensiveness ensures the insights actually lead to change.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'We suspect people are leaving because of [specific issue]' so the AI can include targeted questions without making them obvious. Include 'We have recently changed [policy/manager/structure]' to explore whether recent changes are contributing to turnover.

title: Blog post outline and first draft from a topic
description: Turn any topic into a structured blog post outline and a publish-ready first draft that drives traffic and keeps readers engaged.
toolTips: Use GPT-4o or Claude Sonnet. If you have existing blog posts that reflect your brand voice, paste one in and add 'Match this tone and style' for consistency.
content:
You are an experienced content strategist and blog writer who specialises in creating SEO-friendly, engaging blog content for small and medium-sized businesses. You understand that blog posts need to serve two masters: search engines and human readers.

I need you to create a blog post outline and first draft on the following topic.

Details:
- Topic: [YOUR BLOG TOPIC]
- Target audience: [WHO ARE YOU WRITING FOR, e.g. homeowners, small business owners, parents]
- Primary keyword to target: [MAIN KEYWORD OR PHRASE]
- Desired word count: [e.g. 800, 1200, 1500 words]
- Tone of voice: [e.g. professional but approachable, conversational, authoritative]
- Call to action: [WHAT SHOULD THE READER DO AFTER READING, e.g. book a call, visit a page, download a guide]

Please deliver:

1. A blog post outline with:
   - A compelling H1 title (under 60 characters, includes the primary keyword)
   - 4-6 H2 subheadings that break the content into logical, scannable sections
   - 2-3 bullet points under each H2 summarising what that section will cover

2. A full first draft following the outline, incorporating:
   - The primary keyword naturally in the title, introduction, at least two subheadings, and conclusion
   - Short paragraphs (3-4 sentences maximum)
   - At least one bulleted or numbered list
   - An engaging opening that hooks the reader within the first two sentences
   - A clear call to action in the final paragraph

Constraints:
- Write in UK English throughout.
- Avoid filler phrases like 'In today's fast-paced world' or 'It's no secret that'.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Keep sentences under 25 words where possible for readability.
- Do not keyword-stuff. The primary keyword should appear naturally, not forced.
howToUse: Choose a topic your customers frequently ask about or search for
Fill in the placeholders with your specific details, especially the target keyword
Review the outline first and adjust any subheadings before asking the AI to redraft
Edit the first draft to add your own examples, case studies, or local knowledge
whyItWorks: Separating the outline from the draft gives you a checkpoint to steer the content before a full draft is written. The SEO constraints ensure the post has a chance of ranking, while readability rules keep it accessible for your audience.
makeItYourOwn: Add a line like 'We recently helped a client with [specific example]' so the AI can weave in a real case study. You can also specify 'Include a FAQ section at the end with 3 common questions' for extra SEO value.

title: Website homepage copy for a small business
description: Generate compelling homepage copy that clearly communicates what you do, who you serve, and why visitors should choose you.
toolTips: Claude Sonnet handles structured copywriting well. Paste your current homepage URL or text and ask 'Improve on this' for a tailored rewrite rather than starting from scratch.
content:
You are a conversion-focused website copywriter who specialises in small business homepages. You understand that most visitors decide within 5 seconds whether to stay or leave, so every word must earn its place.

I need you to write homepage copy for my business.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- What we do: [DESCRIBE YOUR CORE SERVICE OR PRODUCT IN ONE SENTENCE]
- Who we serve: [YOUR IDEAL CUSTOMER, e.g. homeowners in Surrey, independent retailers, first-time buyers]
- What makes us different: [YOUR KEY DIFFERENTIATOR, e.g. 20 years experience, same-day response, family-run]
- Location/service area: [WHERE YOU OPERATE]
- Top 3 services or products: [LIST THEM]
- Desired tone: [e.g. friendly and trustworthy, premium and polished, down-to-earth and practical]

Please write the following homepage sections:

1. Hero section: A bold headline (under 10 words), a supporting subheadline (one sentence explaining your value proposition), and a call-to-action button text.

2. 'What we do' section: 80-120 words summarising your services, written for someone who has never heard of you. Use clear, benefit-led language.

3. 'Why choose us' section: 3-4 short bullet points or cards, each with a bold heading and one supporting sentence. Focus on trust signals and differentiators.

4. Social proof section: A placeholder structure for testimonials, plus a suggested prompt I can send to customers to request good testimonials.

5. Call-to-action section: A closing paragraph (2-3 sentences) with urgency or reassurance, plus a final CTA button text.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English.
- Keep all copy scannable: short paragraphs, no walls of text.
- Avoid cliches like 'one-stop shop', 'second to none', or 'go the extra mile'.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Write for a reading age of 13-14 (clear and accessible, not dumbed down).
howToUse: Fill in every placeholder with as much detail as possible for the best output
Share the copy with your web designer or paste it directly into your website builder
Ask a friend or customer to read the hero section and tell you what they think you do. If they cannot answer clearly, refine it
Update the testimonial prompt and send it to 3-5 happy customers this week
whyItWorks: Structuring the output by homepage section mirrors how websites are actually built, making it immediately usable. The 5-second rule context ensures the AI prioritises clarity over cleverness, and banning cliches forces original, specific copy.
makeItYourOwn: If you have competitor websites you admire, paste their homepage text in and add 'I like the tone of this but need it tailored to my business'. You can also add 'Include a brief FAQ section with 3 questions' for extra homepage content.

title: Google Ads copy with headline variations
description: Create high-performing Google Ads copy with multiple headline and description variations ready to test in your campaigns.
toolTips: GPT-4o is strong at generating ad copy variations within character limits. Double-check character counts before pasting into Google Ads, as the AI occasionally goes slightly over.
content:
You are a Google Ads specialist with 10 years of experience managing PPC campaigns for small and medium-sized businesses. You write ad copy that maximises click-through rates while maintaining quality score relevance.

I need you to create Google Search Ads copy for my business.

Campaign details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Product or service being advertised: [WHAT YOU ARE ADVERTISING]
- Target keyword(s): [PRIMARY KEYWORDS YOU ARE BIDDING ON]
- Target audience: [WHO SHOULD CLICK, e.g. homeowners looking for a plumber, first-time buyers in London]
- Unique selling point: [WHAT MAKES YOU STAND OUT]
- Offer or promotion (if any): [e.g. 10% off first order, free consultation, same-day delivery]
- Landing page URL: [THE PAGE PEOPLE WILL LAND ON]
- Geographic target: [CITY, REGION, OR NATIONAL]

Please create:

1. 15 headline variations (each MUST be 30 characters or fewer, including spaces). Mix these types:
   - Keyword-focused headlines (include the target keyword)
   - Benefit-focused headlines (what the customer gains)
   - Trust-focused headlines (experience, reviews, guarantees)
   - Urgency-focused headlines (time-sensitive language)
   - Location-focused headlines (geographic relevance)

2. 4 description variations (each MUST be 90 characters or fewer, including spaces). Each should include a clear call to action.

3. 3 sitelink suggestions with a title (25 characters max) and description (35 characters max each line, 2 lines).

4. 2 callout extension suggestions (25 characters max each).

For each headline and description, show the character count in brackets after it.

Constraints:
- Strictly respect all character limits. This is non-negotiable.
- Write in UK English.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Avoid superlatives like 'best' or 'leading' unless they can be verified (Google policy).
- Include at least one headline and one description that incorporates the geographic target.
howToUse: Fill in your campaign details, paying special attention to the target keywords as these drive relevance
Check every character count before pasting into Google Ads, as the AI sometimes miscounts by 1-2 characters
Use the 15 headlines across 2-3 responsive search ads, mixing different headline types in each
Run the ads for at least 2 weeks before judging performance, then pause the lowest-performing headlines
whyItWorks: Google's responsive search ads work best with diverse headline types. By specifying five distinct headline categories, the prompt ensures variety that Google's algorithm can test. Showing character counts inline makes quality-checking faster before you paste into the platform.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our top competitor is [name] and they advertise [their main message]' so the AI can differentiate your copy. You can also add 'Our best-performing headline so far is [headline]' to give it a benchmark.

title: Facebook ad copy with audience targeting suggestions
description: Write scroll-stopping Facebook ad copy paired with detailed audience targeting recommendations for your campaign.
toolTips: GPT-4o is excellent at generating social ad copy. For best results, describe what your ideal customer is doing or feeling when they would see the ad.
content:
You are a paid social media specialist who creates high-converting Facebook and Instagram ad campaigns for local and regional businesses. You understand the Meta Ads platform inside out.

I need you to create Facebook ad copy and audience targeting recommendations for my business.

Campaign details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- What we are promoting: [SPECIFIC PRODUCT, SERVICE, EVENT, OR OFFER]
- Target customer: [DESCRIBE YOUR IDEAL CUSTOMER]
- Price point: [PRICE OR PRICE RANGE]
- Campaign objective: [e.g. website traffic, lead generation, bookings, event attendance, brand awareness]
- Geographic target: [CITY, REGION, OR RADIUS]
- Budget: [DAILY OR TOTAL BUDGET]

Please create:

1. Three ad copy variations, each with a different angle:
   - Version A: Problem-solution angle (highlight a pain point, then present your offer as the fix)
   - Version B: Social proof angle (leverage reviews, popularity, or community trust)
   - Version C: Urgency or scarcity angle (time-limited or limited availability)

   For each version, provide:
   - Primary text (125 words max, with the hook in the first line before the 'See more' cut-off)
   - Headline (40 characters max)
   - Description (30 characters max)
   - Suggested call-to-action button (from Meta's options: Learn More, Book Now, Shop Now, Sign Up, Get Offer, Contact Us)

2. Three audience targeting recommendations:
   - Audience 1: Interest-based targeting (list specific interests, behaviours, and demographics)
   - Audience 2: Lookalike suggestion (describe the source audience to build from)
   - Audience 3: Retargeting suggestion (who to retarget and with which ad version)

3. One recommendation for ad creative (image or video) that would pair well with each copy version.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English.
- Make the first line of every primary text a scroll-stopper. No soft openings.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Keep language conversational, not corporate.
- Include emoji sparingly (maximum 2 per ad variation).
howToUse: Fill in all campaign details, being as specific as possible about your target customer
Test all three ad variations simultaneously with a minimum budget of five pounds per day per ad
Set up the three audience types and run each for at least 5 days before comparing results
Kill underperformers after 7-10 days and double down on the winning combination of copy and audience
whyItWorks: Three distinct angles ensure you are not guessing what resonates with your audience. Pairing each copy variation with a targeting strategy creates testable combinations. The scroll-stopper constraint addresses the biggest challenge in social advertising: getting people to stop scrolling.
makeItYourOwn: Paste in your best-performing previous ad and add 'Beat this ad with something better'. You can also specify seasonal context like 'This is for our January sale' or 'We are launching this for the summer holidays'.

title: Product or service description that sells
description: Write benefit-driven product or service descriptions that convert browsers into buyers by focusing on what the customer gains.
toolTips: Either tool works well. If you have customer reviews mentioning what they love about the product, paste them in so the AI can echo the language real buyers use.
content:
You are an experienced e-commerce and service copywriter who specialises in writing descriptions that sell. You know that customers do not buy features; they buy outcomes, feelings, and solutions to their problems.

I need you to write a compelling product or service description.

Details:
- Product or service name: [NAME]
- What it is: [BRIEF FACTUAL DESCRIPTION]
- Price: [PRICE OR PRICE RANGE]
- Who it is for: [TARGET CUSTOMER]
- Top 3 features: [LIST THE KEY FEATURES]
- What problem it solves or what benefit it delivers: [THE MAIN REASON SOMEONE WOULD BUY THIS]
- Any proof points: [e.g. number sold, star rating, awards, testimonials, certifications]
- Where this will appear: [e.g. website product page, Amazon listing, brochure, menu]

Please write:

1. A headline (under 15 words) that leads with the primary benefit, not the product name.

2. A short description (50-75 words) for use on category pages or listings where space is limited. This must hook the reader and make them want to click through.

3. A full description (150-200 words) that follows this structure:
   - Opening line that speaks to the customer's need or desire
   - 3-4 benefit statements (each linking a feature to a tangible outcome for the customer)
   - Social proof or trust signal woven in naturally
   - A closing line with a clear call to action

4. A bullet-point feature list (5-6 bullets) formatted for quick scanning, with each bullet leading with the benefit before stating the feature.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English.
- Use 'you' and 'your' throughout. This is about the customer, not the business.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Avoid empty adjectives like 'amazing', 'fantastic', or 'incredible'. Every descriptor must be specific.
- Match the tone to where it will appear (e.g. more formal for a professional services page, more punchy for an online shop).
howToUse: Start with your best-selling or most important product or service
Fill in the proof points section with real data, as this dramatically improves credibility
Use the short description on listing pages and the full description on the dedicated product or service page
Test the headline as a social media post to see if it generates engagement
whyItWorks: Leading with benefits rather than features mirrors how customers actually make decisions. Providing multiple formats (headline, short, full, bullets) gives you copy for every context. The constraint against empty adjectives forces the AI to write with specificity, which builds trust.
makeItYourOwn: Paste in a competitor's description and add 'Write something better than this for my product'. You can also add 'Our customers frequently say [quote from a review]' to ground the copy in real customer language.

title: Press release for a business announcement
description: Write a professional press release for any business announcement, formatted to industry standards and ready to send to local media.
toolTips: Claude follows structural formatting instructions reliably. For best results, provide a quote from the business owner or director to include, as this adds authenticity.
content:
You are a PR professional who writes press releases for small and medium-sized businesses. You understand how journalists work and what makes them actually read and use a press release rather than delete it.

I need you to write a press release for the following announcement.

Details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Announcement: [WHAT YOU ARE ANNOUNCING, e.g. new product launch, office opening, partnership, award win, milestone, hire]
- Why it matters: [WHY THIS IS NEWSWORTHY, e.g. first of its kind in the region, creates 20 new jobs, addresses a gap in the market]
- Key date: [WHEN THIS IS HAPPENING OR HAPPENED]
- Quote from: [NAME AND TITLE OF SPOKESPERSON, e.g. Jane Smith, Managing Director]
- Quote content hint: [WHAT THEY WOULD WANT TO SAY, e.g. excited about growth, proud of the team, committed to the community]
- Target media: [e.g. local newspaper, trade publication, regional BBC, industry blog]
- Location: [YOUR TOWN/CITY AND COUNTY]
- Contact for media enquiries: [NAME, EMAIL, PHONE]

Please write a press release following this structure:

1. Headline: Factual, newsworthy, under 15 words. No puns or marketing language.
2. Subheadline: One sentence adding context to the headline.
3. Dateline: [CITY, Date]
4. Opening paragraph: Who, what, when, where, and why in 2-3 sentences. A journalist should be able to run this paragraph alone as a story.
5. Body paragraph 1: Expand on the details, context, and significance.
6. Quote: A natural-sounding attributed quote (not corporate-speak).
7. Body paragraph 2: Supporting information, statistics, or background.
8. Boilerplate: A standard 'About [Business Name]' paragraph (50-75 words).
9. Ends marker and media contact details.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English.
- Use the inverted pyramid structure (most important information first).
- Do not use em dashes.
- Keep the total press release under 500 words.
- Write the quote so it sounds like a real person speaking, not a corporate statement.
- Avoid superlatives and promotional language. Journalists will bin anything that reads like an advert.
howToUse: Fill in all the details, especially the 'why it matters' section, as this is what makes a journalist care
Review the quote carefully and rewrite it in your own voice if needed
Send to local newspaper editors, regional business journalists, and relevant trade publications
Follow up with a personal email to 2-3 key journalists, referencing the release and offering an interview
whyItWorks: The inverted pyramid structure matches how journalists actually read and edit press releases. By requiring the opening paragraph to work as a standalone story, the prompt ensures the key information is front and centre. Banning promotional language increases the chance a journalist will use it.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'This press release is for [specific publication name]' so the AI can tailor the tone and angle. If you have a relationship with a journalist, add 'The journalist covering this beat is interested in [angle]' for a more targeted approach.

title: Email marketing campaign sequence (4 emails)
description: Create a complete 4-email marketing sequence with strategic timing, subject lines, and conversion-focused copy for any campaign.
toolTips: Claude handles long-form structured output well. Ask for the full sequence in one go rather than one email at a time, so it can ensure the narrative arc and escalation work across all four emails.
content:
You are an email marketing strategist who has built campaigns generating six-figure revenue for e-commerce and service businesses. You understand the psychology of email sequences and how to move subscribers from interest to action over multiple touchpoints.

I need you to create a 4-email marketing campaign sequence.

Campaign details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Campaign goal: [e.g. launch a new product, promote a seasonal sale, re-engage lapsed customers, nurture new subscribers]
- Product or service being promoted: [WHAT YOU ARE SELLING]
- Target audience on this list: [WHO ARE THESE SUBSCRIBERS, e.g. past customers, newsletter sign-ups, enquiries who did not convert]
- Key offer or incentive: [e.g. 20% off, free shipping, free consultation, early access]
- Campaign duration: [e.g. send over 7 days, over 2 weeks, over 1 month]
- Brand voice: [e.g. warm and personal, professional, playful, premium]

For each of the 4 emails, provide:

1. Email purpose (one sentence explaining the strategic role of this email in the sequence)
2. Suggested send timing (e.g. Day 1, Day 3, Day 5, Day 7)
3. Subject line (under 50 characters) plus one alternative subject line for A/B testing
4. Preview text (under 90 characters)
5. Full email body copy (150-250 words per email) with:
   - A compelling opening line
   - Clear value proposition or story
   - One primary call-to-action (linked button text)
   - P.S. line where appropriate

The sequence should follow this arc:
- Email 1: Introduction and value. Build interest without hard selling.
- Email 2: Social proof and credibility. Share results, testimonials, or case studies.
- Email 3: Objection handling. Address the top reasons people hesitate.
- Email 4: Urgency and final call. Create a genuine reason to act now.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Each email must stand alone (not everyone opens every email).
- Keep paragraphs to 2-3 sentences maximum for mobile readability.
- Make subject lines curiosity-driven, not clickbait.
- Include an unsubscribe reminder note at the end of each email.
howToUse: Set up the sequence in your email platform (Mailchimp, Klaviyo, etc.) and schedule according to the suggested timing
A/B test the subject lines on Email 1 with a 50/50 split, then use the winning style for the rest
Replace any placeholder social proof with real testimonials or case studies from your business
Monitor open rates and click rates after each send, and adjust the timing if engagement drops off
whyItWorks: The four-email arc mirrors proven sales psychology: awareness, trust, objection handling, urgency. By defining each email's strategic purpose, the AI creates a sequence that builds momentum rather than repeating the same message four times. A/B test subject lines maximise open rates from day one.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our biggest customer objection is [objection]' so Email 3 directly addresses it. You can also paste in a previous email that performed well and add 'Match this voice and energy level throughout the sequence'.

title: SEO meta titles and descriptions for web pages
description: Generate optimised meta titles and descriptions for your website pages that improve click-through rates from search results.
toolTips: Either tool works. For bulk generation, list all your pages and keywords in one go and the AI will produce meta tags for all of them in a single response.
content:
You are an SEO specialist who writes meta titles and descriptions that maximise click-through rates from Google search results. You understand the balance between keyword optimisation and writing compelling copy that makes people actually click.

I need you to write SEO meta titles and descriptions for the following web pages.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Location: [YOUR TOWN/CITY]
- Industry: [YOUR INDUSTRY]

Pages to optimise (provide as many as you need):
- Page 1: [PAGE NAME] targeting [TARGET KEYWORD]
- Page 2: [PAGE NAME] targeting [TARGET KEYWORD]
- Page 3: [PAGE NAME] targeting [TARGET KEYWORD]
- Page 4: [PAGE NAME] targeting [TARGET KEYWORD]
- Page 5: [PAGE NAME] targeting [TARGET KEYWORD]

For each page, provide:

1. Meta title: Must be under 60 characters (including spaces). Include the target keyword as close to the start as possible. Include the business name only if there is space.

2. Meta description: Must be between 140-155 characters (including spaces). Include the target keyword naturally. End with a call to action or value proposition. Must make the searcher want to click.

3. Character count for each (shown in brackets).

4. A brief note explaining the strategic choice behind each title and description.

Constraints:
- Strictly respect character limits. Show exact character counts.
- Write in UK English.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Every meta description must contain a verb that prompts action (e.g. discover, get, find, learn, book, explore).
- Do not start every description with the same word. Vary the openings.
- Avoid generic phrases like 'Welcome to our website' or 'We are a leading provider'.
howToUse: List all the key pages on your website along with the primary keyword you want each page to rank for
Double-check every character count before updating your website, as the AI occasionally miscounts
Update your meta tags in your CMS (WordPress, Shopify, Squarespace) under each page's SEO settings
Revisit and update meta tags every 6 months or when you notice a page's click-through rate dropping in Google Search Console
whyItWorks: Character limits are enforced because Google truncates anything longer, wasting your carefully crafted copy. Requiring the keyword near the start of the title aligns with how Google weighs title tags. Varying description openings prevents your search results looking repetitive when multiple pages appear.
makeItYourOwn: Check your Google Search Console to find pages with high impressions but low click-through rates. These are your priority pages. Add 'This page currently gets [X] impressions but only [Y] clicks per month' for each page to help the AI understand the gap.

title: Brochure or flyer copy for a local business
description: Create print-ready brochure or flyer copy that grabs attention, communicates your value, and drives people to take action.
toolTips: Either tool works well. Ask the AI to lay out copy by section (front, inside, back) so your designer can place it easily. Specify the format (A5 flyer, tri-fold A4) for appropriately sized copy.
content:
You are a direct response copywriter who specialises in print marketing for local businesses. You know that flyers and brochures have about 3 seconds to grab attention before they end up in the recycling bin, so every word must earn its place.

I need you to write copy for a [FLYER / BROCHURE] for my business.

Details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- What we do: [YOUR CORE SERVICE OR PRODUCT]
- Target audience: [WHO WILL RECEIVE THIS, e.g. local homeowners, people passing our shop, attendees at a trade show]
- Distribution method: [e.g. letterbox drop, handed out at events, displayed in our premises, included in a mailing]
- Format: [e.g. A5 single-sided flyer, A5 double-sided flyer, A4 tri-fold brochure]
- Key message or offer: [WHAT IS THE MAIN THING YOU WANT PEOPLE TO KNOW OR ACT ON]
- Top 3 selling points: [YOUR KEY BENEFITS]
- Contact details: [PHONE, EMAIL, WEBSITE, ADDRESS]
- Call to action: [WHAT SHOULD THEY DO, e.g. call for a free quote, visit our website, use this voucher code]

Please write copy organised by section:

1. Headline: A bold, attention-grabbing statement (under 10 words). Must make the reader want to keep reading.

2. Subheadline: One sentence that expands on the headline and speaks to the reader's need.

3. Body copy: 80-120 words covering your key benefits. Written in short, punchy sentences. Address the reader directly with 'you' and 'your'.

4. Selling points: 3 short bullet points with bold lead-ins (e.g. 'Fast turnaround: most jobs completed within 48 hours').

5. Social proof: A short testimonial placeholder and a trust signal (e.g. 'Rated 4.9 on Google | 200+ five-star reviews').

6. Call to action: Clear instruction on what to do next, with all contact details formatted for print.

7. Any small print needed: [e.g. offer expiry date, terms and conditions].

Constraints:
- Write in UK English.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Keep total copy under 250 words (print space is limited).
- Every sentence must earn its place. Cut anything that does not drive the reader towards the call to action.
- Write at a reading age of 12-13. Clear, direct, no jargon.
howToUse: Choose your format (flyer or brochure) and fill in all the placeholders
Give the copy to your designer or paste it into a Canva template
Read the headline aloud. If it does not make you want to read more, ask the AI for 5 alternative headlines
Add a trackable element (unique phone number, QR code, or voucher code) so you can measure responses
whyItWorks: Organising copy by physical section makes it immediately usable for a designer. The word limit forces conciseness, which is critical for print where every square centimetre costs money. The 3-second attention rule in the brief ensures the AI prioritises impact over completeness.
makeItYourOwn: Specify your brand colours and any design preferences so the AI can suggest how to emphasise key elements. Add 'We are distributing 5,000 of these in [area] next month' for context on the audience.

title: Local SEO content for a specific area
description: Create locally optimised website content that helps your business rank in Google for searches in your target area.
toolTips: Use GPT-4o or Claude Sonnet. For best results, create one page per target area rather than one page covering multiple areas. This signals stronger relevance to Google.
content:
You are a local SEO content specialist who helps businesses rank in Google's local search results and map pack. You understand that local content needs to be genuinely useful and area-specific, not just a generic page with a town name swapped in.

I need you to write a local SEO landing page for my business targeting a specific area.

Details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- Service or product: [WHAT YOU OFFER]
- Target area: [TOWN, CITY, OR NEIGHBOURHOOD YOU WANT TO RANK FOR]
- Your base location: [WHERE YOUR BUSINESS IS BASED]
- Target keyword: [e.g. 'plumber in Reading', 'solicitor near Guildford', 'restaurant in Bath']
- What makes you relevant to this area: [e.g. you have served clients there, it is within your service radius, you have a branch there]
- Any local knowledge: [MENTION LOCAL LANDMARKS, NEIGHBOURHOODS, OR CONTEXT IF YOU HAVE IT]

Please write:

1. Page title (H1): Under 60 characters, includes the target keyword and area name.

2. Meta title and meta description: Following SEO best practices (60 chars / 155 chars).

3. Introduction (100-150 words): Establish your connection to the area. Mention specific local details (neighbourhoods, landmarks, nearby areas) to demonstrate genuine local relevance. Do not just name-drop the area repeatedly.

4. Services section (150-200 words): Describe what you offer in this area, linking services to local needs where possible (e.g. 'Many properties in [area] were built in the 1930s, which means [common issue we solve]').

5. Why choose us for [area] (100-150 words): 3-4 reasons, at least one of which is specifically about your relationship with or proximity to this area.

6. FAQ section: 3-4 questions a local searcher might ask (e.g. 'Do you cover [nearby town]?', 'How quickly can you get to [area]?'). Write full answers of 2-3 sentences each.

7. Call to action: A closing paragraph with clear next steps and contact information.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English.
- Do not use em dashes.
- The area name should appear naturally 4-6 times on the page, not more. Keyword stuffing will hurt rankings.
- Content must be genuinely useful to someone in that area, not a thin page with a location name swapped in.
- Include internal linking suggestions (e.g. 'Link to your main services page here').
- Total word count: 500-700 words.
howToUse: Create one page per target area, starting with your most commercially valuable location
Add real local knowledge after the AI generates the draft, as genuine area-specific detail is what separates good local pages from spam
Add a Google Map embed and your Google Business Profile link to the page
Build links to these pages from local directories, your Google Business Profile, and any local partnerships
whyItWorks: Google's local algorithm rewards content that demonstrates genuine local relevance. The FAQ section targets long-tail local queries that people actually search for. Limiting keyword frequency prevents over-optimisation penalties while still signalling relevance.
makeItYourOwn: Add specific details like 'We have completed [X] jobs in [area] this year' or 'Common issues we see in [area] include [problem]'. Real local data makes pages significantly more effective for both SEO and conversions.

title: Case study framework and writing template
description: Build a compelling case study from a successful project or client engagement, structured to win new business.
toolTips: Claude is strong at structuring narratives. Provide raw notes, emails, or project details and it will organise them into a coherent case study. Use Sonnet for speed.
content:
You are a B2B content writer who specialises in case studies that win new business. You understand that the best case studies follow a story arc and focus on measurable results, not self-congratulation.

I need you to create a case study based on a successful project or client engagement.

Project details:
- Client name (or anonymised descriptor): [CLIENT NAME or 'A mid-sized accountancy firm in Bristol']
- Client's industry: [THEIR INDUSTRY]
- What they came to us for: [THE PROBLEM OR NEED]
- What we did: [DESCRIBE THE WORK, SOLUTION, OR SERVICE YOU PROVIDED]
- Key results or outcomes: [MEASURABLE RESULTS, e.g. 30% increase in enquiries, project delivered 2 weeks early, saved them 15 hours per month]
- Timeline: [HOW LONG THE PROJECT TOOK]
- Client quote (if available): [A REAL QUOTE OR 'Please write a placeholder quote']
- My business name and service: [YOUR BUSINESS AND WHAT YOU DO]

Please create:

1. Case study title: Compelling, results-focused, under 15 words. Format: '[Result achieved] for [client type] through [what you did]'.

2. Executive summary: 2-3 sentences summarising the challenge, solution, and result. This should work as a standalone snippet for social media or email.

3. The challenge (100-150 words): What was the client facing? What was at stake? Make the reader empathise with the problem.

4. The solution (150-200 words): What did you do, step by step? Be specific about your approach without revealing proprietary methods. Focus on decisions and reasoning, not just actions.

5. The results (100-150 words): Lead with the most impressive metric. Include 2-3 measurable outcomes. If you have a client quote, place it here.

6. Key takeaways: 2-3 bullet points summarising what makes this case study relevant to similar prospects.

7. Call to action: A closing sentence inviting the reader to discuss how you could achieve similar results for them.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Total word count: 500-700 words.
- Write in third person ('the client', 'the team'), not first person.
- Focus on the client's transformation, not your brilliance. The client is the hero, you are the guide.
- If writing a placeholder quote, make it sound natural and specific, not generic praise.
howToUse: Choose a project where you have clear, measurable results to showcase
Fill in as much detail as possible, especially the results section
Review the case study with the client before publishing and get their approval
Publish on your website, share on LinkedIn, and include in proposals to similar prospects
whyItWorks: The challenge-solution-results structure mirrors the buyer's journey: they see themselves in the challenge, evaluate your solution, and are convinced by the results. Positioning the client as the hero (not you) makes the case study feel authentic rather than boastful.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'The prospect reading this is likely a [type of business] facing [similar challenge]' so the AI can subtly tailor the narrative to resonate with your target audience. Include any before-and-after data for maximum impact.

title: Seasonal promotion campaign for a solicitor
description: Create a targeted seasonal marketing campaign for a law firm, with messaging that connects legal services to timely client needs.
toolTips: Claude handles nuanced professional services marketing well. Specify any SRA (Solicitors Regulation Authority) advertising rules you need to follow for compliance.
content:
You are a legal marketing specialist who creates tasteful, effective seasonal campaigns for solicitors and law firms. You understand that legal marketing must balance commercial goals with professional standards and client sensitivity.

I need you to create a seasonal promotion campaign for my law firm.

Firm details:
- Firm name: [YOUR FIRM NAME]
- Practice areas to promote: [e.g. conveyancing, wills and probate, family law, commercial property, employment law]
- Season or trigger: [e.g. New Year, spring property market, back to school, tax year end, Christmas, divorce spike in January]
- Target audience: [e.g. first-time buyers, business owners, families, retirees]
- Geographic area: [YOUR REGION]
- Promotion or offer: [e.g. free initial consultation, fixed-fee will writing, reduced conveyancing quote, free guide download]
- Budget level: [LOW: organic social and email only / MEDIUM: add local Google Ads / HIGH: add print and local PR]

Please create:

1. Campaign theme and messaging: A central message that naturally connects the season to the legal service. Explain why this timing makes sense for the target audience.

2. Campaign timeline: A 4-week schedule with specific actions for each week.

3. Content pieces:
   - 3 social media posts (LinkedIn and Facebook) with full copy, each under 150 words. At least one should be educational, not promotional.
   - 1 email to existing clients and contacts (200-250 words) with subject line and preview text.
   - 1 blog post outline (title plus 4-5 section headings) that provides genuine value and subtly connects to your services.
   - 1 Google Ads suggestion (if medium or high budget): 3 headlines (30 chars max) and 2 descriptions (90 chars max).

4. Compliance notes: Flag any content that might need SRA review or could be sensitive. Note where disclaimers may be required.

5. Success metrics: 3-4 specific, measurable KPIs to track campaign performance.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Maintain a professional, trustworthy tone throughout. No hard-sell language.
- Do not make promises about legal outcomes (e.g. 'We will win your case').
- Do not trivialise serious legal matters (e.g. no 'New Year, new divorce!' messaging).
- Ensure all content could reasonably comply with SRA advertising rules.
- The educational content must be genuinely useful, not thinly veiled sales pitches.
howToUse: Choose the next seasonal moment that aligns with one of your practice areas
Fill in all details and run the prompt 8-10 weeks before the season starts to allow time for review and preparation
Have a partner or compliance officer review the output, especially the compliance notes section
Schedule the social media posts and email in advance using your marketing tools
whyItWorks: Connecting legal services to seasonal triggers makes marketing feel timely and relevant rather than random. The compliance notes section addresses the unique regulatory requirements of legal marketing. Mixing educational and promotional content builds trust before asking for action.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Last [season], we saw an increase in enquiries about [service]' to ground the campaign in real data. You can also specify 'Our firm's tone is [formal/approachable/modern]' to match your brand personality.

title: Standard operating procedure from a verbal description
description: Turn a verbal or informal process description into a clear, numbered standard operating procedure that any team member can follow.
toolTips: Claude excels at structuring messy information. Record yourself describing the process on your phone, transcribe it (even roughly), and paste it in. The AI will organise it for you.
content:
You are an operations consultant who specialises in documenting business processes. You turn informal, verbal knowledge into clear, written standard operating procedures (SOPs) that any team member can follow without additional explanation.

I am going to describe a process that currently exists only in people's heads or in rough notes. Please turn it into a professional SOP.

Process details:
- Process name: [NAME OF THE PROCESS, e.g. 'Opening the shop', 'Processing a customer order', 'End-of-day machine shutdown']
- Department or team: [WHO DOES THIS]
- How often it happens: [e.g. daily, weekly, per order, per shift]
- Who typically performs it: [JOB TITLE OR ROLE]
- Any equipment or systems needed: [LIST ANY TOOLS, SOFTWARE, OR EQUIPMENT]
- What triggers this process: [WHAT STARTS IT, e.g. 'A new order comes in', 'Start of the morning shift']
- What the end result should be: [WHAT DOES SUCCESS LOOK LIKE]

Here is my informal description of the process:
[PASTE YOUR VERBAL DESCRIPTION, ROUGH NOTES, OR TRANSCRIPTION HERE. DO NOT WORRY ABOUT IT BEING MESSY.]

Please create an SOP with the following structure:

1. Header: Process name, SOP number [leave as SOP-XXX for me to fill in], version 1.0, effective date [TODAY'S DATE], prepared by [MY NAME], approved by [LEAVE BLANK].

2. Purpose: One sentence explaining why this SOP exists.

3. Scope: Who this applies to and when.

4. Equipment/materials needed: A checklist of everything required before starting.

5. Procedure: Numbered, step-by-step instructions. Each step should be one clear action. Use sub-steps (e.g. 5a, 5b) for complex steps. Include decision points as 'IF [condition], THEN [action]' where the process branches.

6. Quality checks: 2-3 checkpoints where the person should verify they have done things correctly.

7. Troubleshooting: 3-4 common issues and what to do about them (ask me to fill these in if you cannot infer them).

8. Revision history table: A blank table with columns for Version, Date, Changes, and Approved By.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Write for someone doing this process for the first time. Assume no prior knowledge.
- Each step must start with a verb (e.g. 'Open', 'Check', 'Record', 'Notify').
- If my description is ambiguous, flag it with [CLARIFICATION NEEDED: your question] rather than guessing.
- Keep the total SOP under 800 words excluding the header and tables.
howToUse: Record yourself or a team member talking through the process, then paste the transcription into the prompt
Review the output and fill in any [CLARIFICATION NEEDED] flags
Ask the person who actually does this process to walk through the SOP and flag anything missing or wrong
Print and laminate for workstations, or save as a shared document your team can access
whyItWorks: Starting every step with a verb creates clear, actionable instructions. The [CLARIFICATION NEEDED] flags prevent the AI from guessing when information is ambiguous, which is crucial for operational accuracy. Decision points as IF/THEN statements handle process branches clearly.
makeItYourOwn: After generating the SOP, ask 'What steps am I likely missing?' and the AI will identify gaps based on common process patterns. You can also add 'This process has gone wrong before when [describe the failure]' to ensure the SOP addresses known risk points.

title: Health and safety risk assessment checklist
description: Generate a structured risk assessment checklist identifying hazards, risk levels, and control measures for your workplace or activity.
toolTips: Either tool works. This generates a starting framework, not a legally compliant document. Always have a competent person review the output against your specific site conditions and current HSE guidance.
content:
You are a health and safety consultant with 15 years of experience conducting risk assessments for UK businesses. You understand the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974, the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, and HSE's five steps to risk assessment.

I need you to create a risk assessment checklist for the following workplace or activity.

Details:
- Business or site: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME AND TYPE]
- Activity or area being assessed: [e.g. warehouse operations, kitchen, construction site, office, client home visits]
- Number of people affected: [APPROXIMATE]
- Who is at risk: [e.g. employees, contractors, visitors, members of the public]
- Any specific concerns: [e.g. working at height, manual handling, chemical exposure, lone working, young workers]
- Existing control measures already in place: [LIST ANYTHING YOU ALREADY DO]

Please create a risk assessment with the following structure:

1. Assessment header: Activity, date, assessor [LEAVE BLANK], review date (6 months from now).

2. Risk assessment table with columns:
   - Hazard (what could cause harm)
   - Who is at risk
   - Current controls (what is already in place)
   - Risk rating BEFORE additional controls (Likelihood 1-5 x Severity 1-5 = Risk Score)
   - Additional controls recommended
   - Risk rating AFTER additional controls
   - Action owner [LEAVE BLANK]
   - Target date [LEAVE BLANK]

3. Identify at least 8-12 hazards relevant to the specific activity or area I described. Be specific, not generic. For example, 'Slip hazard from grease on kitchen floor tiles' not just 'Slips'.

4. Prioritised action list: Rank the top 5 additional controls by urgency (using the risk scores).

5. Monitoring and review schedule: When and how to review this assessment.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English using UK health and safety terminology.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Reference relevant UK regulations where applicable (e.g. COSHH, PUWER, Work at Height Regulations).
- Use the standard 5x5 risk matrix. Include a key explaining the Likelihood and Severity scales.
- This is a starting framework. Include a disclaimer that this must be reviewed by a competent person and tailored to the specific site conditions.
- Be specific to the activity I described, not generic health and safety boilerplate.
howToUse: Describe your specific workplace or activity in as much detail as possible
Review every hazard in the output against your actual site conditions and add any the AI missed
Have your health and safety lead or a competent person review and sign off the assessment
Display the assessment where workers can access it and set a calendar reminder for the review date
whyItWorks: The structured risk matrix format is the UK standard that HSE inspectors expect to see. Scoring risks before and after controls demonstrates that you have thought about proportionate responses. Specific hazard descriptions (not generic ones) show a genuine assessment of your actual workplace.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'We had an incident last year involving [description]' so the AI can ensure that risk is specifically addressed. You can also add 'Our workforce includes [young workers / non-English speakers / disabled staff]' for more tailored risk considerations.

title: Quality control checklist for a production process
description: Create a detailed quality control checklist for any manufacturing or production process, with inspection points, acceptance criteria, and corrective actions.
toolTips: Claude handles structured, technical documents well. If you have an existing quality procedure or specification, paste it in for a more accurate checklist. Specify your quality management system (e.g. ISO 9001) if you have one.
content:
You are a quality assurance manager with extensive experience in manufacturing environments. You build practical QC checklists that operators can actually use on the shop floor, not theoretical documents that gather dust in a folder.

I need you to create a quality control checklist for the following production process.

Details:
- Product being manufactured: [YOUR PRODUCT]
- Production process: [DESCRIBE THE PROCESS, e.g. CNC machining of steel brackets, assembly of electronic components, food packaging line]
- Production volume: [e.g. 500 units per day, batch of 50, continuous process]
- Key quality standards or specifications: [e.g. dimensional tolerances, weight range, visual appearance, regulatory standards]
- Common defects or issues: [LIST ANY RECURRING QUALITY PROBLEMS]
- Quality system in place: [e.g. ISO 9001, IATF 16949, BRC, none]
- Who will use this checklist: [e.g. machine operators, line supervisors, QC inspectors]

Please create:

1. Checklist header: Product name, process, checklist version [1.0], date, operator name [BLANK], shift [BLANK], batch/lot number [BLANK].

2. Incoming material checks: 3-5 inspection points for raw materials or components before production starts. Each with: what to check, method of checking, acceptance criteria, and pass/fail checkbox.

3. In-process checks: 6-10 inspection points at critical stages during production. For each:
   - Check point description (specific and measurable)
   - Inspection method (visual, gauge, measurement tool, weight check)
   - Acceptance criteria (with specific tolerances or standards)
   - Frequency (every unit, every 10th unit, start of batch, etc.)
   - Pass/fail checkbox

4. Final inspection checks: 4-6 checks before the product leaves production. Include functional checks, visual inspection, packaging, and labelling.

5. Non-conformance actions: A decision tree for what to do when a check fails:
   - Minor non-conformance: [action]
   - Major non-conformance: [action]
   - Critical non-conformance: [action]
   Include who to notify and how to segregate non-conforming product.

6. Sign-off section: Spaces for operator signature, QC inspector signature, date, and any notes.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Every check must be specific and measurable. 'Check quality' is not acceptable. 'Measure outer diameter with caliper, must be 25.0mm +/- 0.1mm' is.
- Keep the checklist practical for shop-floor use. No unnecessary complexity.
- If I have not provided enough detail about tolerances or specifications, use [SPECIFY TOLERANCE] as a placeholder rather than guessing.
- Format for easy printing on A4.
howToUse: Describe your production process in as much detail as possible, including any specifications or tolerances
Review the output with your production team and fill in any [SPECIFY TOLERANCE] placeholders with your actual requirements
Trial the checklist for one week on the shop floor and note any checks that are unclear or impractical
Revise based on operator feedback and formally issue as a controlled document
whyItWorks: Requiring specific, measurable checks eliminates the subjective judgements that cause quality inconsistency. The incoming-in-process-final structure ensures quality is built in at every stage, not just checked at the end.
