The non-conformance decision tree removes ambiguity about what to do when things go wrong.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our most common customer complaint is [complaint]' so the AI can ensure the checklist specifically catches that issue. You can also add 'We are preparing for [ISO audit / customer audit]' to align the checklist with audit expectations.

title: Meeting agenda template with time allocations
description: Create a structured meeting agenda with time allocations, objectives, and action tracking to ensure productive, focused meetings.
toolTips: Either tool works. For recurring meetings, generate the template once and reuse it each week, just updating the specific agenda items.
content:
You are a productivity consultant who helps businesses run meetings that are focused, efficient, and result in clear actions. You believe that every meeting should have a purpose, a structure, and a defined outcome.

I need you to create a meeting agenda for the following.

Meeting details:
- Meeting name: [e.g. Weekly team meeting, Monthly board review, Project kick-off, Client update]
- Meeting purpose: [WHAT THIS MEETING NEEDS TO ACHIEVE]
- Date and time: [DATE AND START TIME]
- Duration: [e.g. 30 minutes, 60 minutes, 90 minutes]
- Attendees: [LIST NAMES AND ROLES]
- Meeting chair: [WHO IS RUNNING THE MEETING]
- Location or platform: [e.g. boardroom, Teams, Zoom]

Topics to cover:
- [TOPIC 1]
- [TOPIC 2]
- [TOPIC 3]
- [TOPIC 4]
- [ADD OR REMOVE AS NEEDED]

Please create a meeting agenda with:

1. Header: Meeting name, date, time, duration, location, chair, attendees.

2. Meeting objective: One clear sentence stating what success looks like at the end of this meeting.

3. Agenda items table with columns:
   - Time (start time for each item)
   - Duration (minutes allocated)
   - Agenda item
   - Type (Information / Discussion / Decision / Action review)
   - Lead (who is presenting or leading this item)
   - Objective for this item (one sentence)

4. Allocate time for each topic I listed, plus:
   - Welcome and check-in (2-3 minutes)
   - Review of previous actions (5 minutes)
   - Any other business (3-5 minutes)
   - Summary of actions and next steps (5 minutes)
   Total must equal the meeting duration I specified.

5. Pre-meeting preparation: A bullet list of what attendees should read, prepare, or bring.

6. Action tracker template: A table with columns for Action, Owner, Deadline, and Status.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English.
- Do not use em dashes.
- If the topics I listed cannot fit in the time available, flag this and suggest which items to defer or shorten.
- Every agenda item must have a clear objective. 'Discuss marketing' is not acceptable. 'Decide on Q2 marketing budget allocation' is.
- Allocate at least 60% of meeting time to Discussion and Decision items, not Information items.
- Keep the agenda to one page when printed.
howToUse: Fill in your meeting details and topics at least 24 hours before the meeting
Send the agenda to all attendees the day before so they can prepare
Use the agenda during the meeting to keep discussions on track and on time
Complete the action tracker during the meeting and circulate within 1 hour of the meeting ending
whyItWorks: Typing agenda items forces clarity about what you actually need from the meeting. Time allocations prevent one topic consuming the entire session. Requiring objectives for each item means every discussion has a defined endpoint, reducing rambling.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our meetings tend to overrun because [reason]' so the AI can build in safeguards. For recurring meetings, ask 'Create a reusable template I can fill in weekly' for a version with permanent structure and changeable content.

title: Project brief template for client work
description: Create a comprehensive project brief that aligns your team and your client on scope, deliverables, timeline, and expectations before work begins.
toolTips: Claude handles structured documents with multiple sections well. Paste in any client emails or notes from discovery calls and ask the AI to extract the key details into the brief format.
content:
You are a project manager who has delivered hundreds of client projects across creative, professional services, and consultancy environments. You know that most project failures stem from poor briefing, not poor execution.

I need you to create a project brief for a client engagement.

Project details:
- Client name: [CLIENT NAME]
- Project name: [PROJECT NAME]
- Your business: [YOUR BUSINESS AND WHAT YOU DO]
- Project type: [e.g. website redesign, brand identity, marketing campaign, consulting engagement, software build]
- Client's stated goal: [WHAT THE CLIENT SAYS THEY WANT]
- Background: [WHY ARE THEY DOING THIS NOW, WHAT TRIGGERED IT]
- Budget: [BUDGET RANGE OR 'TBC']
- Timeline: [DESIRED COMPLETION DATE OR DEADLINE]
- Key stakeholders on client side: [NAMES AND ROLES]
- Key team members on your side: [NAMES AND ROLES]

Please create a project brief with these sections:

1. Project overview: 3-4 sentences summarising the project, its purpose, and the desired outcome. Written clearly enough that someone new to the project could understand it immediately.

2. Objectives: 3-5 specific, measurable objectives. Each should complete the sentence 'This project will be successful if...'

3. Scope:
   - In scope: Specific deliverables and activities included.
   - Out of scope: Things explicitly NOT included (this prevents scope creep).
   - Assumptions: Key assumptions the project plan is based on.

4. Deliverables table: Columns for Deliverable, Description, Format, Due Date, and Approval Required From.

5. Timeline and milestones: Key phases with estimated dates. Include:
   - Kick-off
   - Key review or feedback points
   - Draft delivery
   - Revision rounds (specify how many are included)
   - Final delivery
   - Project close

6. Roles and responsibilities: A RACI-style table (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) for key activities.

7. Communication plan: How and when you will communicate (e.g. weekly status email, fortnightly calls, shared project board).

8. Risks and dependencies: 3-4 risks that could derail the project, with mitigation for each.

9. Sign-off: Space for client and project lead signatures, date, and version number.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Keep the brief under 1,200 words. A brief should be brief.
- Write in a professional but plain English style. No jargon or buzzwords.
- Where I have not provided enough information, use [TO BE CONFIRMED] rather than inventing details.
- The out-of-scope section must include at least 3 items, even if I do not specify them (use common scope creep items for the project type).
howToUse: Fill in the project details from your discovery call or client emails
Review the out-of-scope section carefully as this is your scope creep protection
Walk through the brief with the client in a kick-off meeting rather than just emailing it
Get the client to sign the brief before starting work. This is your reference point if scope disputes arise
whyItWorks: Explicitly defining what is out of scope is the single most effective way to prevent scope creep. The RACI table eliminates confusion about who does what. Measurable objectives give you a clear definition of success to refer back to when the project feels like it is drifting.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our last project with this client had issues with [problem]' so the AI can build in preventive measures. You can also paste in the client's original email or RFP and ask 'Extract the brief details from this'.

title: Staff handover documentation template
description: Create a comprehensive handover document for when a team member is leaving, going on leave, or transitioning responsibilities.
toolTips: Either tool works. Start early: ask the departing or transitioning staff member to brain-dump everything they know, paste it in, and let the AI organise it into a structured handover document.
content:
You are an HR and operations specialist who helps businesses manage staff transitions without losing critical knowledge. You understand that poor handovers cost businesses time, money, and customer relationships.

I need you to create a handover document for a staff transition.

Handover details:
- Person handing over: [NAME AND JOB TITLE]
- Reason for handover: [e.g. leaving the company, going on maternity leave, changing roles, going on holiday for 3 weeks]
- Person taking over: [NAME AND JOB TITLE, or 'TBC']
- Handover date: [WHEN THE TRANSITION HAPPENS]
- Return date (if applicable): [DATE OR 'N/A']
- Department: [DEPARTMENT OR TEAM]

Key areas of responsibility:
- [RESPONSIBILITY 1]
- [RESPONSIBILITY 2]
- [RESPONSIBILITY 3]
- [ADD MORE AS NEEDED]

Please create a handover document with:

1. Overview: Who is handing over to whom, when, and why. Include the handover period dates.

2. Daily responsibilities: A day-by-day or task-by-task breakdown of what needs to happen. For each task:
   - What it is
   - When it needs doing (day/time/frequency)
   - How to do it (step-by-step if the person taking over is unfamiliar)
   - Where to find what you need (files, systems, keys, passwords reference)
   - Who to contact if something goes wrong

3. Weekly and monthly responsibilities: Tasks that do not happen daily but must not be forgotten. Include deadlines.

4. Key contacts: A table of important internal and external contacts relevant to this role. Columns: Name, Organisation/Department, Role, Phone, Email, Context (why you deal with them).

5. Ongoing projects or commitments: Current status, next steps, and deadlines for anything in progress.

6. Systems and access: List of all systems, tools, and platforms used, with login information references (not passwords directly, but where to find them or who to ask).

7. Known issues or watch-outs: Things that are likely to come up, tricky situations, or things that have gone wrong before.

8. Emergency or escalation contacts: Who to call if something urgent or unusual happens.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Write for someone who has never done this role before. Do not assume knowledge.
- Include timestamps or deadlines wherever possible. 'Do the stock check' is not helpful. 'Complete the stock check by 2pm every Friday using the spreadsheet in [shared drive location]' is.
- Keep the document practical and scannable with clear headings and bullet points.
- Do not include actual passwords. Use '[See password manager]' or '[Ask line manager]' references.
howToUse: Have the person handing over fill in as much detail as possible, including things they think are obvious
Sit the incoming person down with the document and walk through it together during the handover period
Ask the incoming person to add notes and flag gaps during their first week
Save the document as a living reference that gets updated as the role evolves
whyItWorks: Structuring by frequency (daily, weekly, monthly) matches how people actually plan their work. Including 'known issues' captures the tribal knowledge that is usually lost when someone leaves. The 'who to contact if something goes wrong' line for every task prevents the new person from being stuck.
makeItYourOwn: Have the departing person record a screen-share video of their key processes and reference the video timestamps in the document. Add 'The biggest mistake a new person could make in this role is [mistake]' to ensure the handover addresses critical risks.

title: Incident report template and analysis guide
description: Create a structured incident report and root cause analysis template for workplace incidents, near misses, or safety events.
toolTips: Claude handles structured compliance documents well. If you have an existing incident report, paste it in and ask for improvements. For RIDDOR-reportable incidents, always consult HSE guidance directly.
content:
You are a health and safety professional with experience in incident investigation and root cause analysis in UK workplaces. You understand RIDDOR requirements, HSE investigation frameworks, and the importance of learning from incidents to prevent recurrence.

I need you to create an incident report template and analysis guide for my workplace.

Workplace details:
- Business type: [YOUR BUSINESS TYPE]
- Industry: [YOUR INDUSTRY]
- Number of employees: [APPROXIMATE]
- Types of incidents most likely: [e.g. slips and trips, machinery injuries, falling objects, chemical exposure, vehicle collisions, near misses]
- Existing H&S system: [e.g. ISO 45001, internal procedures, none]
- Reporting requirements: [e.g. RIDDOR, client reporting obligations, insurance reporting]

Please create:

1. Incident report form with the following fields:
   - Incident reference number [AUTO-FORMAT: INC-YYYY-XXX]
   - Date and time of incident
   - Date and time reported
   - Location (specific area within the site)
   - Reported by (name, role, contact)
   - Injured person(s) details (name, role, employer if contractor)
   - Incident type (checkboxes: Injury, Near Miss, Dangerous Occurrence, Property Damage, Environmental)
   - Severity classification (First Aid, Medical Treatment, Lost Time, Major Injury, Fatality)
   - Description of what happened (narrative section with prompts: What were they doing? What went wrong? What was the immediate outcome?)
   - Immediate actions taken
   - Witnesses (names and contact details)
   - Photographs taken (Yes/No)
   - RIDDOR reportable (Yes/No/Unsure)

2. Root cause analysis section using the '5 Whys' method:
   - What happened (the event)
   - Why 1: immediate cause
   - Why 2: underlying cause
   - Why 3: systemic cause
   - Why 4: organisational cause
   - Why 5: root cause
   Include an example relevant to my industry to demonstrate how to use this method.

3. Corrective actions table with columns: Action, Owner, Priority (Immediate/Short-term/Long-term), Deadline, Status, Verified By.

4. RIDDOR decision guide: A simple flowchart in text form to help determine whether an incident needs reporting under RIDDOR.

5. Lessons learned section: Prompts for what went wrong, what went right (response), what will change, and how the change will be communicated.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Use UK health and safety terminology and reference UK legislation.
- Include a note that RIDDOR-reportable incidents must be reported within the legal timeframe (10 days for most, immediately for fatal and specified injuries).
- Design the form to be completable by a supervisor, not just a H&S professional.
- Include a confidentiality note about data handling.
- Keep the total template under 1,000 words excluding examples.
howToUse: Customise the template for your specific workplace by adding site-specific locations and common incident types
Train supervisors on how to complete the form, especially the 5 Whys analysis
Keep blank copies readily accessible at all work locations
Review completed reports monthly to identify trends and recurring root causes
whyItWorks: The 5 Whys method prevents the common mistake of stopping at the immediate cause (e.g. 'they slipped') and drives investigation to the root cause (e.g. 'no cleaning schedule exists for that area'). The RIDDOR decision guide reduces the risk of missing a legal reporting requirement.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our last three incidents involved [types]' so the AI can tailor the form to your most common scenarios. You can also specify 'We need to report incidents to [client/principal contractor/insurer] as well' for additional reporting sections.

title: Daily site report for a construction foreman
description: Create a structured daily site report template that captures everything a construction foreman needs to record each day on site.
toolTips: Either tool works. Generate the template once and print copies, or paste it into a form builder (Google Forms, Microsoft Forms) for digital completion on site.
content:
You are a construction project manager with 20 years of experience on UK building sites. You know what information is critical to capture each day and how to structure site reports that are useful for project managers, quantity surveyors, and dispute resolution.

I need you to create a daily site report template for a construction foreman.

Project details:
- Project type: [e.g. residential new build, commercial fit-out, refurbishment, civil engineering, housing development]
- Project name: [PROJECT NAME]
- Client: [CLIENT NAME]
- Main contractor: [YOUR COMPANY OR MAIN CONTRACTOR]
- Project duration: [e.g. 6 months, 12 months]
- Typical number of workers on site: [APPROXIMATE]

Please create a daily site report template with:

1. Header section:
   - Project name and reference number
   - Date
   - Report number [DAY-XXX]
   - Weather conditions (morning and afternoon): temperature, precipitation, wind, and whether weather affected work (Yes/No, with explanation)
   - Site hours (start and finish)
   - Completed by (name and role)

2. Labour record:
   - Table with columns: Trade/Company, Number of Operatives, Hours Worked, Area/Activity
   - Total labour count for the day
   - Notable absences or shortages

3. Plant and equipment:
   - Table with columns: Plant/Equipment, Supplier, Hours Used, Area/Activity, Any Issues
   - Deliveries and collections

4. Work completed today:
   - Structured by area or zone of the site
   - Brief description of activities and progress
   - Reference to programme/schedule activities where possible

5. Materials:
   - Deliveries received (what, quantity, supplier, condition on arrival)
   - Materials used
   - Materials wasted or damaged (with reason)

6. Health and safety:
   - Site inductions completed (number)
   - Safety observations or issues noted
   - Incidents or near misses (reference to incident report if applicable)
   - Toolbox talk delivered (topic, attendees)

7. Visitors:
   - Table with columns: Name, Company, Purpose of Visit, Time In, Time Out

8. Issues, delays, and variations:
   - Any delays and their cause (weather, labour, materials, design, client instruction)
   - Verbal instructions received from client, architect, or engineer (record exactly what was said and by whom)
   - Variations or changes to scope (formal and informal)

9. Progress photographs:
   - Checklist prompt: Photos taken of [key areas] (Yes/No)
   - Photo reference numbers

10. Foreman's notes:
    - Free text section for anything that does not fit above
    - Items requiring attention tomorrow
    - Information or decisions needed from the project manager

11. Sign-off: Foreman signature, date, project manager review signature, date.

Constraints:
- Write in UK English using UK construction terminology.
- Do not use em dashes.
- Design for quick completion on site (a foreman should be able to fill this in within 15-20 minutes at the end of the day).
- The 'Issues, delays, and variations' section is critical for contractual records. Include a note reminding the foreman that verbal instructions must be recorded accurately as they may be needed for claims or disputes.
- Keep the template to 2 pages when printed.
- Include a footer note: 'This report forms part of the project record. Complete accurately and submit daily.'
howToUse: Print a stack of blank templates or set up a digital form the foreman can complete on a tablet
Brief the foreman on the importance of the 'Issues, delays, and variations' section for contractual protection
Review reports daily and follow up on any issues, delays, or decisions needed
File reports chronologically as part of the project record. These are valuable in disputes and final account negotiations
whyItWorks: Capturing labour, plant, weather, and delays daily creates a contemporaneous record that is extremely powerful in contractual disputes and extension of time claims. The structured format ensures nothing is missed even when the foreman is tired at the end of a long day on site.
makeItYourOwn: Add your company logo and project-specific zones or areas to the template. If you use a specific programme (e.g. Asta Powerproject, MS Project), add 'Reference programme activity numbers in the work completed section' for easier progress tracking.

title: Competitor analysis framework builder
description: Build a structured competitor analysis comparing your business against key rivals across the dimensions that matter most.
toolTips: Use GPT-4o or Claude Sonnet. If you have competitor websites or reports, paste key excerpts directly into the chat for richer analysis.
content:
You are a senior business strategist with 20 years of experience in competitive intelligence. I need you to build a comprehensive competitor analysis framework for my business.

Here are my details:
- My business: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME AND WHAT YOU DO]
- Industry: [YOUR INDUSTRY]
- My key competitors (list 2-5): [COMPETITOR NAMES]
- What I compete on most: [e.g. price, quality, service, speed, convenience, expertise]

Please create:

1. A comparison matrix table with these columns: Feature/Factor | My Business | [Competitor 1] | [Competitor 2] | [Competitor 3]. Include rows for: pricing model, target customer, unique selling point, online presence strength, key weakness, customer perception, and market positioning.

2. A "where we win" summary listing 3-5 genuine advantages I hold over each competitor, with specific reasoning.

3. A "where we lose" summary listing 2-3 areas where each competitor outperforms us, with honest assessment.

4. Three strategic recommendations based on gaps or opportunities you identify from the analysis.

Constraints:
- Be brutally honest, not flattering. I need real insight, not reassurance.
- Use UK English throughout.
- Base your analysis only on information I provide or that is commonly known. Flag any assumptions clearly with [ASSUMPTION].
- Keep the total output under 800 words excluding the table.
howToUse: Fill in your business details and list your main competitors
If you have information about competitor pricing, reviews, or marketing, paste it in after the prompt for better accuracy
Review the output and challenge anything that feels off by asking 'Why did you rate Competitor X higher on service?'
Use the strategic recommendations as a starting point for your next planning session
whyItWorks: Assigning the role of a strategist with competitive intelligence expertise ensures the AI thinks critically rather than superficially. The instruction to be 'brutally honest' overrides the AI's tendency to be agreeable, and flagging assumptions keeps the output grounded.
makeItYourOwn: Add a line like 'I recently lost a customer to [Competitor X] because [reason]' to give the AI real-world context. You can also paste in competitor Google reviews or website copy for a more informed analysis.

title: Market research summary generator
description: Turn raw market data, articles, or observations into a clear, actionable market research summary for decision-making.
toolTips: Claude handles long documents well. Paste in full articles, reports, or data sets and it will synthesise them effectively. Use Sonnet for speed.
content:
You are a market research analyst who specialises in distilling large amounts of information into clear, decision-ready summaries for business owners who do not have time to read full reports.

I am going to provide you with raw market data, articles, notes, or observations. Please synthesise everything into a structured market research summary.

My business context:
- Business type: [YOUR BUSINESS TYPE]
- Location/market: [YOUR GEOGRAPHIC MARKET]
- What I am trying to decide: [e.g. whether to launch a new product, enter a new area, adjust pricing]

Please structure your summary as follows:

1. Executive summary (3-4 sentences maximum, written for someone with 60 seconds to read)
2. Key market trends (bulleted, with supporting evidence from the data I provided)
3. Customer demand signals (what the data suggests customers want or are moving towards)
4. Competitive landscape snapshot (who is active, what they are doing)
5. Risks and watch-outs (2-3 things that could go wrong)
6. My recommendation (a clear, direct statement on what I should do, with reasoning)

Constraints:
- Write in plain English, no jargon or marketing speak.
- Clearly distinguish between facts from the data and your inferences. Label inferences as [INFERENCE].
- Use UK English and UK market conventions.
- Keep the total summary under 600 words.

Here is my raw data/information:
[PASTE YOUR DATA, ARTICLES, NOTES HERE]
howToUse: Gather your raw information: this could be articles, survey results, notes from customer conversations, or industry reports
Paste everything after the prompt, even if it is messy or unstructured
Replace the business context placeholders so the AI tailors the summary to your situation
Use the recommendation section as a starting point for discussion with your team or partners
whyItWorks: The structured output format ensures every summary covers the same ground, making it easy to compare across different research exercises. Labelling inferences separately from facts prevents the AI from presenting guesses as certainties, which is critical for business decisions.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'I am leaning towards [option A] but want you to challenge that assumption' to get a more balanced analysis. You can also specify 'Focus especially on [price sensitivity / demographic trends / seasonal patterns]' to sharpen the output.

title: SWOT analysis with strategic actions
description: Generate a thorough SWOT analysis that goes beyond listing items and recommends concrete strategic actions for each quadrant.
toolTips: Either tool works well here. For a follow-up, ask 'Now prioritise these actions by impact and effort' to create a quick action plan.
content:
You are a business strategy consultant who has helped hundreds of SMEs conduct meaningful SWOT analyses that actually lead to action. Most SWOTs gather dust because they list things without saying what to do about them. Yours will be different.

Please conduct a SWOT analysis for my business.

Business details:
- Business name: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME]
- What we do: [BRIEF DESCRIPTION]
- Industry: [YOUR INDUSTRY]
- Number of employees: [APPROXIMATE SIZE]
- How long we have been operating: [YEARS IN BUSINESS]
- Our biggest challenge right now: [MAIN CHALLENGE]
- Our biggest recent win: [RECENT SUCCESS]

For each SWOT quadrant, provide:
- 4-6 specific items (not generic statements like 'strong brand' but specific ones like 'established reputation with local builders since 2015')
- For each item, a one-line strategic action: what to do about it

Format the output as four clear sections:
- Strengths: how to leverage each one
- Weaknesses: how to mitigate or fix each one
- Opportunities: how to capture each one
- Threats: how to defend against each one

Finish with a 'Top 3 priorities' section that identifies the three most impactful actions from across all four quadrants.

Constraints:
- Be specific to my business context, not generic.
- Use UK English.
- Avoid consultant jargon. Write as if explaining to the business owner directly.
- Keep the total output under 700 words.
howToUse: Fill in your business details honestly, including challenges and wins
The more specific you are about your situation, the more tailored the output will be
Share the Top 3 priorities with your team or business partner as a conversation starter
Revisit every quarter by running the prompt again with updated details
whyItWorks: Traditional SWOTs fail because they are descriptive, not prescriptive. By requiring a strategic action for every single item, this prompt forces the AI to think about implications rather than just categorisation. The 'Top 3 priorities' section prevents analysis paralysis.
makeItYourOwn: Add context about upcoming changes like 'We are considering [expansion/new hire/price increase]' so the SWOT reflects your current decision-making needs. You can also add competitor information for a more outward-looking analysis.

title: Customer persona creator from real data
description: Build detailed, actionable customer personas based on your actual customer data rather than guesswork.
toolTips: Claude is excellent at synthesising qualitative data. Paste in customer reviews, support emails, or survey responses for the richest personas.
content:
You are a customer research specialist who builds data-driven personas that marketing and sales teams can actually use. You avoid fictional fluff and focus on real behavioural patterns.

I need you to create [NUMBER, e.g. 2-3] detailed customer personas for my business based on the information I provide.

My business:
- What we sell/do: [YOUR PRODUCT OR SERVICE]
- Price range: [YOUR PRICING]
- How customers typically find us: [e.g. Google search, referrals, social media, walk-ins]
- Our best customers (describe them): [WHO BUYS MOST / STAYS LONGEST / REFERS OTHERS]
- Our worst-fit customers (describe them): [WHO COMPLAINS, LEAVES, OR IS UNPROFITABLE]

For each persona, include:
1. Name and demographic snapshot (age range, location type, job/life situation)
2. What problem they are trying to solve when they come to us
3. What they care about most (e.g. price, speed, quality, trust, convenience) ranked in order
4. How they make buying decisions (impulse, research-heavy, recommendation-driven, etc.)
5. Their biggest objection or hesitation before buying
6. The message that would resonate most with them (one sentence)
7. Where to reach them (channels, platforms, physical locations)
8. Lifetime value indicator: high, medium, or low, with reasoning

Constraints:
- Ground every persona in the data I provide. Do not invent characteristics that are not supported by my input.
- Make personas distinct from each other, not slight variations of the same person.
- Use UK English and UK-relevant references.
- Flag anything you are inferring rather than drawing directly from my data with [INFERRED].
- Keep each persona under 250 words.
howToUse: Gather what you know about your customers: reviews, emails, sales data, survey responses, or even your own observations
Paste this information after the prompt for richer, more accurate personas
Use the 'message that would resonate most' line directly in your marketing copy or ads
Print the personas and keep them visible when making marketing or product decisions
whyItWorks: Most AI-generated personas are generic fiction. This prompt anchors everything to real data by requiring you to provide customer information and flagging inferences. The ranked priorities and objection fields make these immediately useful for marketing and sales, not just decorative documents.
makeItYourOwn: Paste in 5-10 customer reviews (positive and negative) as additional context. The AI will spot patterns you might miss. You can also add 'Include a persona for a customer segment we should be targeting but currently are not' to discover growth opportunities.

title: Trend analysis report for your industry
description: Identify and analyse the key trends shaping your industry with a focus on practical implications for your business.
toolTips: For the most current trends, use ChatGPT with browsing enabled or paste in recent articles. Claude's knowledge has a training cutoff, so provide recent data where possible.
content:
You are an industry analyst who writes trend reports for business owners, not academics. Your reports are practical, direct, and focused on what business owners should actually do in response to trends.

Please write a trend analysis report for my industry.

Context:
- My industry: [YOUR INDUSTRY]
- My business size: [e.g. sole trader, 5 employees, 50 employees]
- My geographic focus: [e.g. local, regional, UK-wide, international]
- Time horizon I care about: [e.g. next 6 months, next 1-2 years, next 5 years]

Structure the report as follows:

1. Industry snapshot: 3-4 sentences on where the industry stands right now.

2. Top 5 trends: For each trend, provide:
   - Trend name and one-line description
   - Evidence: what is driving this trend
   - Impact on small businesses specifically (not just large corporates)
   - Action to take: one concrete thing a business my size could do in response
   - Urgency rating: Act now / Watch closely / Long-term consideration

3. One contrarian view: a trend that everyone talks about but may be overhyped, with your reasoning.

4. Summary: three sentences on what to focus on first.

Constraints:
- Write for a busy business owner, not a boardroom. No jargon.
- Be specific to my industry and business size. Do not give advice that only applies to large corporations.
- Use UK English and UK market context.
- Flag anything based on general knowledge rather than recent data with [GENERAL KNOWLEDGE].
- Keep the total report under 900 words.
howToUse: Fill in your industry, business size, and geographic focus
For more current analysis, paste in 2-3 recent industry articles after the prompt
Pay special attention to the 'Act now' urgency items and discuss them with your team
Run this prompt quarterly to stay on top of shifts in your market
whyItWorks: The urgency rating system forces the AI to prioritise rather than just list everything as important. The contrarian view section counteracts the AI's tendency to agree with conventional wisdom, giving you a more balanced perspective. Specifying your business size ensures advice is actually relevant to you.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'I have been hearing a lot about [specific trend] and want your honest assessment of whether it matters for a business like mine' to get targeted analysis on something specific. You can also paste in a competitor's recent blog post or announcement to analyse what trends they are betting on.

title: Survey data interpreter and insight extractor
description: Turn raw survey results into clear insights and actionable recommendations without needing a data analyst.
toolTips: Claude handles large data pastes well. Export your survey results as CSV or plain text and paste them directly. For very large datasets, summarise the key statistics first.
content:
You are a research analyst who specialises in interpreting survey data for small businesses. You translate numbers into stories and stories into actions.

I have conducted a survey and need help understanding what the results mean for my business.

Survey context:
- Purpose of the survey: [e.g. customer satisfaction, employee engagement, market research]
- Who responded: [e.g. existing customers, website visitors, staff]
- Number of responses: [TOTAL RESPONSES]
- When it was conducted: [DATE/PERIOD]

Please analyse the data I provide and deliver:

1. Top 3 headlines: the most important findings, written as clear statements (e.g. '72% of customers would recommend us, but only 45% would describe our pricing as fair')

2. What is going well: 3-4 positive findings with supporting data points

3. What needs attention: 3-4 areas of concern, ranked by severity, with supporting data

4. Surprising findings: anything in the data that is unexpected or contradicts common assumptions

5. Recommended actions: 5 specific things to do based on the findings, ordered by priority

6. What to ask next: 2-3 follow-up questions the survey raises that you should investigate further

Constraints:
- Only draw conclusions supported by the data. Do not speculate beyond what the numbers show.
- Present percentages and numbers clearly. Avoid vague language like 'most people' when you can say '68%'.
- Use UK English.
- Write for a business owner, not a statistician. Explain any statistical concepts in plain language.
- Keep the total analysis under 700 words.

Here are my survey results:
[PASTE YOUR SURVEY DATA / RESULTS HERE]
howToUse: Export your survey results from your survey tool (Google Forms, Typeform, SurveyMonkey etc.)
Paste the results after the prompt, including the questions and response data
If you have open-text responses, include those too as they often contain the richest insights
Use the 'Recommended actions' section to create a simple action plan
whyItWorks: Survey data often sits unanalysed because business owners lack time or confidence to interpret it. This prompt provides a complete analytical framework that separates positive findings from concerns, surfaces surprises, and ends with clear actions. The 'what to ask next' section ensures continuous improvement.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Compare these results to our last survey in [month/year] where [key finding]' to get trend analysis. You can also add 'I expected [specific outcome] - tell me if the data supports or contradicts this' for hypothesis testing.

title: Industry report summariser and action finder
description: Condense a lengthy industry report into key takeaways and specific actions relevant to your business.
toolTips: Claude can process very long documents. Paste in the full report text for best results. If the report is a PDF, copy and paste the text content.
content:
You are a business advisor who reads industry reports so your clients do not have to. Your job is to extract what actually matters for small and medium businesses and ignore the filler.

I am going to give you an industry report. Please read it and provide:

1. One-paragraph summary (under 80 words): what this report is about and why it matters.

2. Five key takeaways: the most important findings, written as clear, specific bullet points. Include the data point or statistic that supports each one.

3. What this means for my business: translate the findings into implications for a business like mine.
   - My business: [BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF YOUR BUSINESS]
   - My size: [NUMBER OF EMPLOYEES OR REVENUE BAND]

4. Three things to do: specific, actionable steps I should take based on this report, starting with the most urgent.

5. One thing to ignore: identify something in the report that sounds important but is not relevant or actionable for a business my size.

Constraints:
- Be direct and concise. Cut through any waffle in the original report.
- Use UK English.
- Only reference data and findings from the report I provide. Do not add external information.
- Keep the total output under 500 words.

Here is the report:
[PASTE THE REPORT TEXT HERE]
howToUse: Copy the text from your industry report (from a PDF, email, or website)
Paste the full report text after the prompt
Fill in your business description so the takeaways are personalised
Share the output with your team to save everyone from reading the full report
whyItWorks: The 'one thing to ignore' instruction is key. It signals to the AI that not everything in the report is relevant, encouraging critical rather than summarising thinking. Tying takeaways to your specific business size prevents generic advice that only applies to larger organisations.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'I am particularly interested in [topic area]' to focus the summary. If you receive multiple reports, run each through this prompt and then ask 'Now compare the key findings from these three summaries and identify any contradictions or common themes'.

title: Pricing research and positioning analysis
description: Research and analyse pricing in your market to find the right position for your product or service.
toolTips: For current competitor pricing, use ChatGPT with browsing or paste in screenshots/data from competitor websites. The AI cannot check live prices without browsing access.
content:
You are a pricing strategist who helps small businesses find the right price point. You understand that pricing is about positioning and psychology, not just covering costs.

I need help analysing pricing in my market and determining where I should position myself.

My business details:
- What I sell: [YOUR PRODUCT OR SERVICE]
- Current price: [YOUR CURRENT PRICE / PRICE RANGE]
- My costs per unit/job: [APPROXIMATE COST TO DELIVER]
- My target customer: [WHO YOU ARE SELLING TO]
- How I am currently positioned: [e.g. budget, mid-range, premium, luxury]
- Competitors and their prices (if known): [LIST WHAT YOU KNOW]

Please provide:

1. Pricing landscape map: place me and my competitors on a simple value-for-money scale (budget to premium) with brief reasoning.

2. Price sensitivity analysis: based on my target customer, how sensitive are they likely to be to price changes? What non-price factors matter most to them?

3. Three pricing strategies I could consider:
   - For each: the approach, the price point or change, the expected impact, and the risk.
   - Include at least one option I probably have not considered.

4. Pricing psychology tips: 3 specific tactics relevant to my product/service (e.g. anchoring, bundling, charm pricing, tiered pricing).

5. Recommendation: which strategy I should pursue and why, given my business context.

Constraints:
- Be specific with numbers. Do not just say 'increase your prices'. Say 'consider moving from [X] to [Y]'.
- Use UK English and UK market context (GBP, UK consumer behaviour).
- Acknowledge where you are making assumptions and mark them [ASSUMPTION].
- Keep the total output under 800 words.
howToUse: Fill in your pricing details as accurately as possible, including costs
List competitor prices if you know them, or describe their positioning if not
Test the recommended strategy on a small segment before rolling out broadly
Re-run this prompt every 6-12 months as market conditions change
whyItWorks: Most business owners set prices based on costs or gut feeling. This prompt forces a strategic approach by considering competitors, customer psychology, and positioning together. Requiring specific numbers rather than vague advice makes the output immediately actionable.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'I last changed my prices in [date] and customers reacted by [description]' to give the AI real pricing history. You can also add 'I am considering [specific change] and want you to stress-test it' for a focused analysis.

title: Local area analysis for estate agents and service businesses
description: Create a detailed local area profile covering demographics, competition, footfall, and opportunity for any UK location.
toolTips: Use ChatGPT with browsing enabled for the most current local data. Alternatively, paste in ONS data, local council reports, or Rightmove/Zoopla area guides.
content:
You are a location analyst who helps businesses understand local markets. You combine demographic data, economic indicators, and local knowledge to create area profiles that drive business decisions.

Please create a local area analysis for the following location.

Details:
- Location: [TOWN, CITY, OR POSTCODE AREA]
- My business type: [WHAT YOU DO]
- Why I need this analysis: [e.g. considering opening here, already based here and want to understand the market, evaluating for a client]
- Radius of interest: [e.g. the high street, 5-mile radius, the whole town]

Please cover:

1. Area overview: population estimate, demographic profile (age, income level, family composition), and character of the area in 3-4 sentences.

2. Economic profile: employment types, average household income, property price indicators, and economic health signals.

3. Competition snapshot: what similar businesses exist in the area, how saturated the market is, and any obvious gaps.

4. Footfall and accessibility: transport links, parking, high street health, and any major employers or attractors nearby.

5. Opportunities: 3 specific opportunities for a business like mine in this area.

6. Risks: 3 specific risks or challenges to be aware of.

7. Verdict: a clear recommendation on whether this area is strong, moderate, or weak for my type of business, with reasoning.

Constraints:
- Use UK-specific data sources and context.
- Be honest about the limitations of your knowledge. State your data cutoff and flag anything that may have changed recently.
- Avoid generic descriptions. Be as specific to this location as possible.
- Use UK English throughout.
- Keep the total output under 800 words.
howToUse: Specify the exact location you want analysed, ideally with a postcode or clear area name
Paste in any local data you have (council reports, census data, Rightmove area guides) for more accurate results
For estate agents: use this to create area guides for clients or assess new instruction opportunities
For retailers/hospitality: use this before signing a lease to validate your location choice
whyItWorks: Location decisions are some of the most expensive a business makes. This prompt structures the analysis to cover every factor that matters, from demographics to competition to accessibility. The honest verdict at the end forces a clear conclusion rather than leaving you to interpret ambiguous data.
makeItYourOwn: For estate agents, add 'Also include: average property prices by type, rental yields, and recent development activity in the area'. For food and drink businesses, add 'Include information about the local dining scene, average spend per head, and any upcoming events or developments that could affect footfall'.

title: Supplier comparison matrix builder
description: Create a structured comparison of potential suppliers to make confident, evidence-based procurement decisions.
toolTips: Paste in supplier quotes, website information, or review data for the most accurate comparison. Either tool works well for this structured task.
content:
You are a procurement specialist who helps small businesses evaluate and compare suppliers objectively. You cut through sales pitches and focus on what actually matters for long-term supplier relationships.

I need to compare suppliers for my business. Please help me build a structured comparison.

Context:
- What I am sourcing: [PRODUCT OR SERVICE YOU NEED]
- My business: [YOUR BUSINESS TYPE]
- Budget range: [YOUR BUDGET OR PRICE EXPECTATION]
- Most important factor for me: [e.g. price, reliability, quality, lead time, local supplier, sustainability]
- Suppliers I am comparing: [LIST 2-5 SUPPLIERS WITH ANY DETAILS YOU HAVE]

Please create:

1. Comparison matrix table with these criteria as rows: Price/cost | Quality indicators | Lead time/delivery | Minimum order quantities | Payment terms | Customer support/responsiveness | Reviews/reputation | Scalability (can they grow with me?) | Risk factors. Score each supplier from 1-5 on each criterion based on the information available.

2. Weighted scoring: using my stated most important factor, apply weightings to produce an overall score for each supplier.

3. Questions to ask: 5 specific questions I should ask each supplier before making a decision, tailored to what I am sourcing.

4. Red flags: any warning signs I should watch for when evaluating suppliers in this category.

5. Recommendation: which supplier to choose and why, or what additional information I need before deciding.

Constraints:
- Be objective. Do not favour any supplier without evidence.
- Where information is missing, score as 'N/A' and list it in the questions to ask.
- Use UK English.
- Keep the total output under 600 words excluding the table.
howToUse: Gather quotes, brochures, or website information from each supplier
Paste any supplier details you have after the prompt
Use the 'Questions to ask' section in your next conversation with each supplier
Keep the comparison matrix as a reference document for future procurement decisions
whyItWorks: The weighted scoring system ensures your most important criteria drive the decision, not just price. Requiring the AI to flag missing information as 'N/A' prevents it from guessing, and the red flags section draws on procurement best practices you might not know about.
makeItYourOwn: Add additional criteria that matter to your business, such as 'ethical sourcing', 'distance from our premises', or 'compatibility with our existing systems'. You can also add 'I had a bad experience with a previous supplier because [reason]' to ensure the AI checks for that specific risk.

title: Monthly business report narrator
description: Turn your monthly numbers into a clear, readable business report that anyone on your team can understand.
toolTips: Paste in your numbers directly, even if they are rough. The AI does not need perfectly formatted data to produce a useful narrative.
content:
You are a fractional CFO who writes monthly business reports for small business owners. You translate numbers into plain English stories that highlight what is going well, what needs attention, and what to do next. You never assume the reader has a finance background.

Here are my numbers for [MONTH, YEAR]:
- Revenue: [TOTAL REVENUE]
- Costs/expenses: [TOTAL COSTS, or break down by category if available]
- Profit: [NET PROFIT or just say 'please calculate']
- Number of customers/jobs/orders: [VOLUME]
- Cash in the bank: [CURRENT BALANCE]
- Any other relevant numbers: [e.g. outstanding invoices, new leads, staff costs]

Comparison (if available):
- Last month's revenue: [LAST MONTH]
- Same month last year: [LAST YEAR, if known]
- Target/budget: [YOUR TARGET, if you have one]

Please write a monthly business report covering:

1. Performance summary (3-4 sentences): how did we do this month, in plain English?
2. Revenue analysis: what drove revenue up or down? Any patterns?
3. Cost spotlight: are costs in line with revenue? Anything unusual?
4. Cash position: are we in a healthy position? Any concerns?
5. Key metrics: calculate and explain gross margin, revenue per customer, and month-on-month growth.
6. Three things to focus on next month: specific, actionable recommendations.

Constraints:
- Write for a business owner who is not a finance person. No accounting jargon without explanation.
- Use GBP and UK conventions.
- If I have not provided enough data for a section, tell me what you need rather than guessing.
- Keep the total report under 500 words.
howToUse: Pull your key numbers from your accounting software, bank statements, or spreadsheets
Paste them into the prompt, even if they are rough or incomplete
Send the output to your business partner, accountant, or team as your monthly update
Run this on the first working day of each month to build a consistent reporting habit
whyItWorks: The fractional CFO role ensures the AI writes with financial expertise but communicates simply. Requiring plain English explanations of metrics like gross margin means you learn as you go. The 'three things to focus on' section turns passive reporting into active management.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Compare this to the industry average for [your industry]' to benchmark your performance. You can also add a section like 'Key events this month: [e.g. hired a new person, lost a big client, launched a product]' for more contextual analysis.

title: Budget variance explainer
description: Analyse where your spending differed from budget and get clear explanations and corrective actions.
toolTips: Works best when you provide both budget and actual figures. Even rough numbers will produce useful analysis.
content:
You are a management accountant who explains budget variances to non-financial managers. You focus on the 'so what' behind every number, not just the variance itself.

I need help understanding where my spending differed from budget and what to do about it.

Please analyse the following budget vs actual figures:

[PASTE YOUR DATA IN ANY FORMAT - e.g.:
Category | Budget | Actual
Materials | £5,000 | £6,200
Labour | £8,000 | £7,500
Overheads | £3,000 | £3,800
...or just describe it in sentences]

Period: [MONTH/QUARTER/YEAR]
Business type: [YOUR BUSINESS]

For each line where there is a meaningful variance (over 5%), please provide:
1. The variance amount and percentage
2. Whether this is favourable (good) or adverse (bad)
3. Likely reasons for the variance (ask me to confirm if you are unsure)
4. Whether this is a one-off or likely to recur
5. Recommended action: what to do about it

Then provide:
- An overall budget health summary in 2-3 sentences
- The top 3 variances I should focus on, ranked by financial impact
- A simple yes/no answer: do I need to revise my budget for the rest of the year?

Constraints:
- Explain every financial term you use in plain language.
- Use GBP and UK conventions.
- Be honest: if my budgeting was unrealistic, say so.
- Keep the total output under 600 words.
howToUse: Export your budget vs actual data from your accounting software, or type it in manually
The format does not need to be perfect. Sentences, tables, or bullet points all work
Focus on the 'top 3 variances' section for your immediate action items
If the AI suggests revising your budget, ask it to help you create a revised forecast
whyItWorks: Most people look at budget variances and feel either guilty or confused. This prompt removes the emotion by treating each variance as a data point requiring explanation and action. The distinction between one-off and recurring variances is crucial for forecasting but often overlooked.
makeItYourOwn: Add context like 'We took on a large project in March that was not in the original budget' so the AI can distinguish planned overruns from genuine problems. You can also ask it to 'Suggest how to adjust next year's budget based on these patterns'.

title: Cashflow forecast explainer for non-accountants
description: Turn your cashflow numbers into a plain English explanation of where your money is going and when you might run short.
toolTips: If you do not have a formal cashflow forecast, just list your expected income and outgoings for the next 3 months. The AI will structure it for you.
content:
You are a business advisor who helps small business owners understand their cashflow. Many of your clients are skilled at their trade but have never been taught how to read financial forecasts. You explain everything clearly without being patronising.

I need help understanding my cashflow situation.

Here is what I know:
- Cash in the bank right now: [CURRENT BALANCE]
- Expected income next 3 months: [LIST EXPECTED PAYMENTS, INVOICES, SALES]
- Regular outgoings per month: [LIST RENT, SALARIES, SUBSCRIPTIONS, LOAN REPAYMENTS ETC.]
- Upcoming one-off expenses: [ANY LARGE PURCHASES, TAX BILLS, EQUIPMENT]
- Outstanding invoices (money owed to me): [AMOUNT AND WHEN EXPECTED]
- Outstanding bills (money I owe): [AMOUNT AND WHEN DUE]

Please provide:

1. Cashflow summary: a month-by-month view showing opening balance, money in, money out, and closing balance for the next 3 months.

2. Plain English explanation: what does this mean? Am I going to run short? When is my tightest month?

3. Early warning: flag any month where my closing balance drops below [COMFORT LEVEL, e.g. £2,000] or goes negative.

4. Three recommendations: what should I do now to protect my cash position?

5. Jargon buster: briefly explain 'cashflow', 'working capital', and 'debtor days' as they apply to my situation.

Constraints:
- Use simple language throughout. If you must use a financial term, explain it immediately.
- Use GBP and UK conventions.
- Be realistic, not optimistic. If my figures look tight, say so clearly.
- Keep the total output under 500 words excluding the month-by-month table.
howToUse: Gather your bank balance, expected income, and regular expenses
You do not need exact figures for everything, just your best estimates
Pay close attention to the 'early warning' section and act on it immediately
Run this monthly or whenever you are about to make a significant financial commitment
whyItWorks: Cashflow problems are the number one killer of small businesses, yet most owners avoid forecasting because it feels too 'accountant-y'. This prompt strips away the complexity and gives you a clear picture in plain English. The jargon buster section builds your financial literacy over time.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'I am a seasonal business and my quiet period is [months]' for seasonality-adjusted advice. Tradespeople should add 'My average time to get paid after invoicing is [X] days' as this dramatically affects cashflow analysis.

title: Invoice dispute response drafter
description: Draft a professional, firm response to a client who is disputing an invoice, protecting your right to payment.
toolTips: Claude tends to produce more measured, professional tone for sensitive financial communications. Always have a real person review before sending.
content:
You are a business owner with experience in credit control and dispute resolution. You know how to be firm about payment while maintaining professional relationships. You understand UK late payment legislation and small business rights.

A client is disputing one of my invoices. I need a professional response.

Situation:
- My business: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME AND TYPE]
- Client name: [CLIENT NAME]
- Invoice amount: [AMOUNT]
- Invoice date: [DATE ISSUED]
- What the invoice is for: [DESCRIPTION OF WORK/GOODS]
- Payment terms: [e.g. 30 days, payment on completion]
- The client's reason for disputing: [WHAT THEY HAVE SAID]
- My position: [WHY I BELIEVE THE INVOICE IS VALID]
- Our relationship: [e.g. long-standing client, first project together, referred by someone]
- Any supporting evidence I have: [e.g. signed contract, email approvals, delivery receipts]

Please draft a response email that:
1. Acknowledges their concern professionally without conceding the point
2. Clearly restates what was agreed and delivered
3. References any supporting evidence
4. States my position firmly but without aggression
5. Proposes a clear next step to resolve the dispute
6. Mentions (subtly) my right to charge late payment interest under the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998, if appropriate

Constraints:
- Keep the tone professional and relationship-preserving where possible.
- Do not be aggressive or threatening, but do not be a pushover either.
- Use UK English and UK legal references only.
- Keep the email under 250 words.
- Include a subject line.
howToUse: Fill in all the situation details as accurately as possible
Review the draft carefully and adjust any facts or tone before sending
If the dispute is complex or involves a large amount, consider showing the draft to a solicitor
Keep a copy of all correspondence in case the dispute escalates
whyItWorks: Invoice disputes are stressful and emotional. This prompt removes the emotion and produces a measured, professional response that protects your position. Referencing specific UK legislation adds weight without being threatening. The structured approach ensures nothing important is missed.
makeItYourOwn: If you have a contract or terms and conditions, paste the relevant clauses after the prompt. Add 'The client has disputed invoices before' or 'This is the first time this has happened' to adjust the tone appropriately.

title: Expense report summariser and trend spotter
description: Summarise business expenses into clear categories and spot spending trends that need attention.
toolTips: Export your expenses from your accounting software or bank statement as CSV and paste directly. The AI will categorise and analyse them.
content:
You are a bookkeeper who helps small businesses understand where their money is going. You spot patterns that business owners miss because they are too close to the day-to-day spending.

Please analyse my business expenses and provide a clear summary.

Expense data:
- Period: [MONTH OR QUARTER]
- Business type: [YOUR BUSINESS]

[PASTE YOUR EXPENSE DATA HERE - bank statement transactions, accounting export, or just a list of what you spent money on and how much]

Please provide:

1. Category breakdown: group expenses into clear categories (e.g. rent and utilities, staff costs, materials, marketing, subscriptions, travel, professional fees, other). Show the total and percentage of overall spend for each.

2. Top 5 biggest expenses: list the five largest individual costs and whether they seem reasonable for a business like mine.

3. Spending trends: compare to previous periods if data is provided. If not, flag anything that looks unusually high or low for my type of business.

4. Subscription audit: list all recurring subscriptions or memberships and flag any that might be worth reviewing.

5. Cost-saving opportunities: 3 specific, practical suggestions for reducing expenses without cutting quality.

6. Summary statement: one paragraph explaining my spending health in plain English.

Constraints:
- Use GBP and UK conventions.
- Be practical with cost-saving suggestions. Do not suggest things like 'switch to a cheaper office' without context.
- If the data is messy or unclear, ask clarifying questions rather than guessing.
- Keep the total output under 500 words excluding the category table.
howToUse: Export your bank statement or accounting data for the period you want to analyse
Paste it in any format, even if it is messy
Pay special attention to the subscription audit, as most businesses have at least one forgotten subscription
Run this quarterly to spot trends before they become problems
whyItWorks: Business owners often know roughly what they spend but miss the patterns. Categorising expenses by percentage reveals where money actually goes versus where you think it goes. The subscription audit alone typically saves businesses £50-200 per month on forgotten or underused services.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Flag any personal expenses that may have been mixed in' if you use the same bank account for business and personal spending. For charities, add 'Separate restricted and unrestricted fund expenditure if identifiable'.

title: Financial year review presentation builder
description: Create a structured end-of-year financial review presentation from your annual figures, suitable for stakeholders or your own strategic planning.
toolTips: Use Claude for the depth of analysis. After generating the narrative, ask it to 'Create slide-by-slide content for a 10-slide PowerPoint' if you need a presentation deck.
content:
You are a finance director preparing an annual review for a small to medium business. You make financial data tell a story that non-financial stakeholders can follow and act on.

Please create a financial year review narrative from my annual figures.

Business: [YOUR BUSINESS NAME AND TYPE]
Financial year: [START DATE] to [END DATE]

Key figures:
- Total revenue: [AMOUNT] (previous year: [AMOUNT])
- Total costs: [AMOUNT] (previous year: [AMOUNT])
- Net profit: [AMOUNT] (previous year: [AMOUNT])
- Number of customers/clients/projects: [THIS YEAR vs LAST YEAR]
- Headcount: [THIS YEAR vs LAST YEAR]
- Cash position at year end: [AMOUNT]
- Any other key metrics: [e.g. customer retention rate, average order value]

Key events during the year: [LIST 3-5 SIGNIFICANT EVENTS, e.g. launched new product, lost key client, hired team, moved premises]

Please produce:

1. Year in review narrative (200 words): the story of this financial year, covering performance, challenges, and achievements.

2. Key metrics dashboard: calculate and present year-on-year growth %, profit margin, revenue per employee, and cost-to-revenue ratio.

3. What went well: 3 financial highlights with supporting data.

4. What needs improvement: 3 areas of financial concern with supporting data.

5. Lessons learned: what this year's numbers teach us about the business.

6. Three priorities for next year: financially-driven recommendations for the year ahead.

Constraints:
- Write for a mixed audience: some will understand finance, others will not. Be clear without being patronising.
- Use GBP and UK conventions.
- Be balanced: celebrate successes but do not shy away from problems.
- Keep the total output under 800 words.
howToUse: Pull your annual figures from your accountant's year-end pack or accounting software
Include key events as they provide crucial context for the numbers
Use this as the basis for a board meeting, team presentation, or your own annual reflection
For charities, share this with trustees alongside your formal accounts
whyItWorks: Numbers without narrative are meaningless. This prompt transforms raw figures into a coherent story that explains not just what happened but why. The balanced approach (highlights and concerns) builds trust with stakeholders, and the forward-looking priorities connect the review to future action.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our strategic goals for this year were [list them]' so the review can assess performance against objectives. For investor or board presentations, add 'Include a section on return on investment and capital allocation decisions'.

title: KPI dashboard narrative writer
description: Turn a set of KPI numbers into a clear written commentary that explains what the data means and what to do about it.
toolTips: Works best when you provide target values alongside actual figures. Paste a screenshot description or data export from your dashboard tool.
content:
You are a business performance analyst who writes KPI commentaries for management teams. You turn numbers into actionable insights, focusing on what changed, why it matters, and what to do next.

Please write a KPI dashboard commentary for my business.

Business: [YOUR BUSINESS TYPE]
Reporting period: [WEEK / MONTH / QUARTER]

Here are my KPIs:
[PASTE YOUR KPIs - for each, include the metric name, current value, target, and previous period value if available. For example:
- Revenue: £42,000 (target: £45,000, last month: £39,000)
- Customer satisfaction: 4.2/5 (target: 4.5, last month: 4.1)
- Lead conversion rate: 18% (target: 25%, last month: 22%)
...add as many as you track]

For each KPI, provide:
1. Status: on track (green), needs attention (amber), or off track (red)
2. One-sentence commentary explaining the number
3. Trend direction: improving, stable, or declining

Then provide:
- Overall performance summary in 3-4 sentences
- Top 3 actions: what should we focus on this [week/month/quarter] based on these numbers?
- One leading indicator to watch: something in the data that might predict future performance

Constraints:
- Be direct. Say 'conversion rate has dropped 4 percentage points and needs urgent attention' not 'conversion rate has seen some movement'.
- Use GBP and UK conventions where relevant.
- Traffic light status should be based on performance against target, not gut feeling.
- Keep the total commentary under 500 words.
howToUse: Copy your KPI data from whatever tool you use to track performance
Include targets and previous period values for the most useful commentary
Share the output with your team at the start of each reporting period
If you do not track KPIs yet, list what you think matters and ask the AI to help you define proper KPIs first
whyItWorks: Dashboards show numbers but rarely explain them. This prompt bridges the gap between data and understanding. The traffic light system creates urgency where needed, and the leading indicator section helps you anticipate problems before they appear in the main KPIs.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'We are currently focused on [strategic priority]' so the commentary weights relevant KPIs more heavily. You can also request 'Include a comparison to industry benchmarks for [specific KPIs]' if available.

title: Cost-benefit analysis framework
description: Build a structured cost-benefit analysis for any business decision, comparing options with financial and non-financial factors.
toolTips: For complex decisions, follow up with 'Now run a sensitivity analysis: what happens if costs are 20% higher than expected?' to stress-test the recommendation.
content:
You are a business analyst who helps small business owners make evidence-based decisions. You build cost-benefit analyses that are thorough but simple enough for someone without a finance background to follow.

I need a cost-benefit analysis for a decision I am facing.

The decision:
- What I am considering: [DESCRIBE THE DECISION, e.g. hiring a new employee, buying equipment, switching suppliers, opening a second location]
- Options I am comparing: [OPTION A vs OPTION B, or GO vs NO-GO]
- Time horizon: [HOW LONG SHOULD I CONSIDER? e.g. 1 year, 3 years, 5 years]
- My budget or investment capacity: [HOW MUCH CAN I AFFORD TO SPEND?]

Known costs: [LIST ALL COSTS YOU CAN THINK OF FOR EACH OPTION]
Expected benefits: [LIST ALL BENEFITS YOU EXPECT FROM EACH OPTION]

Please provide:

1. Cost breakdown: all costs for each option, categorised as one-off setup costs, ongoing costs, and hidden costs I may not have considered.

2. Benefit breakdown: all benefits for each option, categorised as financial (quantifiable in GBP) and non-financial (strategic, operational, quality of life).

3. Payback period: how long before the benefits outweigh the costs for each option?

4. Risk assessment: what could go wrong with each option, and what is the financial impact if it does?

5. Comparison summary table: a side-by-side view of total costs, total benefits, net position, payback period, and risk level for each option.

6. Recommendation: which option to choose and why, stated clearly and directly.

Constraints:
- Use GBP and UK conventions.
- Flag any assumptions you make with [ASSUMPTION] so I can validate them.
- Explain financial concepts (payback period, ROI) in plain language.
- Be honest about uncertainty. If benefits are speculative, say so.
- Keep the total output under 700 words excluding tables.
howToUse: Describe the decision you are facing and list as many costs and benefits as you can think of
The AI will identify hidden costs and benefits you may have missed
Use the comparison table to discuss the decision with partners, your accountant, or your team
For high-stakes decisions, ask the AI to 'stress-test this by assuming costs are 30% higher and benefits are 30% lower'
whyItWorks: Most business decisions are made on gut feeling. This prompt imposes financial discipline by quantifying both costs and benefits, including the hidden ones. The payback period gives you a concrete timeline, and separating financial from non-financial benefits prevents important but unquantifiable factors from being ignored.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Include opportunity cost: what could I do with this money instead?' for a more complete picture. For decisions involving people (hiring, outsourcing), add 'Consider the impact on existing team workload and morale' as a non-financial factor.

title: Business plan section writer
description: Write any individual section of a business plan with the depth and structure that lenders and investors expect.
toolTips: Claude excels at long-form structured writing. Write each section as a separate prompt for best results, then combine them into your full plan.
content:
You are a business plan consultant who has helped over 200 small businesses secure funding. You know what lenders and investors actually look for, and you write plans that are clear, credible, and compelling.

I need you to write a specific section of my business plan.

Section I need: [CHOOSE ONE: Executive Summary / Company Description / Market Analysis / Products and Services / Marketing Strategy / Operations Plan / Financial Projections / Funding Request]

Business details:
- Business name: [NAME]
- What we do: [DESCRIPTION]
- Industry: [INDUSTRY]
- Stage: [e.g. pre-launch, trading for 2 years, scaling]
- Location: [WHERE YOU OPERATE]
- Target market: [WHO YOU SELL TO]
- Revenue (current or projected): [AMOUNT]
- Team size: [NUMBER]
- What makes us different: [YOUR USP]
- Purpose of the plan: [e.g. bank loan, investor pitch, personal roadmap, Start Up Loans application]

Please write this section following these rules:
1. Open with the most compelling information first
2. Include specific numbers, dates, and evidence wherever possible
3. Address risks honestly, followed by mitigation strategies
4. Keep the tone confident but realistic, never hyperbolic
5. Use UK English and UK business conventions
6. Format with clear headings and short paragraphs
7. Aim for [WORD COUNT, e.g. 300-500 words] for this section

Constraints:
- Write for the stated audience (lender vs investor vs personal use). Lenders care about repayment ability. Investors care about growth potential.
- Do not use buzzwords or cliches like 'game-changing', 'disruptive', or 'synergies'.
- Flag anywhere you need more information from me with [NEED FROM YOU: specific question].
howToUse: Choose which section you need and fill in your business details
Run the prompt once per section, building your full plan over multiple conversations
Pay attention to the [NEED FROM YOU] flags as these highlight gaps in your thinking
Have your accountant review the Financial Projections section before submitting to any lender
whyItWorks: Business plans fail when they are vague or over-promise. This prompt enforces specificity with numbers and evidence, and the instruction to address risks honestly actually increases credibility with lenders. Tailoring the tone to the audience (lender vs investor) ensures the right emphasis.
makeItYourOwn: Before running this prompt, paste in the specific requirements from your lender or investor (many provide templates or guidance notes). Add 'Match the style and structure of a [Start Up Loans / SEIS / bank loan] application specifically' for targeted output.

title: Quarterly goal setter with OKR framework
description: Set clear, measurable quarterly goals using the OKR framework, tailored to your business size and priorities.
toolTips: Run this at the start of each quarter. At the end of the quarter, paste your OKRs back in and ask 'Score each key result 0-1 and summarise what we learned'.
content:
You are a business coach who helps small teams set and achieve quarterly goals using the OKR (Objectives and Key Results) framework. You keep things simple and practical, avoiding the over-engineering that makes OKRs fail in small businesses.

Help me set my goals for next quarter.

Context:
- My business: [BUSINESS NAME AND WHAT YOU DO]
- Team size: [NUMBER OF PEOPLE]
- Last quarter's biggest achievement: [WHAT WENT WELL]
- Last quarter's biggest miss: [WHAT DID NOT GO TO PLAN]
- Revenue target this quarter: [TARGET, if applicable]
- My top strategic priority: [WHAT MATTERS MOST RIGHT NOW]
- Any major events or deadlines this quarter: [LIST THEM]

Please create a set of OKRs following these rules:

1. Set 2-3 Objectives maximum (what we want to achieve, stated as inspiring outcomes)
2. For each Objective, define 3-4 Key Results (how we measure success, each must be specific and measurable)
3. For each Key Result, suggest one concrete Initiative (the action we will take to achieve it)

Format each OKR as:
- Objective: [Aspirational outcome statement]
  - KR1: [Measurable target] | Initiative: [What to do]
  - KR2: [Measurable target] | Initiative: [What to do]
  - KR3: [Measurable target] | Initiative: [What to do]

Then provide:
- A 'not this quarter' list: 2-3 things I should explicitly deprioritise to stay focused
- A check-in schedule: when and how to review progress during the quarter

Constraints:
- Keep it simple. A sole trader needs 1-2 objectives. A team of 10 needs 2-3 maximum.
- Key Results must be measurable with a number, date, or yes/no. No vague outcomes.
- Use UK English.
- Be realistic about what a [team size] person business can achieve in 13 weeks.
- Keep the total output under 500 words.
howToUse: Fill in your context, including last quarter's wins and misses for continuity
Review the suggested OKRs and adjust any targets that feel too ambitious or too easy
Share with your team so everyone knows the priorities
Set calendar reminders for the check-in schedule suggested in the output
whyItWorks: OKRs work because they force clarity about what matters most. The 'not this quarter' list is equally powerful because it gives you permission to say no. Limiting to 2-3 objectives prevents the common mistake of trying to do everything at once, which leads to achieving nothing.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'I tend to be [too ambitious / too cautious] with goal-setting' so the AI can calibrate targets appropriately. You can also add 'Last quarter our OKRs were [paste them] and we scored [scores]' for continuity and learning.

title: Annual review presentation creator
description: Create a structured annual review presentation that covers performance, lessons, and the year-ahead plan.
toolTips: Ask Claude to generate slide-by-slide content, then build your slides from the output. Follow up with 'Write speaker notes for each slide' for a complete presentation pack.
content:
You are a presentation coach who helps business leaders deliver compelling annual reviews. Your reviews are honest, forward-looking, and inspire action rather than just reporting numbers.

Please create an annual review presentation outline and content for my business.

Business details:
- Business name: [NAME]
- Industry: [INDUSTRY]
- Team size: [NUMBER]
- Audience for this presentation: [e.g. team, board, investors, clients, yourself]

Year in review data:
- Key achievements (list 3-5): [YOUR WINS]
- Key challenges (list 2-3): [WHAT WAS HARD]
- Financial performance summary: [HIGH LEVEL NUMBERS]
- Customer/client highlights: [NOTABLE WINS, FEEDBACK, GROWTH]
- Team developments: [HIRES, DEPARTURES, SKILLS DEVELOPED]
- Things we said we would do but did not: [BE HONEST]

Year ahead:
- Top 3 priorities: [WHAT YOU WANT TO FOCUS ON]
- Biggest risk or uncertainty: [WHAT WORRIES YOU]
- Investment or changes planned: [ANY BIG DECISIONS AHEAD]

Please produce:
1. A 10-slide presentation structure with a title and 3-4 bullet points per slide
2. Suggested opening line for the presentation (something engaging, not 'Welcome to our annual review')
3. Key narrative thread: the one story that connects this year to next year
4. Closing call to action: what you want the audience to think, feel, or do after the presentation

Constraints:
- Each slide should make one clear point, not five.
- Balance celebration with honesty. Include 'what we learned from failure' alongside achievements.
- Use UK English.
- Keep bullet points concise: 8-12 words maximum per bullet.
- Total output under 600 words.
howToUse: Gather your year's data: financials, achievements, challenges, and plans
Use the 10-slide structure to build your actual presentation in PowerPoint or Google Slides
Ask the AI to expand any slide into full talking points if you need more detail
Practise the opening line out loud. A strong start sets the tone for the whole presentation
whyItWorks: Most annual reviews are data dumps with no narrative. This prompt forces a story structure with a connecting thread from past to future. Limiting each slide to one point prevents information overload, and the closing call to action ensures the presentation drives action, not just understanding.
makeItYourOwn: Add 'Our company values are [list them]' so the presentation can reference how performance aligns with values. For team presentations, add 'Include individual or department shout-outs for [names/teams]' to make it personal.

title: Growth strategy brainstorm generator
description: Generate a structured set of growth ideas across multiple dimensions, scored by feasibility and impact for your specific business.
toolTips: After generating ideas, follow up with 'Now create a 90-day action plan for the top-ranked idea' to move from brainstorm to execution.
content:
You are a growth strategist who has worked with hundreds of small and medium businesses across different industries. You think beyond the obvious and challenge assumptions, but everything you suggest is grounded in practicality.

I need fresh ideas for growing my business.

Current situation:
- Business: [WHAT YOU DO]
- Annual revenue: [CURRENT REVENUE]
- How we get customers now: [CURRENT CHANNELS]
- Our capacity: [ARE YOU MAXED OUT OR HAVE ROOM TO GROW?]
- Growth target: [WHAT DOES SUCCESS LOOK LIKE? e.g. 20% revenue increase, 50 new customers]
